sources.title: Dustin Howes's 7-step checklist for launching and scaling an affiliate program
sources.originalTitle: The 30+ Point Ultimate Checklist for Launching and Scaling an Affiliate Marketing Program
sources.summary: Dustin Howes walks through his 30+ point checklist for building an affiliate program: research, tech stack decisions, creation, announcement, recruitment, management and reporting. His core argument is that programs fail because they are set up poorly and then ignored, and that good partners need onboarding, assets and ongoing attention to produce revenue.

principles.text: Most affiliate programs fail from poor setup and neglect, not because the product is bad.
principles.quote: most of the time uh it's that I see programs fail because it's set up poorly and it's just ignored

principles.text: Good affiliates don't just show up; you must build an environment and resources that keep them excited.
principles.quote: good Affiliates don't just show up they don't just join the program and make magic happen it is hard work optimizing your program and creating an environment that is inviting to those Partners

principles.text: Start with competitive research: sign up for rival programs and benchmark commissions before setting your own.
principles.quote: go sign up for their programs see what they're doing right see what they're doing wrong how much they are offering in commissions you'll need to stay competitive with these payouts

principles.text: Set commissions by what you can afford to give partners and still profit as a company.
principles.quote: figure out what you can afford to give partners and still profit as a company

principles.text: Polish onboarding before announcing: signup page, welcome emails and assets shape the first impression.
principles.quote: this is why we have to be all squared away before or you make the big announcement and tell the people your program is ready signup page needs to be tidy

principles.text: Treat the affiliate manager as a leader who helps partners succeed, and give top performers VIP attention.
principles.quote: the affiliate manager has to be that leader that helps the troops succeed

sources.title: How to Recruit Affiliates at Scale: live Alfie demo hosted by Dustin Howes
sources.originalTitle: How to Recruit Affiliates at Scale
sources.summary: Dustin Howes hosts a live School of Chaos webinar where the XP Flow team demos Alfie, an AI tool that finds, scores and emails affiliates from just a brand URL. Dustin's own contributions are framing: affiliate recruitment has been spreadsheet work, and AI should enhance partnership managers rather than replace them. Most substantive material comes from guests Matt and Beth.

principles.text: Manual affiliate recruitment (spreadsheets, guessing domains, cold emails to generic inboxes) is the old default that automation should replace.
principles.quote: I've spent 17 years in the affiliate space working out of spreadsheets, guessing at domains and firing emails into info at boxes that nobody reads.

principles.text: Show real, unscripted product demos on a blank account, because polished demos where nothing breaks aren't credible.
principles.quote: Most product webinars are going to show you this beautiful demo that really doesn't exist and nothing ever breaks.

principles.text: AI in affiliate management should enhance the partnership manager, not replace the human relationship work.
principles.quote: This is an enhancer, not a replacement. And that's what this industry is leaning towards.

sources.title: Dustin Howes: the 15-step affiliate partnership process, from recruitment to repeat campaigns
sources.originalTitle: 15 Steps to Affiliate Manager Success
sources.summary: Dustin Howes walks through the 15 steps an affiliate takes from discovering a program to ranking content, earning sales and renegotiating terms. His core point is that this process takes time and only works if the manager actively holds the hand of high-potential affiliates and knows how long to spend on each step.

principles.text: Recruiting is a dance: affiliates either find your program or you find them, so you must actively recruit.
principles.quote: this is a dance you've got to get out there and recruit to help them find your program

principles.text: Entice affiliates to review and join with better commissions, landing pages and free products; it is not instant.
principles.quote: you might be enticing them with bigger commissions with landing pages with free products whatever it may be they have to review your product and your affiliate program and make sure it's a good fit for them

principles.text: Good affiliates do heavy keyword and content research, then replicate winning content and make it better.
principles.quote: they found a winner that they're gonna go after see what the kind some content is actually working and they're gonna have to replicate it and make it better

principles.text: Monetization takes time: affiliates usually promote multiple brands, so placement of your links in each piece matters.
principles.quote: they're probably promoting more than one brand at a time so monetization of each content piece is super important

principles.text: Watch reporting for up-and-coming affiliates who start bringing in sales, and connect with them to replicate success.
principles.quote: if you're doing all the right things with your reporting affiliate managers should be looking at their up-and-comers and connecting with the guys that are starting to bring in sales

principles.text: Negotiate as a give and take: they ask for the moon, you give a little, and you meet in the middle.
principles.quote: they're going to ask for the moon you're going to want to give them just a little bit and you guys got to meet in the middle somehow to make magic happen

sources.title: Affiliate recruitment masterclass: automate discovery and outreach, spend time on relationships
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Recruitment Masterclass
sources.summary: Dustin Howes walks through an eight-step affiliate partnership funnel and argues the top of it (discovery, outreach) absorbs 80% of a manager's time and should be automated. He covers personas, a three-list prospecting system, a five-email sequence, bargaining chips, call prep, hybrid negotiation and nurturing, while pitching his product Alfie.

principles.text: Automate the top of the affiliate funnel so you can spend time on relationships.
principles.quote: this top part is the part that you want to automate so that you can spend more time on the relationship portion of what affiliate marketing is.

principles.text: Build three prospect lists: a 25-partner wish list, keyword lists, and competitor-traffic lists, not one unprioritized list.
principles.quote: I like to do it in three fashions. First is a wish list. This is 25 dream affiliate partners that I'm never going to stop until they give me a hard note.

principles.text: Run a five-email sequence over two weeks; a 20% response rate means you're winning.
principles.quote: those five emails over two weeks, you're trying to get a 20% response rate. If you get that, you're absolutely winning.

principles.text: Open with a bargaining chip (sponsorship, backlink, free product, co-branded page), not a generic program invite.
principles.quote: The ones that are saying, "Hey, this is our affiliate program. Come join." Those get deleted.

principles.text: Use LinkedIn alongside email; creators respond there far more than on Instagram.
principles.quote: I get responses on LinkedIn so much more often than I do on Instagram.

principles.text: Negotiate hybrid deals (flat fee plus commission) and ask for proof of audience and conversion.
principles.quote: Hybrid is almost always the right fit. So, we want to give them a flat fee and and pay for their time.

sources.title: How to recruit and activate high-quality affiliates: personas, budget, outreach, onboarding
sources.originalTitle: How to Recruit and Activate High-Quality Affiliates (Proven Playbook with Dustin Howes)
sources.summary: Dustin Howes lays out an affiliate recruitment playbook: fix conversion first, build partner personas, prioritize quality over count, fund an exploratory budget, personalize outreach, and onboard affiliates with a welcome sequence and resource hub. He also covers screening red flags and CPA vs revenue share.

principles.text: Affiliate recruitment is real, ongoing work, not a set-and-forget channel.
principles.quote: তারা ভাবে লোকজন এমনিতেই এসে আমাদের প্রচার করবে, কিন্তু এর পেছনে কতটা পরিশ্রম করতে হয় তা তারা বোঝে না।

principles.text: Make sure your site converts before sending affiliates traffic, or you burn the relationship.
principles.quote: আপনার একটি উচ্চ কনভার্টিং ওয়েবসাইট এবং ল্যান্ডিং পেজ থাকা উচিত, যেখানে আপনি অ্যাফিলিয়েটদের ট্রাফিক পাঠাতে সাহায্য করতে পারেন এবং তারা কনভার্ট হবে।

principles.text: Build partner personas like you build an ICP; each type has different motivations and needs a different approach.
principles.quote: প্রতিটি ধরণ আলাদা এবং প্রতিটি পার্টনার পারসোনাকে কাছে পাওয়ার উপায়ও হবে ভিন্ন।

principles.text: Affiliate count is a vanity metric; a few top partners drive most revenue, so know and tier them.
principles.quote: আপনার প্রোগ্রামে কতজন অ্যাফিলিয়েট আছে তা গুরুত্বপূর্ণ নয়। এটা কেবল লোক দেখানো পরিসংখ্যান।

principles.text: An exploratory budget to pay creators upfront multiplies response rates.
principles.quote: যদি উত্তর হ্যাঁ হয় এবং আপনার এক্সপ্লোরেটরি বাজেট থাকে, তবে আমি গ্যারান্টি দিচ্ছি যে আপনার রেসপন্স রেট নাটকীয়ভাবে, এমনকি বহুগুণ বেড়ে যাবে।

principles.text: Most programs miss the welcome sequence; send a five-email sequence in the first five days.
principles.quote: আমি প্রথম ৫ দিনে পাঁচটি ইমেইলের একটি সিকোয়েন্স রাখতে পছন্দ করি

sources.title: Affiliate Nerd Out: Why AI is already separating winning affiliate programs from stalled ones
sources.originalTitle: AI Shifts That Will Separate Winning Affiliate Programs from the Rest
sources.summary: Dustin hosts a panel (Adam Riemer, Lacy Thompson, Matt Fray) on AI in affiliate marketing. His own contributions are framing: AI is already here, hesitation is the main risk, and paying affiliates for appearing in LLM answers is an emerging model. Most of the substantive insight comes from the guests, not Dustin.

principles.text: AI is already here and is quietly sorting affiliate programs into winners and stallers over the next three years.
principles.quote: AI is not coming for affiliate. It is already here and it is quietly separating the programs that'll dominate the next three years from the ones that are going to stall out.

principles.text: Freezing out of fear or hesitation is the main failure mode for affiliate managers facing AI.
principles.quote: Most affiliate managers hear AI and they picture either this magic button that's going to threaten their job. So, they freeze.

principles.text: Paying affiliates for appearing in LLM search results is a new payment model likely to grow.
principles.quote: That is a very new payment method in the affiliate space that I think is going to blow up.

sources.title: B2B affiliate program playbook: audit first, recruit outbound, coach partners (Dustin Howes panel)
sources.originalTitle: The $10M Partner Playbook: How to Build a B2B Affiliate Program from Scratch
sources.summary: Dustin hosts a panel with affiliate operators from HubSpot/Instantly, an affiliate agency and a tracking platform. His own contributions: audit before recruiting, respond fast to partner interest, build co-branded landing pages, coach partners, treat affiliate types differently, and pitch internally for test budget.

principles.text: Audit the existing program before chasing new partner recruitment.
principles.quote: auditing the program is an absolute must.

principles.text: Raise partner conversion with co-branded landing pages built for them.
principles.quote: optimizing conversion rate for your affiliates is absolutely optimal, like, for your program. Build them a co-branded landing page that's going to convert better and you're going to be in a much better spot.

principles.text: Jump on any call a partner requests immediately; don't screen them first.
principles.quote: If you get a response from an affiliate and they want a call, jump on that call immediately. Like, no questions asked.

principles.text: Segment affiliates by funnel position and pay each type appropriately instead of treating all the same.
principles.quote: every affiliate is a little bit different and treating them all the same way is the wrong answer.

principles.text: Coaching partners is an undervalued part of affiliate management that benefits both sides.
principles.quote: Coaching is a big part of affiliate management that people don't recognize how important it is to and spending that time with the affiliates is extraordinarily valuable to them and to your program

principles.text: Make recruitment emails show the opportunity, create urgency, and end with an ask to get on a call.
principles.quote: you're presenting what the possibility is here. Two, you're giving me a time frame to get into this exclusive opportunity. And three, you're giving me a question and trying to get me on a call to open this door

sources.title: Affiliate manager mindset: ask for help, stay organized, be valuable (Erica deForge-Sarza on Affiliate Nerd Out)
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Manager Education 101:The Subtle Art of Not Giving a f* - affiliate manager edition
sources.summary: Dustin Howes hosts Erica, who was thrown an affiliate program in 2020 and ended up running a huge budget by age 25. Dustin mainly frames the episode and endorses her points: don't fear looking stupid, ask for help and forgiveness, lean on community, and don't pretend you know everything. Most tactical advice is Erica's.

principles.text: Affiliate managers with a few years of experience often think they know everything; the more years you add, the more you see how little you knew.
principles.quote: affiliate managers that get two to three years experience in this space uh feel like they know everything and they're not willing to to learn

principles.text: Don't fear looking stupid; ask follow-up questions openly.
principles.quote: I don't mind feeling stupid whatever

principles.text: Once settled in a role, ask forgiveness rather than permission and take chances, but not in your first three months.
principles.quote: let's ask for forgiveness rather than permission

principles.text: Community is essential for affiliate managers working alone; it keeps you from falling behind day to day.
principles.quote: as long as you're getting your community aspect um from some Outlet whether that be friends that that you actually can hug or if that's virtual

principles.text: Confidence, and acting like you know what you're doing, matters in the affiliate manager role.
principles.quote: being confident in this role is an important part of it and just acting like you know what you're doing

principles.text: Reaching out and introducing yourself pays off; Dustin wants to mentor people who approach him.
principles.quote: those are the ones I want to Mentor

sources.title: Affiliate manager hurdles: activating publishers, filtering applications, and motivating partners
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Manager Job Biggest Hurdles
sources.summary: Dustin Howes (solo, guest no-show) walks through common affiliate manager hurdles gathered from LinkedIn responses: publisher education/activation, application overload and fraud, "lazy" affiliates, and finding long-term partnerships. His core fix is making education easy and paying for partners' time.

principles.text: Make partner education effortless: free samples/trials plus short, tailored videos shortcut the path from cold email to activation.
principles.quote: making it as easy as possible for them to get the education uh is essential so share with them some videos

principles.text: Show prospective partners exactly how you'd fit into their content with a personalized screen-share video.
principles.quote: share a video that is a little video catered to them and how you think you guys can work as a partnership

principles.text: Buy a partner's hour of consulting; it builds loyalty, yields feedback, and can lead to promotion.
principles.quote: it could be a really good investment for your company to buy somebody's hour for 200 300 dollars

principles.text: Treat a flood of applications as a good problem; auto-decline low-value countries, with a decline note inviting appeals.
principles.quote: one of my favorite Solutions here is to Auto decline certain countries

principles.text: Unresponsive affiliates aren't lazy; they're unmotivated, so fix motivation by paying for their time.
principles.quote: lazy is not in the equation if you are a good affiliate with high traffic and high value

principles.text: Durable partnerships come from many content affiliates and SEO; find who ranks for your keywords and reach out.
principles.quote: the long-term value is really in Google and ranking on SEO so uh work harder and use semrush to find out who's ranking for the keywords

sources.title: Scaling as a Consultant in Affiliate: Dustin Howes hosts Adam Weiss
sources.originalTitle: Scaling as a Consultant in Affiliate
sources.summary: Dustin Howes hosts Adam Weiss, a publisher-side affiliate consultant, on Affiliate Nerdout. Weiss carries the consulting playbook; Howes contributes short remarks on network profile keywords, community value, and networks as a career entry point.

principles.text: Advertisers on affiliate networks should load their profile with the keywords they want to be found for, because publishers search by keyword.
principles.quote: if you're on an affiliate network uh you better be stuffing keywords on your like profile page like with all the keywords you can possibly get in there utilize them because when Publishers are going to search a keyword you better show up

principles.text: Affiliate managers often forget to set the right keywords on their network profile for what they want to rank for.
principles.quote: too often do I see affiliate managers just forget this aspect on a network to like put in the right keywords for whatever you're trying to rank for organically

principles.text: Industry community and the right contacts at publications are valuable because the space has many moving parts and people change roles constantly.
principles.quote: having the right connections at all those companies all those Publications is really important and one of the greatest things about martech uh record and the Forum that we have there on that slack channel is the community

principles.text: Nothing prepares you for affiliate marketing except doing it; a network job is a strong way in without prior industry experience.
principles.quote: it's because I didn't have any industry expertise nothing could prepare you for what affiliate marketing is except for uh you know doing your best to prepare for those kinds of interviews

sources.title: AI tools for affiliate managers: recruitment, outreach, fraud checks and onboarding (with Vic Giurgiu)
sources.originalTitle: Best AI tools for affiliate managers with Vic Giurgiu
sources.summary: Dustin hosts Vic Giurgiu, who walks through AI tools for affiliate recruitment, cold email, fake follower detection and onboarding. Dustin's own contributions are short practical takes: use lookalike search to replicate winners, train the algorithm with thumbs up, keep the human relationship in partnerships, and stay focused on one product.

principles.text: Clone your best affiliates: find a good one, then use lookalike search to find more like them.
principles.quote: if I find a good affiliate and I want to replicate it that's the the thing I use

principles.text: Train recommendation algorithms by rating results so future partner searches get better.
principles.quote: I give thumbs up to ones I'm looking for and I want to train that algorithm to find more results like that in the future but that's just me but that's a good practice

principles.text: Automation should not replace the human side of partnership marketing.
principles.quote: the last thing we want to do in Partnership marketing is take away the aspect of face Toof face and the partnership relationship

principles.text: Cut the click-heavy manual work of finding creator contact info; automating it saves real time.
principles.quote: one of the most annoying things about finding YouTubers is how many clicks you have to do to get to their email address with a recapture this is skipping all of that

principles.text: Stay hyperfocused on one product rather than chasing every new idea.
principles.quote: I want you hyperfocused on ay stash and like making that product so much better

principles.text: Avoid burnout; protect life experiences because you have a whole career to work.
principles.quote: I don't want you living behind a computer and burin out because you have your entire life to go and work

sources.title: Affiliate Nerd Out: network settings and affiliate manager skills for international ecom programs
sources.originalTitle: International affiliate program setup for Success
sources.summary: Dustin hosts affiliate agency owner Ish and shares his own bar for choosing affiliate networks (flexible commissions, locking periods, two-tier), how product feeds now serve content affiliates, and how to staff affiliate management by pairing relationship and data skills.

principles.text: Don't use a network that locks you into a flat commission; payout flexibility per partner type is non-negotiable.
principles.quote: anything that has a flat feed that you can't change is not a network for me like I need that flexibility with all the partners

principles.text: Tailor locking periods to partner type; trusted native-ad buyers should be paid faster than the standard window.
principles.quote: the guys I work with that are buying native ads they want to be paid a lot quicker and I can trust them if I have old relationship with them I want that locking period be 10 days rather than 30 days for the regular sales

principles.text: Use two-tier commissions to motivate affiliates to recruit other affiliates into the program.
principles.quote: I like having an ability to recruit Affiliates into a program and be able to be paid in perpetuity with those I like giving the option the Affiliates I'm working with to invite other Affiliates

principles.text: Running multiple networks is an acceptable fix when one network can't serve both coupon and content partners; accept some overlap.
principles.quote: I hate suggesting doing multiple networks but sometimes that's the solution right if maybe you work with all coupon sites over here on a web share and then you work with all content sites on a CPA over here

principles.text: Product feeds matter beyond shopping platforms; content affiliates use feeds to build calls to action easily.
principles.quote: it's not just for Content shopping platforms anymore to pull in all the products I think it's more these days for the content Affiliates to make it easier on them

principles.text: Pair a relationship-strong affiliate manager with a data-strong teammate to cover each other's gaps.
principles.quote: if you hire a relationship Guru make sure you hire a data head to put to fill those gaps of that person to make a one really good affiliate manager

sources.title: B2B affiliate marketing: why coupon tactics fail and agency strength lives in relationships
sources.originalTitle: B2B Affiliate Marketing Best Practices
sources.summary: Dustin Howes hosts Adam Glazer of Partner Commerce on how B2B affiliate programs get built, from discovery to a go-to-market plan to partner personas. Most of the substance comes from the guest; Dustin's own contribution is framing on why B2B differs from B2C and where agencies get their edge.

principles.text: An affiliate agency's real power is its network of relationships, which lets it hit the ground running for new clients.
principles.quote: Everybody, every agency out there, their power is in their rolodex. It's the guys that they know that they can come back to when they bring on new clients to help hit the ground running.

principles.text: B2C affiliate programs lean on coupons and loyalty because those wins are easy and conversion rates are high.
principles.quote: There's a tendency in B TOC to get caught up in the coupons, loyalty and that game because it's easy. It's really easy to get those wins.

principles.text: Coupon-site tactics don't transfer to B2B because business buyers don't shop for business tools on coupon sites.
principles.quote: There's not people searching on coupon sites for what business that they want to go to.

principles.text: B2B is an underserved area of affiliate marketing, so specialist agencies that focus on it stand out.
principles.quote: B2B is one of those underserviced industries in the affiliate space and you guys specialize it in.

sources.title: How Dustin Howes builds a "perfect partner 500" affiliate recruitment list
sources.originalTitle: How to Find Hidden Affiliate Partners That Actually Convert
sources.summary: Dustin walks through his six-step process for building a list of 500 targeted affiliate partners for a brand. He shows how to mine competitor backlinks, ranking content and influencer databases, enrich contacts, and score and prioritize partners by persona.

principles.text: Run a repeatable six-step process: learn the brand, audit the program, build personas, gap analysis, list of 500, email templates.
principles.quote: First off, my first step is always learning about the brand. Second step is auditing their existing program. Next, we build out partner personas

principles.text: Mine competitor backlinks, especially the sponsored ones, since those show who they partner with on a performance basis.
principles.quote: I like going into that area of sponsored because now we know that they are partnered with them on some kind of performance basis.

principles.text: Find content already ranking for your category keywords and pull its authors as outreach targets, skipping giant retailers.
principles.quote: we can see who's out here ranking. And this is results at 80 million. We don't need to export all of that, but we can export the first 100 and put it into a CSV.

principles.text: Filter influencers tightly: mid-size follower count, 2% engagement baseline, in-country, with email, and the keyword in their content.
principles.quote: I want to find specifically Instagrammers with 20,000 to 200,000 followers I find and make sure you add you know the percentage of engagement 2% is a good baseline

principles.text: Score every prospect 1 to 5 on partner type, category fit, follower range and geography, and only list fours and fives.
principles.quote: I give each one of these a score of one to five... And I'm only putting fours and fives on the sheet.

principles.text: Categorize targets into personas and subcategories, then confirm with the client and prioritize time per segment.
principles.quote: I can categorize each one of these and prioritize. So, I can get Minecraft influencers and build a list of 50 of them and only do, you know, 20 of the toys.

sources.title: Affiliate Nerd Out AMA: help-first mentoring and AI as an edge for affiliate managers
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Nerd Out: Ask Me Anything
sources.summary: A casual live show where Dustin Howes hosts affiliate industry friends in short guest slots. Most of the substance comes from guests; Dustin's own contributions are a help-first view of relationships, the idea that AI users (not AI itself) will take jobs, and his pitch for affiliate manager training.

principles.text: AI won't replace affiliate managers; the people who use AI well will.
principles.quote: AI is not going to come and take our jobs as AMs uh but uh the people that are using AI will

principles.text: Admire and copy a help-others-first approach; being generous with time builds career-long relationships.
principles.quote: I'm taking that fundamentally sound like help others first kind of mentality and that's always been great

principles.text: Share knowledge publicly, and interview peers, to spread the word about what you do and build authority.
principles.quote: I'm interviewing people like you to to spread the word about what we're doing out here

principles.text: Back training with a guarantee and live coaching to lower the buyer's risk.
principles.quote: growth guaranteed or I'm going to give you your money back

sources.title: Dustin Howes hosts Robert Glazer: Why partnerships are the future of marketing
sources.originalTitle: Why Partnerships Are The Future of Marketing
sources.summary: Dustin Howes interviews Robert Glazer (Acceleration Partners) on the evolution of partnership marketing, AI and the agency model, and career paths. Most insight is Glazer's; Dustin's own contributions are brief reflections on relationships, podcast side benefits, and course-selling difficulty.

principles.text: The relationship side of partnerships matters more than the tech side.
principles.quote: I lean on the partnership side of things and love the relationship factor of this industry more than I do the tech side of it

principles.text: A podcast started to drum up business can become a learning engine and a network builder.
principles.quote: it turned into a two-fold uh really educational like it's fulfilling my educational portion of of me upskilling and then secondarily my connections throughout this industry have grown immensely throughout this time

principles.text: Selling a course for a problem people don't think they have is very hard.
principles.quote: beating my head against the wall trying to get people to buy a product that they don't think they need

principles.text: The wanted automation: tools that match a brand to fitting affiliates and handle outreach for you.
principles.quote: I'm just waiting for that AI to show up that says hey here's your brand here are all of the Affiliates in this database that will fit into your exact Niche

sources.title: Affiliate Nerd Out: Why creator outreach needs budget and creative freedom, with Gigi Robinson
sources.originalTitle: Storytelling that will turn cold outreach into paid partnerships  with Gigi Robinson
sources.summary: Dustin hosts creator Gigi Robinson, who explains how she pitches brands, negotiates paid sponsorships and why she avoids affiliate-only deals. Dustin's own contributions are brief: creators deserve pay, influencers sit at the top of the funnel, and recorded kickoff calls document scope.

principles.text: Creators deserve to be paid for their time and effort, and pure affiliate deals can be unfair to them.
principles.quote: every influencer and Creator out there deserves to get paid for their time and efforts and AFF marketing can be unfair in that kind of concept

principles.text: Influencers work the top of the funnel; affiliate closers convert the demand they create.
principles.quote: influencers traditionally are at that top of the funnel right or brand recognition and then there are other closers in the affiliate game that we rely on in the affiliate Channel

principles.text: Use influencers to bring customers in the door, then retarget them to close the sale.
principles.quote: influencers they have their place of getting that brand or that potential customer in the door to start off and then being retargeted in different kinds of Fashions to close that deal

principles.text: Record kickoff calls and keep notes so agreed scope is documented and revisions can be handled with proof.
principles.quote: another great thing about the zoom call is you can record that and you can have a note taker and document hey this is what we decided on

principles.text: To get a creator's response, bring a real budget and give them creative freedom.
principles.quote: I've got budget and you have creative freedom and that's the way to get a response from you

sources.title: Affiliate software pricing: why "unlimited" rarely means unlimited
sources.originalTitle: The Truth About “Unlimited” Affiliate Software
sources.summary: Dustin Howes interviews the CEO of TrackDesk about hidden ceilings in affiliate platform pricing. His framing: "unlimited" on a pricing page is a hook, and click caps, contact-sales walls and overages are where growing programs get burned. Most substance comes from the guest; Dustin's contribution is the buyer's checklist.

principles.text: Treat "unlimited" on an affiliate software pricing page as a claim to verify, not a fact.
principles.quote: I've been burned by this before in some of my affiliate programs where unlimited on the pricing page doesn't really mean unlimited.

principles.text: Ask vendors on the record where their unlimited promise has a ceiling, such as click caps or contact-sales walls.
principles.quote: Every vendor in this category says unlimited somewhere in their pricing page. Fewer of them will tell you on the record where that promise actually has a ceiling.

principles.text: Pricing surprises hit hardest once the program starts working, so evaluate what happens to the bill at scale before signing.
principles.quote: That gap is exactly where a lot of growing programs get burned.

principles.text: Click-based overage pricing is risky because forced or fraudulent clicks inflate usage, and not every vendor will reverse them.
principles.quote: There could be force clicks. There could be some kind of nefarious actions going on and not every network is will listen when you try to bring that up and try to get those reversed.

sources.title: Beyond the Click: measuring incremental lift across influencers and affiliates (host framing)
sources.originalTitle: Beyond the Click: Measuring Incremental Lift with Influencers & Affiliates
sources.summary: Dustin hosts a panel on the "constellation strategy": pairing influencer reach with affiliate retargeting and measuring publisher-level incrementality. His own contribution is mostly framing and questions; the substantive tactics come from the panelists (Kim Murray, Annie Laro, Tom Wthbone).

principles.text: Influencer buzz alone isn't enough; brands need measurable action and a scalable growth approach.
principles.quote: in a world where influencer buzz alone isn't enough and affiliate conversions are increasingly scrutinized out there, brands need more connection, measurable action, scalable approach to growth.

principles.text: Pair influencer content distribution with affiliate retargeting to generate demand and close the loop with data.
principles.quote: This session is all about aligning influencer content distribution strategies with affiliate retargeting to not only generate demand, but to close the loop with databased performance.

principles.text: Pulling back a performance campaign for being 'too successful' makes little sense when you only pay on results.
principles.quote: some campaigns are too successful. brands say like we're paying too much for affiliate but it's on performance. That seems like ludicrous talk to me.

sources.title: Affiliate compliance: why monitoring is ignored until it breaks (Dustin Howes with Complyy)
sources.originalTitle: How Smart Brands Avoid FTC Nightmares with Affiliate Compliance Management
sources.summary: Dustin Howes hosts Joe Campanella of Complyy on AI-driven FTC compliance monitoring for affiliate programs. Dustin's own points are short: compliance gets ignored until something breaks, monitoring gets exponentially harder as programs scale, and affiliate managers should automate it rather than do it by hand.

principles.text: Affiliate compliance is neglected until something breaks, so build it in before a problem forces you to.
principles.quote: affiliate compliance is usually ignored until something actually breaks.

principles.text: Compliance monitoring gets exponentially harder as the program grows, so start early rather than waiting for scale.
principles.quote: exponentially harder to monitor as your program gets bigger and bigger. So affiliate managers, it's never a bad time to start thinking about monitoring this to save your program.

principles.text: Don't manually police affiliates; automate the monitoring with tools.
principles.quote: Nobody's got time to be going out there and manually doing this.

principles.text: Affiliate managers should look for tools that make them better at their job.
principles.quote: affiliate nerdout is all about finding the tools that are going to help affiliate managers and program managers be better at their job.

sources.title: Affiliate commission structures: staying competitive, fraud risk and partner communication (with Bob Sparkins)
sources.originalTitle: Setting the Right Performance Based Commission Structures with Bob Sparkins
sources.summary: Dustin interviews Bob Sparkins of Leadpages on moving from a flat 30% lifetime commission to a performance-based tier. Dustin's own takeaways cover keeping offers competitive, explaining complex structures simply, why rev share reduces fraud versus CPA, and how to put yourself in affiliates' shoes.

principles.text: Don't let your commission structure go stale; competitors' payouts keep moving, so you have to stay competitive.
principles.quote: things have changed on the internet your competitors have changed their payouts are changing all the time and like you need to stay competitive

principles.text: If your commission structure is complicated, explain it in a short video in the first email to new affiliates.
principles.quote: that doesn't mean you can't like make a two minute video for your first email and like explain that commission structure to all of your Affiliates like that would be the first thing I do

principles.text: Rev share lowers fraud risk; a big upfront CPA invites self-submitted signups until you catch them.
principles.quote: if they get a 200 payout and they have to pay thirty dollars for a subscription they're going to do that all day long until you catch them

principles.text: Tell affiliates about program changes in advance and ask for feedback so they feel heard.
principles.quote: hey this change is coming uh we would like your feedback on it uh they want to felt feel heard first of all

principles.text: Counter CPA requests by showing affiliates lifetime value and what the tiered commission earns over time.
principles.quote: your lifetime value is x amount of months your average commission with this 40 tier is this much you're going to make four times as much money with this commission structure in place

principles.text: Affiliate managers should try being an affiliate themselves to build empathy with partners.
principles.quote: you could just go out and try to be an affiliate and see how hard it is for yourself uh so that you can put yourself in their shoes

sources.title: B2B Partner Recruitment: Dustin Howes's takes on picking a network and negotiating budget
sources.originalTitle: B2B Partner Recruitment: The Good, the Bad, and the In-Between
sources.summary: Dustin hosts Get Response's affiliate head on B2B partner recruitment and migration off an in-house program. His own contributions are brief: judge affiliate networks by reachable partners, not vanity counts, raise experimental budget early, and let product features power partner landing pages.

principles.text: Judge an affiliate network by partners you can realistically reach, not an inflated headline affiliate count.
principles.quote: sales reps will try to drop a vanity metric of how many affiliates are in the platform, right? And I like that it's a a neat number that's like not out of reach.

principles.text: No single affiliate platform is best; each has nuances, so pick by your program's particular needs.
principles.quote: I'm a big fan of partner stack. I'm a big fan of impact and everflow. Like they all have their nuances that I need for a particular

principles.text: Raise the need for upfront or experimental partner budget during the interview; it signals creativity and sets up the program.
principles.quote: I think that's a solid plan like early on in the interview process and it shows that you're creative as well.

principles.text: Your product's own strengths, like easy landing page building, are what your biggest advocates can use to promote you.
principles.quote: I would figure, you know, the biggest uh advocates of your platform are going to be the ones that can build these kinds of things pretty easily.

sources.title: Dustin Howes on affiliate marketing: relationships first, email, content focus, courses and AI
sources.originalTitle: Dustin Howes on Building Strong Affiliate Marketing Relationships
sources.summary: Dustin Howes, an affiliate manager and course creator, shares what he teaches about running affiliate programs and being a successful affiliate. Core ideas: relationship-first partner management, focus on one strength before expanding, email as the cheapest conversion channel, and embracing AI while editing it with your own voice.

principles.text: Treat affiliates as people, not numbers; relationships drive program results.
principles.quote: Affiliates are not just a number on a page and in your program and with dollar bill signs they are actual people that you need to be participating with and helping out as much as you can

principles.text: Prioritize your top affiliates but don't ignore the low tier; spot potential to grow them.
principles.quote: you have your favorites in your program and you need to be paying attention to them more than the the folks down at the bottom of the list that are are just barely making any sales but you can't ignore them either

principles.text: Email is the cheapest route to conversions, and affiliate is often second; start collecting emails early.
principles.quote: email is your cheapest way to conversions uh and that has been consistent for any company that I've ever worked for

principles.text: Master one brand and medium before moving to the next, then reuse the lessons.
principles.quote: get really good at something first before you move on to something else that's the important factor here is focus on something and one brand get it really tightened up

principles.text: Amplify content that works with small paid budgets, e.g. a YouTube video or transactional keyword ads.
principles.quote: if you make a good YouTube video spend 50 $100 to amplify that video and get more views to it

principles.text: Adopt AI in your workflow but edit heavily to keep a human voice.
principles.quote: the people that adapt to what AI is doing right now and add it into their workflow are the people that are going to be successful

sources.title: 15 Steps To Success For An Affiliate Manager: Nurturing High-Potential Partnerships
sources.originalTitle: 15 Steps To Success For An Affiliate Manager
sources.summary: Dustin Howes walks through the 15-step journey an affiliate manager takes from finding a partner to replicating wins with them. His core claim is that time management is the biggest success metric: spend time nurturing high-potential partnerships and be patient while content ranks.

principles.text: Time management is the biggest success factor for an affiliate manager, not years of experience or revenue growth.
principles.quote: The biggest success metric is… Time Management.

principles.text: Spend your time nurturing high-potential partnerships; the hard part is execution.
principles.quote: The answer is easy: Spend time nurturing high potential partnerships. The execution is the hard part.

principles.text: Affiliate programs take time to build; they are not like paid ads that give instant results.
principles.quote: Affiliate programs are not grown overnight. You can’t just turn them on like Facebook ads and see instant results.

principles.text: Give affiliates everything they need to sell: free product, reviews, converting landing pages and earnings proof.
principles.quote: Set them up with free products and share other reviews with them that highlight great selling points. Show them which landing pages are converting best and share how much some of your affiliates are making.

principles.text: Be patient while affiliate content ranks; managers and executives must believe in the process.
principles.quote: Affiliate managers (and executives) need to be patient here and believe in the process.

principles.text: Once a partner is winning, replicate content with that same partner rather than starting from scratch.
principles.quote: Convincing someone with money in their pocket of doing more is a much easier conversation than starting from scratch.

sources.title: What an affiliate manager does: recruiting, activation, relationships, compliance, optimization, and hiring options
sources.originalTitle: What Does An Affiliate Manager Do?
sources.summary: Dustin Howes breaks the affiliate manager role into six core jobs (recruit, activate, build relationships, enforce compliance, optimize, direct creative) and compares three ways to staff it: in-house, agency, or a trained junior marketer. He stresses that affiliate programs don't grow on their own and that relationships are the core asset.

principles.text: Fill the affiliate pipeline every week; program success depends on growing the affiliate network.
principles.quote: It is vital for every affiliate manager to fill their pipeline by recruiting new partners every week.

principles.text: Recruiting affiliates is not enough; activate them with information, incentives and tools, starting with a welcome email sequence.
principles.quote: It’s one thing to have hundreds of affiliates on your roster. But it’s another thing to keep all affiliate accounts active.

principles.text: Invest in partner success and relationships; helping partners win makes them vested in your program and builds a lasting network.
principles.quote: When you spend your time helping partners succeed, you become vested in their journey and they become vested in yours.

principles.text: Compliance monitoring protects brand image and payouts and ensures the program's longevity.
principles.quote: Compliance is an integral part of affiliate program management. It ensures the longevity and success of your program.

principles.text: Hit and exceed revenue goals to earn more budget from executives for exploratory campaigns.
principles.quote: When revenue goals are reached and exceeded, executives are more likely to invest additional marketing budget into exploratory campaigns.

principles.text: Choose staffing by stage: in-house for committed growth, an agency to scale on its affiliate network, or a trained junior as the cost-effective option.
principles.quote: Training one of your junior marketers is one of the most cost-effective ways of getting an affiliate manager for your program.

sources.title: Dustin Howes's affiliate marketing blueprint: how to audit, scrub, and scale a new affiliate program
sources.originalTitle: The Ultimate Affiliate Marketing Blueprint For Affiliate Managers
sources.summary: A 10-step playbook Dustin follows when taking on any new affiliate program: audit first, define partner personas, scrub unproductive partners, layer in quick-win technology partners, then chase review placements, paid-search publishers and media buyers. He stresses judging partners by traffic and revenue produced rather than by partner count or brand name.

principles.text: Start every program with a thorough audit; it makes you the expert and builds client trust.
principles.quote: The auditing process is the foundation for successful client engagement.

principles.text: Partner count is a vanity metric; focus on partner productivity and remove dormant partners with no potential.
principles.quote: The number of affiliates in your program is a vanity metric.

principles.text: Define partner personas (type, job title, how to find them, motivation) before recruiting.
principles.quote: You need to drill down and find out what type of partner they are, what their job title is, how to find them, and their motivation to partner with you.

principles.text: Use abandonment and retargeting partners for quick wins while slower content partners ramp up.
principles.quote: retargeting and abandonment partners can bring incremental value to a program during that time.

principles.text: Optimize on-site conversion first: affiliates send more traffic to pages they know will convert.
principles.quote: If affiliate partners see a high quality site and landing page, they know it will convert their traffic, so they are more likely to send you more.

principles.text: Judge review placements by traffic and trust delivered, not publisher prestige; niche sites can beat premium names.
principles.quote: Whether it’s Forbes or a small personal finance website, what's most important is how much traffic the site drives to your client's affiliate program.

sources.title: Affiliate management tools: how Dustin Howes builds an affiliate program tech stack
sources.originalTitle: The Ultimate List Of Affiliate Management Tools
sources.summary: Dustin Howes catalogs affiliate management tools by function: recruitment, tracking, CRM, automation, AI, communication, payments and fraud. The core idea is that manual program management doesn't scale, and the right stack saves time, improves accuracy and unlocks growth. Much of the piece is a tool list with affiliate links, so the durable insight is thin.

principles.text: Automate the most tedious work first; recruitment tooling saves the most time.
principles.quote: This is my favorite category. Not just because I'm a nerd with it, but because I feel like they save the most time from the most tedious work.

principles.text: Manual affiliate management doesn't scale; the right tools add time savings, insight and automation.
principles.quote: These tools not only save you time and effort but also provide valuable insights and automation capabilities that can significantly impact your program's success.

principles.text: Pick tools to fit your program's goals and scale; your tech stack can make or break results.
principles.quote: The effectiveness of your affiliate program hinges on selecting the right tools tailored to your goals and program scale.

principles.text: Tailor landing pages to the affiliate's audience to lift conversion; a celebrity-specific lander raised conversion 200%.
principles.quote: This lander speaks to her fans and to the benefits that she finds valuable. It also includes her recognizable face, her accolades, and a quote.

principles.text: Combine tools (scraping plus data enrichment) to build affiliate prospect lists at scale.
principles.quote: Scraping Instagram followers at scale. Combine this with Upfluence or Influencers Club

sources.title: From affiliate manager to C-suite: how to turn channel expertise into executive leadership
sources.originalTitle: From Affiliate Manager To C-Suite: Breaking The Professional Ceiling
sources.summary: Dustin Howes recaps his conversation with Partner Gap CEO Vik Ratomske on moving from data analyst to executive. The core idea is to treat the affiliate role as executive training, prove relationship value with hard data, and learn to delegate and pick your battles.

principles.text: Treat an affiliate role as executive training, not a dead end.
principles.quote: You shouldn't see your current role as a dead end. Instead, treat it as the ultimate training ground for executive leadership.

principles.text: Back intangible relationship value with concrete data executives can see.
principles.quote: You can't just say a partner is important. You have to show how three years of connection turned into wealth for the brand.

principles.text: Educate leadership on how the channel supports the whole business to win buy-in.
principles.quote: If you are struggling to get buy-in, you have to become an educator.

principles.text: Stay broad across channels to become the most versatile marketer.
principles.quote: Don't narrow yourself to just one channel like media buying or content. Be an expert on traditional affiliate strategies, but stay open to every new trend.

principles.text: Use a pause button when negotiations get emotional and unproductive.
principles.quote: If a conversation becomes unproductive, use the “pause button.” Suggest revisiting the topic in ten minutes or the next day.

principles.text: At executive level, delegate and focus on the big picture rather than tasks.
principles.quote: You have to learn to delegate and focus on the big picture.

sources.title: Affiliate fraud prevention: Dustin Howes's practitioner playbook for detecting and handling affiliate fraud
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Fraud Prevention: A Practitioner's Guide
sources.summary: Dustin Howes, who started his affiliate career policing fraud at CJ Affiliate 17+ years ago, defines affiliate fraud as anyone breaking brand T&Cs to earn a commission. He lays out red flags, seven fraud types, an evidence-first escalation path, and daily, weekly and quarterly monitoring habits. Most fraud is opportunistic, not sophisticated.

principles.text: Define fraud as any T&C violation made to earn a commission, sophisticated or not; vague terms are unenforceable.
principles.quote: “Affiliate fraud is anybody breaking the terms and conditions established by the brand to make a dollar.”

principles.text: The goal is managing fraud, not eliminating it: catch it early and be a harder target than the next program.
principles.quote: “You can't stop hustlers from hustling.”

principles.text: Rule out tracking misconfiguration, attribution windows and cookie overrides before accusing a partner.
principles.quote: “Outright scamming is rare. More common issues are attribution windows, cookie overrides, self-referrals getting blocked, or conversions being marked as ineligible in fine print.”

principles.text: Very short click-to-purchase times signal a stolen last click; investigate anything under five minutes.
principles.quote: “If something's happened within five minutes from their first click all the way to checkout, that means that somebody's doing something serious and stealing that last click somehow.”

principles.text: Lock down evidence before contacting or freezing any affiliate; with evidence the conversation is easy.
principles.quote: “Collect that evidence and make sure that it's locked tight before we do anything else.”

principles.text: Fraud prevention is a system of daily habits, not a tool; tools only help you scale the system.
principles.quote: you don't need expensive tools to catch fraud. You need a system.

sources.title: Why ecommerce affiliate tools fail SaaS: the $200 CPA mistake at WP Engine
sources.originalTitle: 3 Critical Reasons Ecommerce Tools Can't Track Recurring Revenue
sources.summary: Dustin explains why ecommerce-style affiliate tracking breaks for subscription businesses, drawing on a conversation with FirstPromoter's Tautvydas Vasiliauskas. He covers subscription-native commission structures, long B2B sales cycles, and a personal lesson from paying a flat $200 CPA at WP Engine on $30 plans that cancelled.

principles.text: A flat CPA invites gaming: partners send cheap-plan customers who cancel after one payment.
principles.quote: People figured out they could send us a customer on a $30 plan, collect the full $200 commission, and the customer would cancel the next month.

principles.text: Subscription businesses need commission tracking that follows the customer lifecycle, not a single transaction.
principles.quote: If you have a subscription pricing for your product and you want to do partner marketing, you need a subscription-native commission tracking tool.

principles.text: Pull renewals, refunds, chargebacks and upgrades straight from billing data to avoid manual reconciliation.
principles.quote: No manual reconciliation. No spreadsheet gymnastics. The commission engine just reflects what's actually happening with the customer's subscription.

principles.text: Design the reward model around your customer lifecycle: delay payouts, weight first payment, or pay recurring.
principles.quote: You have to always structure the reward model around your business case.

principles.text: Set commission rules per partner, not just per campaign, so top partners can run different structures.
principles.quote: You can delay commissions until a customer hits their third month of subscription.

principles.text: For long B2B or freemium sales cycles, track the lead itself rather than a short click-to-purchase cookie window.
principles.quote: you need a tool that tracks the lead itself, not just a short click-to-purchase window.

sources.title: Affiliate tracking software: what it does and the 8 platforms Dustin Howes recommends
sources.originalTitle: Mastering Affiliate Tracking Software
sources.summary: Dustin Howes explains why affiliate programs need dedicated tracking software, what makes a platform good, and ranks eight platforms by best-fit use case (SaaS, SMB ecommerce, enterprise, mobile, coupons, budget). Includes pricing and pros/cons per tool.

principles.text: Dedicated tracking software replaces manual spreadsheet tracking and gives accurate attribution of clicks, leads and commissions.
principles.quote: This is the stuff that transforms you from “I think I made sales today?” to “Oh hey, here are my clicks, conversions, and commissions neatly organized in a dashboard.”

principles.text: A good platform tracks accurately in real time, is easy for both businesses and affiliates, and is customizable.
principles.quote: It should be able to track clicks, conversions, and other metrics accurately. Real-time analytics are important for businesses to make quick, informed decisions.

principles.text: Fraud detection and integrations with CRMs and ecommerce tools are essential selection criteria.
principles.quote: Built-in fraud detection tools are essential to prevent fraudulent activities and ensure fairness.

principles.text: Choose tracking software by fit: Everflow overall, PartnerStack for SaaS, ShareASale/Awin for SMB ecommerce, Impact for big programs.
principles.quote: Not recommended for SMBs with less than $10 million in revenue.

principles.text: Match the tool to the program's strategy, e.g. Refersion for coupon/vanity code programs, TUNE for mobile, FirstPromoter for tight budgets.
principles.quote: Refersion excels at simplifying tracking for programs focused on coupon strategies, thanks to its ability to create vanity codes for partners.

principles.text: Pick a tool that fits your workflow; guesswork is unnecessary when precise attribution is available.
principles.quote: Don’t settle for guesswork when precision is just a dashboard away.

sources.title: Best affiliate software for subscription businesses: billing-synced commissions compared
sources.originalTitle: 7 Best Affiliate Software For Subscription Businesses
sources.summary: Dustin ranks seven affiliate platforms for subscription businesses, arguing that commissions must follow the billing lifecycle (renewals, upgrades, downgrades, cancellations) rather than a one-time sale webhook. He picks FirstPromoter as best overall and lists the features that matter. The piece is heavily affiliate-link driven.

principles.text: Subscription commissions must follow the billing lifecycle, not a one-time sale event, or you over/underpay affiliates.
principles.quote: commissions follow the actual lifecycle of the subscription: renewals, upgrades, downgrades, and cancellations all adjust payouts automatically instead of you reconciling a spreadsheet every month.

principles.text: Generic ecommerce affiliate tools only track the initial sale and leave you adjusting everything after manually.
principles.quote: a generic, ecommerce-first affiliate tool will typically only track the initial sale and leave you to manually adjust everything that happens afterward.

principles.text: Choose a tool with native billing-provider sync, lifecycle-aware commissions, self-serve setup, transparent pricing, fraud protection, and room to grow.
principles.quote: Native billing-provider sync** (Stripe, Chargebee, Paddle, Recurly, Braintree) – not just a one-time “purchase” webhook

principles.text: Match the platform to your model: simple Stripe-only SaaS wants the cheapest simple tool; full B2B partner motions need a partner ecosystem platform.
principles.quote: If your business is Stripe- or Paddle-only and you want the absolute simplest, cheapest way to get started, **Rewardful** is a strong runner-up.

principles.text: Partner activation after signup is where most affiliate programs stall, so use emails, contests and leaderboards.
principles.quote: broadcast emails, contests, and leaderboards to keep partners producing after signup, where most programs stall

principles.text: Subscription businesses are common targets for self-referral abuse, so fraud protection should be built in.
principles.quote: Fraud protection** built in, since subscription businesses are a common target for self-referral abuse

sources.title: Affistash review: why Dustin Howes backs it as the affiliate manager's partner-discovery and CRM tool
sources.originalTitle: Affistash Review: The Ultimate Affiliate Manager Super Tool
sources.summary: Dustin Howes reviews Affistash, an affiliate partner discovery and CRM SaaS he helped shape and later became CMO of. He lays out its feature set, SMB target buyer, pricing and competitive positioning. This is a promotional review by an interested party, not a general framework.

principles.text: Find affiliate partners who already rank for your target keywords; they are proven performers in your niche.
principles.quote: This real-time insight allows you to target affiliates who are already performing well in your niche, increasing the likelihood of successful partnerships.

principles.text: Mine competitors' backlinks to find sites already in affiliate relationships, then sway them to your brand.
principles.quote: This feature allows you to tap into established affiliate relationships and potentially sway them to your brand.

principles.text: Clone a winning partnership by finding lookalike partners based on your best partner's URL.
principles.quote: Have a successful partnership you'd like to replicate? Affistash can find hundreds of similar partners based on any given ideal partner URL

principles.text: Centralize partner tracking in one CRM and use AI for personalized outreach and drip sequences to save time.
principles.quote: Managing multiple partnerships can quickly become chaotic.

principles.text: SMB brands with limited resources benefit most from tools that automate partner discovery and relationship management.
principles.quote: These businesses often struggle with limited resources and manpower, making Affistash's time-saving and efficiency-boosting features particularly valuable.

principles.text: Use traffic data on prospective partners to make data-driven decisions about which affiliates to pursue.
principles.quote: Understanding the traffic potential of your partners is crucial.

sources.title: Affiliate Manager Training Course: how Dustin Howes packages 12+ years of affiliate program know-how
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Manager Training Course
sources.summary: Sales page for Dustin Howes's Affiliate Manager Mastermind, a 10-day, one-hour-a-day course on affiliate program setup, recruitment, fraud prevention and reporting. It shows how he frames the affiliate manager role and the value of a well-run affiliate channel.

principles.text: A good affiliate program is a major revenue source and typically your cheapest paid channel.
principles.quote: A good affiliate program will represent 20% of the revenue from the marketing efforts. It will also likely be the lowest CPA of all your marketing channels (besides organic).

principles.text: An affiliate manager is a partnership development role, with many small daily tasks that compound.
principles.quote: An affiliate manager is a partnership development representative of the company. Their focus is to grow the affiliate program, but there are dozens of little tasks to be done each day to maximize their efforts.

principles.text: The biggest pitfall for affiliate managers is not knowing where to focus; recruiting is never finished.
principles.quote: The biggest pitfall an affiliate manager faces is not knowing where to focus their efforts. The job of the affiliate manager is never done because they can always be recruiting more partners.

principles.text: Build the program affiliates actually want to join; design it to attract partners.
principles.quote: Create the affiliate program that affiliates WANT to join.

principles.text: Teach with templates and a checklist so people can execute immediately after learning.
principles.quote: A powerful affiliate program checklist, complete with templates for recruitment, welcome sequences, legal terms, and more.

principles.text: Implement strategies while they are fresh; short daily sessions fit around a full-time job.
principles.quote: Just one hour per day for 10 consecutive weekdays will make you a certified affiliate manager.

sources.title: How to recruit and activate high-quality affiliates: Dustin Howes's 5-step playbook
sources.originalTitle: How to Recruit High-Quality Affiliates (and Activate Them)
sources.summary: A Rewardful webinar recap where Dustin Howes lays out a five-step system for affiliate programs: define ideal partner personas, recruit outbound, personalize outreach, vet applicants, then onboard so partners earn their first commission fast. Recruitment is treated as ongoing pipeline work, not a one-time task.

principles.text: Recruitment and activation are the engine of an affiliate program, not an afterthought.
principles.quote: Too many brands expect affiliates to just show up, grab a link, and go. Recruitment and activation end up last on the task list—yet they’re the engine of the program.

principles.text: Know your ideal customer before defining your ideal affiliate; write partner personas before pitching.
principles.quote: No ICP means no IAP.

principles.text: Optimize for revenue concentration, not affiliate count; a few partners drive most sales.
principles.quote: Vanity metrics (total affiliates) don’t matter, revenue concentration is real.

principles.text: Fund an exploratory budget (fee, free product, commission) to lift response rates from competitive partners.
principles.quote: Exploratory budget (even modest) dramatically lifts response rates.

principles.text: Skip mass blasts; send targeted, human outreach that shows you looked and offers value.
principles.quote: Skip the mass blast. Aim for targeted, human messages.

principles.text: Treat affiliate activation like product onboarding, aiming at the first commission.
principles.quote: Treat affiliate activation like product onboarding: the “aha” moment is their first commission.

sources.title: Affiliate networks drop the ball: stay hands-on with data and stand out in job hunts
sources.originalTitle: Affiliate Marketing Unfiltered: Dodgy Networks, Job Hunts, and Smart Moves
sources.summary: Dustin recaps a Real Talk Friday chat with Christen Evans on affiliate network failures (an eight-month tracking outage billed on estimates, removed affiliates still earning via bookmarked links). He also shares how a three-minute video and dedicated page got him a job interview, and urges early Q4 prep.

principles.text: Network quirks and estimated commissions can cause major headaches, so monitor your affiliate data diligently and stay hands-on.
principles.quote: Stay Hands-On with Data: Network quirks like "bookmarked links" and estimated commissions can cause major headaches. Diligent monitoring is key.

principles.text: Networks should flag tracking problems early; long outages billed on generic estimates are hard to verify and unfair.
principles.quote: The network should have flagged the issue much earlier instead of blindsiding them with a massive invoice.

principles.text: Stand out in a competitive job market with a creative, personalized approach such as a short video and dedicated page.
principles.quote: I made a three-minute YouTube video and a dedicated page explaining why I’d be a great hire. It got me in the door and landed that crucial first interview.

principles.text: Prepare for Q4 early: lock in placements and finalize strategies before the holiday rush.
principles.quote: Prepare for Q4 Early: The holiday rush is coming fast. Now’s the time to lock in placements and finalize strategies.

sources.title: Dustin Howes at CJU 2026: filming Affiliate Nerd Out on the road in Santa Barbara
sources.originalTitle: I took Affiliate Nerd Out on the road to CJU 2026 in Santa Barbara, and I filmed everything.
sources.summary: A LinkedIn post and video diary from Dustin Howes covering CJU 2026. He shares practical travel tips and a candid verdict on the event app, meeting pacing and sponsor-heavy content, while interviewing attendees about why in-person networking events matter.

principles.text: Skip the conference hotel; cheap nearby lodging gets you the same event for far less.
principles.quote: You don't want to stay at the same hotel as conference, which is ridiculous money.

principles.text: Event tech and meeting pacing can sink networking value; give people a usable scheduling app and time between meetings.
principles.quote: The event app was probably the biggest hit this conference took. It was clunky, it was not user friendly. It was very difficult to schedule meetings

principles.text: Conference education should help practitioners improve, not just promote the host's ecosystem; bring in outside voices.
principles.quote: I would love to see more outside content from contributors outside of the CJ ecosystem.

principles.text: Be honest in event coverage: share the good and the not-so-good so your audience trusts your verdict.
principles.quote: yes, I’m sharing the good and the not-so-good.

principles.text: Compact, walkable venues make networking effortless.
principles.quote: One end of the conference to the other took less than a 3 minute walk. Super convenient when you're trying to network throughout the event.

principles.text: Mix scheduled meetings with unstructured social settings to multiply connections.
principles.quote: Maybe 10 meetings and another 10 on the side. Now it's off to the beach party to see more folks and mingle.

sources.title: The Phia Scandal: what forced-click fraud means for affiliate marketing
sources.originalTitle: The Phia Scandal: What it really means for affiliate marketing.
sources.summary: Promo post for a live panel on the alleged Phia forced-click scheme. Dustin frames it as different from Honey-style credit theft: clicks and commissions were allegedly manufactured, leaving merchants as the victims. Light on detail, mostly a teaser with fraud-spotting and network-policy takeaways.

principles.text: Manufactured clicks are a distinct, worse fraud than stealing credit for another publisher's click.
principles.quote: They allegedly did not just take credit for another publishers click the way Honey was accused of doing. It allegedly created clicks.

principles.text: Forced-click schemes leave tells in the data: implausibly high click-through and conversion rates.
principles.quote: How to spot the tells of a forced-click scheme, including implausibly high click-through rate and conversion rate

principles.text: In both credit theft and manufactured commissions, the merchant ends up as the victim paying for sales not earned.
principles.quote: How Honey-style credit theft differs from Phia-style manufactured commissions, and why merchants end up as the victims

principles.text: Each affiliate network enforces fraud differently, so merchants should know where their network draws the line.
principles.quote: Where each network draws the line: Awin's soft click, Impact's per-program paid PQ, and CJ's NQ team and software ban in subaffiliate programs

sources.title: B2B affiliate recruitment: respond fast, measure influence, coach partners
sources.originalTitle: An affiliate replied to your recruitment email. They said yes.
sources.summary: Final part of Dustin Howes's series on building a B2B affiliate program from scratch. He argues for instant follow-up when an affiliate says yes, attribution that captures both influence and conversion, and hands-on coaching of partners who promote but don't convert.

principles.text: When an affiliate says yes to recruitment, get on the call immediately; speed to lead decides whether interest survives.
principles.quote: Speed to lead is everything in affiliate recruitment.

principles.text: Interest decays within a day or two; delay means the affiliate has moved on.
principles.quote: Wait a day or two and that interest is already gone. They've moved on with their life.

principles.text: Your tech stack must measure influence and conversions together; last-touch attribution misleads and leads to bad cuts.
principles.quote: if you cannot measure influence and conversions at the same time, you're dead. Last-touch attribution will lie to you.

principles.text: Don't cut a channel just because it shows few last-touch conversions; understand its role in the buying journey first.
principles.quote: One brand killed their Facebook ads because conversions looked low. Sales dropped 25%.

principles.text: Coach partners who promote but don't convert: find where they're stuck and give them angles that work.
principles.quote: If someone is promoting but not converting, hop on a call. See where they're getting stuck. Give them the angles that work.

principles.text: Affiliate marketing is a relationship business, so invest in personal contact with partners.
principles.quote: It's a relationship business.

sources.title: Why SaaS affiliate programs need subscription-native tracking and delayed commissions
sources.originalTitle: I used to run affiliate programs without subscription-native tracking, and it almost cost me.
sources.summary: Dustin Howes recounts how a flat $200 CPA at WP Engine got gamed by buyers of a $30 plan who cancelled in month two. In a conversation with FirstPromoter's head of marketing, he reinforces that SaaS affiliate programs need subscription-native tracking, flexible and delayed commissions, and lead-based attribution for long B2B sales cycles.

principles.text: A flat CPA on a cheap subscription plan invites gaming: people buy, cancel in month two, and keep the commission.
principles.quote: At WP Engine, we set a $200 CPA... and got burned. People bought the $30 plan, canceled month two, and pocketed the commission.

principles.text: Forcing ecommerce-style tracking onto subscription billing breaks continuity, recurring logic and protection against abuse.
principles.quote: That's the exact problem SaaS affiliate programs run into when they try to force ecommerce-style tracking onto subscription billing. No continuity, no recurring logic, no protection.

principles.text: Set the CPA by balancing what you can afford, what attracts partners, and what protects customer lifetime value.
principles.quote: We had to make a strong decision, what's the CPA that we need to give out, that we can afford to give out, be appealing enough to get people's attention and yet not take it back on the lifetime value of the customers.

principles.text: Pick an affiliate platform for flexibility: different partner types, like coupon sites and content creators, should be paid differently.
principles.quote: I'm not going to pay the coupon sites the same as I'm going to play the content and the content creators. It's just not going to happen.

principles.text: Use delayed and tiered commissions so you stop overpaying people who churn fast.
principles.quote: Delayed and tiered commission structures (so you stop overpaying people who churn fast)

principles.text: Long B2B sales cycles need lead-based attribution, not just click-to-sale cookie tracking.
principles.quote: Why long B2B sales cycles need lead-based attribution, not just click tracking

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes walks through his 30+ point checklist for building an affiliate program: research, tech stack decisions, creation, announcement, recruitment, management and reporting. His core argument is that programs fail because they are set up poorly and then ignored, and that good partners need onboarding, assets and ongoing attention to produce revenue.

chunks.heading: Why affiliate programs fail and what the "fish" lesson means
chunks.text:
- Dustin says most affiliate programs fail because they are "set up poorly and just ignored", not because the product is bad. He compares them to raising kids: nurtured programs treat you well, ignored ones "turn into a turd".
- Good affiliates "don't just show up" and make magic happen. They are fickle, get excited about a niche, and drift away if they lack resources or a good onboarding experience.
- Any program not set up by a trained manager has affiliates "falling through the cracks".
- He argues setup alone won't grow a program. The manager must be taught the functions, per the "teach a man to fish" adage.
- His payoff claim for doing it right over 12 months: up to 20% additional revenue, an "army of sales reps" on commission, a cost per acquisition cheaper than any other channel except email, and the highest-quality customers with the best lifetime value.
- His background: 13+ years in affiliate, including Commission Junction, impact, publishers, agencies and merchant programs. At WP Engine he grew the program about 60% year over year consistently.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Research and the 30/60/90/180/365 plan
chunks.text:
- Run a competitive analysis chart: which platform competitors use, their offers, their application process, and their commissions. Sign up for their programs and note what they do right and wrong.
- Calculate your standard and maximum commission rates. Stay competitive, and work out what you can afford to give partners while the company still profits. If you can't out-pay competitors, find something else to offer.
- Take demos with at least three tracking platforms before choosing.
- Decide in-house vs outsourced (agency) management.
- Build partner personas, like customer avatars, to define who you're targeting.
- Write a 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365-day plan with growth expectations and accountability for the affiliate manager. Do this before hiring the person or company to manage it.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Program decisions (payouts, visibility, CRM, platform)
chunks.text:
- Pick a payout model: cost per click, lead or sale. He calls CPA-style models the easiest and most efficient.
- Define the standard payout and the absolute maximum you'd pay premium partners. Set a base rate and a VIP rate, plus any bonuses or volume/sale incentives.
- Decide whether the program is public or invite-only.
- Choose a CRM for partnerships ("you will need a CRM"). You can piggyback on the company CRM or separate partnerships into their own.
- Choose a platform: a big network gives big publisher pools and strong reports; a small platform saves money but means you do all the recruiting yourself.

chunks.heading: Steps 3 and 4: Build the program, then announce it
chunks.text:
Build everything before announcing, because the program is "an extension of your brand".

- Application responders (automated replies, some platforms allow only one or two).
- Welcome email flow that sets the tone, explains where assets are and how to grab a link.
- Branded signup page: the first impression.
