- Banners and links library with landing page variations.
- Program terms and conditions.
- Partner assets folder with banners, links, blog posts and examples of affiliates already doing good work.
- Recruitment email templates per persona, as a message sequence.
- Third-party tools to expand reach.

His bar analogy: an unstaffed bar with no bouncer or bartender attracts dishonest people and makes honest ones cautious. A greeted, served guest becomes loyal.

Announcement tactics:
- Company newsletter, blog, social and forums.
- Invite customers, since they're evangelists.
- Put the affiliate program link in the site footer, "the first place I look when I'm an affiliate".

chunks.heading: Step 5: Recruitment
chunks.text:
- Build a partner list: use Semrush to find sites ranking on Google, Hunter.io for contact emails, and look at competitors' traffic sources and backlinks.
- Email with a goal of 50 per week and scale up, then schedule calls.
- Come to calls flexible, with talking points on why the program is worth promoting.
- He mentions using a tool called Rona for recruiting and time management.
- Most programs fail by not dividing time between recruiting and activating interested affiliates.
- Good managers look for potential before the affiliate makes sales and nurture the relationship, acting as the leader who helps the troops succeed.

chunks.heading: Step 6: Ongoing program management
chunks.text:
- Update assets, approve or deny applications daily, and initiate the automated welcome sequence with a first link.
- Send a newsletter at least monthly to stay top of mind.
- Run incentive campaigns that motivate new content and sales.
- Give VIP treatment to top performers: "every teacher has favorites".
- Keep banners and links fresh, with links, landing pages and banners for every new product.

chunks.heading: Step 7: Reporting KPIs for executives
chunks.text:
Because the manager's work has many intangibles, build reports that show effort and results.

- Daily: transactions, program performance, traffic spikes. Investigate anything out of place.
- Weekly: week-over-week results and best-selling days.
- Weekly/monthly: top links and banners, best-selling SKUs, best coupons, partner conversion rates vs average.
- Also track lifetime value and AOV per partner to identify who drives the best traffic.
- Investigate dips and spikes per partner versus the prior month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes hosts a live School of Chaos webinar where the XP Flow team demos Alfie, an AI tool that finds, scores and emails affiliates from just a brand URL. Dustin's own contributions are framing: affiliate recruitment has been spreadsheet work, and AI should enhance partnership managers rather than replace them. Most substantive material comes from guests Matt and Beth.

chunks.heading: Alfie's origin and the problem Dustin says it solves
chunks.text:
- Dustin has 17 years in affiliate marketing, much of it "working out of spreadsheets, guessing at domains and firing emails into info@ boxes that nobody reads."
- He says this describes most affiliate managers' jobs, current or past.
- He presents Alfie (from XP Flow) as the tool that replaces that manual recruitment work, and says he has "never been so excited about a product."
- He frames the goal as freeing partnership managers to be more human: relationships and strategy instead of reporting and spreadsheet labor.
- He stresses the tool "is an enhancer, not a replacement" for affiliate managers and agencies, and that it is not meant to replace the networks (tracking and payments).

chunks.heading: Why recruitment stayed manual and what has changed
chunks.text:
- Dustin's co-presenters' framing, which he endorses by hosting and agreeing, is that affiliate is relationship driven rather than "coin operated" like paid search or programmatic.
- AI now handles the messy parts: sifting millions of affiliates, structuring unstructured data, finding contacts, and drafting personalized outreach.
- Old workflow he describes: three screens open at once, with separate tools for finding contacts, checking traffic, finding similar sites, reading the site for placement ideas, and writing the email.
- Alfie puts all of this in one interface.
- Data brokers who used to sell spreadsheets of finance affiliates at conferences are made obsolete by on-demand matching.

chunks.heading: Setting up a recruitment campaign from just a URL
chunks.text:
Live demo steps, run on a blank install using Robinhood as the brand:

1. Add an advertiser by entering only the brand URL. Alfie analyzes the site and generates a recruitment prompt, keywords (for example "best apps for beginners"), categories and verticals. This replaces hours of bullpen brainstorming.
2. Optionally add targeting to the prompt: US audience, gender skew, age.
3. Answer onboarding questions: affiliate network (the tool is network agnostic), signup link, commission (demo used 20%), cookie duration (90 days), extras like seasonal bonuses and creative refresh cadence, and an email signature. These become merge fields in outreach templates.
4. Launch the campaign. It uses a prompt, up to 10 keywords (add your own), IAB categories (700 available), affiliate types (content sites, review and comparison sites, influencers, and so on, toggled on or off), geo, age range, audience size and gender.

- Dustin says multiple campaigns can target different affiliate types or traffic, so different promos can go to different groups.

chunks.heading: How discovery, verification and fit score work
chunks.text:
- Results come from a verified data lake of roughly 75,000-80,000 affiliates, plus live web curation that finds long-tail content sites not visible in the networks.
- Dustin points out that network marketplace data is only as good as what affiliates entered themselves and goes stale when owners leave. Alfie's data is verified contact and site data.
- Every result includes an affiliate drawer with a summary, why it was selected, best contact (multiple contacts can be chosen), traffic and authority metrics (otherwise pulled manually from tools like SimilarWeb or SEMrush), geo reach (for example 96% US), and audience age, gender and income signals.
- A verified check mark means Alfie detected affiliate links and disclaimers. Unverified content sites can still be good fits but require a different conversation (teaching them about affiliate programs).
- Fit score is out of 100 (the demo showed a 90, "exceptional match"). It reflects data completeness, keyword and category match, and geo and demographic criteria.
- Dustin: after 10 years with tools in this space (he names FiveIQ and MediaRails), "this is the most sophisticated search functionality that I've ever seen," and the fit score is "not something you can easily replicate" with Claude or ChatGPT.
- Rejecting an affiliate with a reason trains Alfie, and rejected affiliates can be restored later.

chunks.heading: Outreach sequences and the affiliate workflow
chunks.text:
- The pipeline stages are Outreach, Engage, Deploy and Convert.
- Approved affiliates go into an autoresponder-style sequence with prefilled templates and merge tags (bonuses, benefits).
- Cadence in the demo: first email, follow-up 3 days later, third email 6 days later. The sequence stops automatically on reply.
- Emails send from an Alfie mail domain by default (name plus a number tied to the campaign and affiliate). Custom DNS can make mail come from your own domain.
- Engage: reply from an inbox, or have Alfie draft replies that you can edit or ask to make more casual.
- Deploy: send links, creatives and IO, set postbacks. Convert is currently a status field, with optimization suggestions planned.
- Once running, the work happens in the background so managers can focus on strategy.

chunks.heading: Response rates reported on the webinar
chunks.text:
Figures come from the Alfie team and Dustin presents them as results of the platform:

- Cold outreach over the last 38 days of signups: 3.8% response rate.
- Alfie recruiting affiliates for the Alfie program itself: 7.9%.
- Some clients reach as high as 25%.
- Inbox placement is in the high 90s percent.
- The team's services group got a reply from the New York Times for an up-and-coming brand client.
- Dustin notes the demo replies were mocked up for speed, so the live demo did not reflect real response rates.

chunks.heading: Current limits and roadmap
chunks.text:
- Currently strongest on content affiliates. Social and influencer affiliates are on the roadmap.
- No export, API or CSV import yet (an MCP is in the works and CSV import is planned).
- It does not yet optimize publisher revenue or score on activation. Network integrations (for activation data and automatic deploy stages) are coming.
- Organizations and teams for agencies are "days away," and AI-personalized sequences are in design.
- It works for B2B and SaaS too, with Alfie's own program as the example.
- Alfie offers a 14-day free signup with no credit card at alfie.io.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes walks through the 15 steps an affiliate takes from discovering a program to ranking content, earning sales and renegotiating terms. His core point is that this process takes time and only works if the manager actively holds the hand of high-potential affiliates and knows how long to spend on each step.

chunks.heading: The 15-step affiliate partnership lifecycle
chunks.text:
Dustin frames affiliate management as a long, hands-on process in which a manager has to "hold the hand" of a high-potential affiliate. He walks through 15 steps, grouped into four phases, and says knowing how much time to spend on each step is crucial.

- **Phase 1 (steps 1-4): getting the affiliate into the program.**
- **Phase 2 (steps 5-9): research, content and monetization.**
- **Phase 3 (steps 10-12): ranking, clicks and sales.**
- **Phase 4 (steps 13-15): connection, negotiation and a new campaign.**

He stresses that none of this happens instantly and that these steps do not complete on their own without the manager's involvement.

chunks.heading: Phase 1: recruiting the affiliate and getting them to join
chunks.text:
- **Step 1, find or be found.** Dustin calls this "a dance." The manager has to get out and recruit so affiliates can find the program. The affiliate may already be searching a niche or running a site about it, and either they find you or you find them.
- **Step 2, review.** The affiliate has to review the program and agree to its terms. The manager can entice them with bigger commissions, landing pages or free products. The affiliate checks that the product and program are a good fit.
- **Step 3, join.** The manager either sends a link or talks the affiliate into signing up on whatever network or platform the program runs on. The affiliate accepts the terms agreed in earlier discussions.
- **Step 4, a separate stage.** The transcript does not name this step clearly, but he says it is "not an easy task" and "these kinds of things don't happen instantaneously."

chunks.heading: Phase 2: how a good affiliate researches and builds content
chunks.text:
Dustin describes what a good affiliate does after joining, so a manager knows what is happening behind the scenes.

- **Step 5, keyword research.** The affiliate researches what is currently ranking on Google, YouTube or wherever they publish.
- **Step 6, content research.** They review all the content about the target keywords. They find a winner to go after, see which content actually works, then replicate it and make it better. He says a lot of research goes into this step for good affiliates.
- **Step 7, create the content.** They decide the format and length, such as a 500-word or 10,000-word blog post, or a one-minute video versus a 15-minute tutorial. Everyone's process differs. The goal is content that produces clicks and sales.
- **Step 8, optimize.** They work out how to rank at the top of Google. He says this takes time and strategy: "can't just slop this together."
- **Step 9, monetize.** They place affiliate links in the content. They are probably promoting more than one brand at a time, so monetizing each piece matters and takes time.

chunks.heading: Phase 3: ranking, clicks and sales
chunks.text:
- **Step 10, rank.** The content has to rank on Google or other platforms before clicks come through. Good affiliates know how to rank faster and have domain authority greater than most content already out there. Some buy their placement at the top of Google.
- **Step 11, clicks.** Clicks must arrive in large volume.
- **Step 12, sales.** Clicks have to convert. Depending on the medium, conversion rate could be 2% or 15%.

chunks.heading: Phase 4: connecting, negotiating and repeating
chunks.text:
- **Step 13, connect with the affiliate manager.** Managers should use reporting to watch their up-and-comers and reach out to the ones starting to bring in sales. The goal is to replicate what is working, so he suggests getting on a call.
- **Step 14, negotiate.** Topics include landing pages and commission rate, anything that gives the affiliate more exposure to the program. He calls it a give and take: affiliates "ask for the moon," the manager gives a little, and both meet in the middle.
- **Step 15, create a new campaign.** Once the content-ranking-sales formula works, repeat it with the same affiliate because the relationship is established. For that affiliate, go back to phase 2 and repeat steps 5 through 9. For new affiliates, start from step 1.

chunks.heading: Resource Dustin points to
chunks.text:
- He promotes his affiliate manager course at performancemarketingmanager.com, which teaches these steps and how to manage programs properly.
- He says he has run this process "time and time again" with affiliates in his own programs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes walks through an eight-step affiliate partnership funnel and argues the top of it (discovery, outreach) absorbs 80% of a manager's time and should be automated. He covers personas, a three-list prospecting system, a five-email sequence, bargaining chips, call prep, hybrid negotiation and nurturing, while pitching his product Alfie.

chunks.heading: The affiliate partnership funnel and where time goes
chunks.text:
Dustin uses an eight-step partnership funnel, honed over the years:
- Discovery, outreach, express interest, call scheduled, negotiation, applied and aligned, content active, revenue active.
- The goal is to move every affiliate down this funnel.
- About 80% of an affiliate manager's time is absorbed in the top steps (finding contacts and affiliates).
- Junior managers work the top; senior managers work negotiation and relationship steps and must train the next generation for those calls.
- Dustin wants the top part automated so more time goes to relationships. His line: don't fear AI; "AI isn't going to be replacing the human side of affiliate marketing. It's actually protecting it."
- He argues managers who adapt to AI fastest are the ones who survive layoffs in a tough job market.

chunks.heading: Strategy: ICP, partner personas and three target lists
chunks.text:
- Start from the ICP and work backwards: where does the ICP hang out online?
- Build a partner persona sheet per partner type (job title, motivation, ideal content such as a "best of" listicle vs. full product review, subtypes like lifestyle or mommy bloggers).
- Build three lists rather than one undifferentiated blast:
  1. **Wish list:** 25 dream partners he never stops pursuing until he gets a hard no. Research them heavily and aim for touchpoints with about five a week.
  2. **Keyword list:** sites ranking for the keywords the brand wants to rank on, aligned with buyer intent.
  3. **Competitor traffic list:** sites ranking for competitors' keywords. They already have the traffic and can switch to promoting you with the right pitch.
- Prioritize non-branded terms ("best sleeping product") over branded terms. Still monitor branded terms so bad actors don't bid on trademarks and steal credit for sales you'd get anyway.
- Rebuild lists regularly (a VA can do it) because people change companies fast and a list goes stale within a year.

chunks.heading: Discovery channels and tools
chunks.text:
- **Content sites:** drop in around 50 keywords from the SEO team and find who ranks.
- **YouTube:** descriptions give an easy click path; YouTubers are great affiliates.
- **LinkedIn and social:** a "hidden gem." Creators who ignore DMs on Instagram (even with 100,000 followers) respond on LinkedIn because they're trying to network and grow there.
- **Closed communities:** for Facebook groups, befriend an admin and ask what top-of-group placement costs for a month. It may be about $100 and is "totally worth it."
- Tools he named, with his stated prices:
  - Semrush for keywords (~$140/month)
  - Similarweb for site metrics (~$200/month)
  - Channel Crawler for YouTube (~$60/month, includes fake-follower checks)
  - Favicon for LinkedIn discovery and traffic value (~$160/month)
  - Hunter.io for contact enrichment (~$50/month)
- He estimates the old manual method takes at least 10 minutes per spreadsheet line for someone good, 20 for someone not.

chunks.heading: Outreach: spray-and-pray vs. personalized
chunks.text:
- **Spray and pray** is for low-priority, long-tail affiliates: a five-email sequence over about two weeks. Hitting a 20% response rate means "you're absolutely winning." Sending about 50 emails a day gets results.
  - Email 1: short and punchy, ends with a question. Thursday is a good start day.
  - Email 2: quick follow-up.
  - Email 3: longer, with program context and how you'd work together.
  - Email 4: almost always uses a gift or joke. He uses the "Hello" gift from Lionel Richie and says it gets more responses than his other emails because it makes people laugh.
  - Email 5: the hard ask: "give me a yes or a no... tell me to kick rocks."
  - Suggested spacing: 3, 5, 7, then 6 days between sends; cadence is flexible.
- **Personalized** is for the high-value 25: reference specific content and hand-craft both the first email and follow-ups.
- Build a separate template per persona (YouTubers, bloggers and media buyers shouldn't get the same pitch). Test one variable at a time (subject, opener, ask), measure replies, keep winners and retire the rest.
- Use Claude to draft templates and generate many variants. Use Instantly (~$50/month) for sequencing.

chunks.heading: Bargaining chips that get attention
chunks.text:
- As an affiliate himself (dustin.com), he gets about a dozen partnership emails a day. Emails saying "this is our affiliate program, come join" get deleted; ones saying "we're open to running a relationship how you want" stand out.
- Chips to offer:
  - Sponsorship money (gets attention)
  - Backlinks (gold for bloggers)
  - Free product
  - Co-branded landing pages. At Inflection he built a page showing the prospect's own branding for high-value partners and got incredible responses.
  - Audience exchanges or collaborations
  - Deeper discounts
- The goal is to offer something immediately rather than just point to the program.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn networking and fast response handling
chunks.text:
- He keeps LinkedIn Sales Navigator (~$120/month, subscribed about 10 years) and uses Sales Connector to automate outreach; he connects with at least 100 people a week.
- Combining LinkedIn and email lifts response rates. He gave a figure of 43% but admitted it was made up from experience, so treat it as anecdotal.
- When someone responds:
  - Reply fast ("speed equals professionalism") and match their tone and length.
  - Thank them, get to the point, answer questions, and immediately drop a Calendly link to kill scheduling back-and-forth.
- He uses SaneBox (~$10/month) for inbox organization and HubSpot or HighLevel as CRM/PRM.

chunks.heading: Discovery calls, negotiation and nurture
chunks.text:
- **Before the call:** research the person in Sales Navigator and LinkedIn, run their site through Claude for a brief and goals, and find something personal to connect on.
- **On the call:** help first, since "no one really cares about what you want." Spend about five minutes on small talk, ask questions, share creative ideas, close with action items. Record with Granola (or Fireflies) and push notes to the CRM, with Claude drafting follow-ups.
- **Negotiation** should be win-win. Pure performance-only deals put all the risk on the affiliate and "you're starting off on the wrong foot."
  - Ask for their media kit; it's a door opener and signals a sale.
  - Hybrid is almost always right: a flat fee for their time plus commission.
  - A small paid placement (e.g. $100 newsletter slot) gets your foot in the door for commission work later.
  - Everything is negotiable; verify claims with screenshots, Google Analytics or conversion stats.
  - Off-peak rates are cheaper, notably Q1 and Q3.
- **Nurture after approval:** a five-day drip: welcome and product info; "my door is always open"; all assets in one place; "anything else I can do for you?" Evergreen content is what drives long-term revenue, and it won't happen overnight. Do favors, check in more often with more important partners, and document content wins to report to executives.

chunks.heading: Alfie (XP Flow) and the consolidated stack
chunks.text:
Dustin is VP of Product Marketing at XP Flow, and this section reflects his product pitch.
- He says the tools above total at least $450/month, versus Alfie at $100/month.
- Alfie claims:
  - A database of 80,000 verified, tagged affiliates
  - Keyword-based discovery with a fit score from seven touchpoints
  - Contact enrichment, AI-written five-email sequences with automated personalized openers
  - Traffic intel and a built-in PRM that is early-stage ("give us two months")
  - Results in as little as 10 minutes, with 50 ready leads per campaign (one example campaign had 144 loaded)
- Takeaways: recruiting never ends, LinkedIn is underused, and use tools that multiply your effort.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes lays out an affiliate recruitment playbook: fix conversion first, build partner personas, prioritize quality over count, fund an exploratory budget, personalize outreach, and onboard affiliates with a welcome sequence and resource hub. He also covers screening red flags and CPA vs revenue share.

chunks.heading: Why affiliate recruiting stalls
chunks.text:
- Dustin says the biggest cause is expectations. Businesses think "we have a great product, let's build an affiliate program" and assume affiliates will show up, take a link and promote.
- Recruitment ends up last on the affiliate manager's list. Managers who inherit an existing program spend their time on current affiliates, so activation and new recruiting get pushed down.
- He blames some networks and platforms for marketing affiliate as set-and-forget. Networks cite thousands or millions of affiliates but don't say that very few fit your business.
- Reaching the few who can promote you is hard through a platform. In his experience there is no substitute for direct, hands-on searching for the best affiliates in your niche.
- Don't launch a program out of desperation or as your primary channel. The company should be established first, with a high-converting website and landing pages. If traffic doesn't convert, you damage relationships and affiliates move to your competitors.
- Train affiliate managers on the company, the ICP and the sales cycle. He admits that as a young manager he knew too little about the company and tried to dodge it. Knowing which affiliates actually close sales, not just bring top-of-funnel curiosity, is a key part of learning.

chunks.heading: Build partner personas and target quality over quantity
chunks.text:
- The biggest mistake he sees is not creating partner personas. Write about five types, like you would for customers: content affiliates, bloggers, listicle sites, influencers on a specific topic or hashtag.
- First work out each persona's motivation to work with you, and don't build a list yet. Motivations differ:
  - Small bloggers will work for free if the pitch is right.
  - Big publications won't work for free; you buy sponsorship unless your product is truly unique and they already have content on it.
  - Influencers with 1,000 to 10,000 followers may work for free gifts or a little content. Above 10,000 you may need to offer sponsorship upfront.
- Each type needs a different approach.
- Program size is a vanity stat. A few affiliates deliver most sales. He described a customer program earning roughly 300K a month in commissions, with about 6,000 affiliates, perhaps 200 earning anything, and the top 10 accounting for about half of historical revenue.
- He cites Nathan Barry (ConvertKit), who framed it as 95-5: not that 5% bring 95% of sales, but that 95% of affiliates bring no traffic or revenue.
- His goal as a manager is to move toward 80-20. Know most active sellers personally and tier them: bottom (potential), middle (extra attention), top (do everything for them). Ask top-tier affiliates monthly how you can help.
- Diversify across partner types, and aim at the moon with big influencers only with realistic expectations. A million-follower influencer won't promote you for free; you negotiate and build trust.

chunks.heading: Where to find affiliates, in priority order
chunks.text:
1. Bloggers, listicle writers and content creators ranking on Google for your target keywords. List the ranking sites, find the right person, and keep pursuing a spot on the list until they say no. Ask what motivates them, since you only find out by asking.
2. Media buyers. Harder to find, but they know how to bring quality traffic at volume. Monitor messaging so it matches your brand and isn't misleading.
3. Email marketers who have built lists for years.
4. LinkedIn influencers for B2B and SaaS. Reviews bring less traffic but high-quality customers and good conversion.
5. Community admins, a good source of traffic.
6. Coupon, loyalty and toolbar sites at the bottom of the funnel. Often forced into programs; the industry's "closers".
7. YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and podcasters, which he treats as one influencer category with different channels.

chunks.heading: Tools for finding and reaching partners
chunks.text:
- Afy Stash is his first choice. Enter a competitor URL or your own to see which keywords affiliates rank for, then get contact details. It saves a lot of list-building time.
- Upfluence for influencer marketing; search by hashtag for large lists.
- Phantom Buster is underused in the affiliate community. Pull the followers of competitors' brands, download them with follower counts, then follow and engage the best ones. Example pitch: you like product X, here is a better and cheaper one your audience may like, want to promote it?
- Semrush, Similar Web, Hunter.io and Ahrefs (domain authority) as Chrome extensions.
- Waalaxy for LinkedIn outreach automation, used for B2B clients and SaaS influencers.
- He has a guide to the roughly 50 tools he uses at dustinous.com/tools.
- Find the decision-maker. A 100,000-follower influencer likely has someone handling partnerships; use LinkedIn or the website to find them.

chunks.heading: Outreach and negotiation
chunks.text:
- Decide first whether you have an exploratory budget and can buy sponsorships. He strongly recommends moving budget from other channels into exploring affiliate. With a budget, he says response rates rise dramatically, even several-fold.
- Without budget, offer free gifts (influencers must actually use the product; for SaaS, have them work with it and build a tutorial), backlinks for content publishers (they value them for SEO), and EPC and conversion rate data so they can decide.
- He finds 10K to 50K follower influencers the most effective on commission when shown EPC and conversion.
- Sponsorship also de-risks the affiliate: they create content and traffic hoping it converts. Paying for their time shows you value it. Often only a few hundred dollars, not much negotiation. For thousands, negotiate down by raising commission or cutting the upfront fee.
- Run a test budget with a few partners, then build case studies showing what they earned versus what they would have earned on commission. Use them as social proof and to justify lower upfront fees.
- Email structure of three parts:
  1. Why their content is great and why you like it (personal).
  2. What your product is and what you offer.
  3. A closing question, such as whether it fits their audience or whether they have time to promote it.
- Avoid AI tells: the words "dip", "dive" and "delve", em dashes, and emojis. He uses Matt McWilliams' tool for email drafts but still humanizes the output.
- Expect 10% or less response rate at scale; targeted, personal outreach can reach 20% or more.
- Run outreach over three channels (DM, email, LinkedIn friending) on three different days to raise response.
- Warm approach for small niche creators: comment on their posts, praise a specific piece, and send something useful, like a video on how to monetize with a $10 tool. He then treats them as friends.
- On LinkedIn creators who prefer sponsored posts: build friendships and give value. He says it's a long road if you can't afford upfront budget, and he tries to be everyone's friend, with favors coming back naturally.
- Don't pay upfront to people without a meaningful audience; offer them the affiliate program.

chunks.heading: Screening applications
chunks.text:
- Keep the application short: name, company, URL, social links, and an open box on how they will promote. Skip tax info and anything intrusive.
- Red flags:
  - A website that isn't theirs (e.g. someone entering Google).
  - A site that clearly doesn't fit your niche (cat blog for a SaaS), unless their promotion plan convinces you.
  - Sites that don't show what they do.
  - Inflated traffic claims (100K email subscribers on a tiny blog).
  - Spelling mistakes.
  - Certain countries he is wary of accepting from.
- Green flags: content fits your niche, audience matches your ICP, quality content, they know how to write CTAs, and their brand quality matches yours.
- He gives people the benefit of the doubt and watches borderline applicants more closely once sales arrive.

chunks.heading: Activation and onboarding
chunks.text:
- Most programs miss the welcome sequence. He suggests five emails over the first 5 days:
  1. Welcome, who the affiliate manager is, how to reach them.
  2. Their affiliate link, delivered fast.
  3. Marketing assets and resources.
  4. Success stories of other affiliates, plus contact info and a booking link.
  5. How the brand works and how to maximize earnings; the final email says to reach out anytime.
- Keep assets in one easily accessible, organized folder: email swipes, product summaries, best marketing strategies, banners, deep links.
- Use two one-pagers: one for recruiting ("why join") and one for post-signup onboarding with marketing details. A Notion page works too.
- Think of affiliate onboarding like product onboarding; the "aha" moment is their first commission.
- Ongoing activation: bonus structures and volume-based incentives, backlinks to their best content, occasionally paying for traffic to top-performing affiliate sites, sharing campaign wins in your newsletter, and promoting the program on social media to reach fans who didn't know it existed. He says 100 long-tail affiliates making a few sales each add up.

chunks.heading: Commission, CPA and sponsorship decisions
chunks.text:
- Commission versus flat fee depends on the brand, upsell ability and lifetime value.
- Best answer is often to offer both: revenue share or CPA.
- If revenue share, cap it at 12 months; retaining the customer is the brand's job.
- If CPA, he suggests something like the first three months of revenue. With a six-month lifetime value, paying three months works for both sides.
- He has seen programs pay up to 200% of first-month revenue, and a company paying up to $100 CPA on a $60 product, accepting the loss because of future upsells and lifetime value.
- Sponsorship rates: no fixed formula. With about 1,000 to 10,000 Instagram followers, he generally wouldn't sponsor and would stay in the affiliate program with free gifts. Above that, think in hundreds and thousands, scaling with size and engagement rate; rates vary a lot by niche (finance, travel, tech, B2B SaaS).
- To persuade advertisers who expect CPA-only: reframe budget from PPC (e.g. a few thousand dollars, he mentions $3,000), show affiliates' data on what they cost, name the first five partners and the expected sales.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts a panel (Adam Riemer, Lacy Thompson, Matt Fray) on AI in affiliate marketing. His own contributions are framing: AI is already here, hesitation is the main risk, and paying affiliates for appearing in LLM answers is an emerging model. Most of the substantive insight comes from the guests, not Dustin.

chunks.heading: Prediction: small, AI-run affiliate programs will beat big teams
chunks.text:
- Dustin's bold prediction (also voiced by Matt Fra, whom he echoes): "the next great affiliate program is not going to be built by the biggest team." It will be built by the smallest, most efficient team of AI experts within 18 months.
- A one-person program running AI will outrecruit a 10-person team running spreadsheets. "Headcount stops being the moat."
- He expects the days of huge affiliate teams to end: "small, nimble, and extremely profitable."
- AI is not a traffic channel like social, mobile, influencer or toolbars. It is a layer underneath everything: how partners get found, how work gets done, how buyers decide.
- He frames the industry as a "partnership operating system": affiliate is a pricing model that partners with every channel, not a channel itself.
- Winners "automate the work and elevate the judgment"; losers "automate the judgment and keep doing the work."

chunks.heading: Where affiliate value is moving: LLM visibility and flat fees
chunks.text:
- Publishers are losing click traffic to AI overviews and LLMs. A cited test showed hiding AI overviews raised organic clicks by almost 40% and cut zero-click searches by 35%.
- Publishers are already pivoting from chasing traffic to communicating the value they bring to brands, and pushing for flat-fee deals instead of CPC or CPA, because LLMs feed off their content.
- Dustin sees new payment models emerging. He cited a conversation with Mero about paying affiliates on LLM searches where the brand shows up, which he expects "is going to blow up."
- The panel's view of the mechanism: LLMs personalize results per user and source from trusted sites, authors and creators, so affiliates with trusted authors and creators are positioned to win information retrieval.
- Most LLM answers produce no clicks, so measurement lags. Visibility tools exist, and users often jump from an LLM to Google or Bing, which makes the influence partly visible.
- Local businesses win in LLMs the same way they won in SEO: real reviews (Yelp, Google), testimonials, content and inbound links. "Go be a good business and the LLM will pick you up."

chunks.heading: Attribution, incrementality and fraud
chunks.text:
- The real long-term threat is last-click thinking. Affiliate gets bucketed with paid search and paid social, yet partnerships that add the most incremental value rarely get last-click credit.
- Brands refusing to pay for what they "can't measure" will kill the ecosystem. Example from an agency audit: a program that put branded paid search above affiliates and refused to pay partners on branded-search clicks.
- Attribution will likely improve as LLM platforms monetize and want to show sponsors results (source=chatgpt on outbound clicks, Shopify integrations). The open question is incentive: platforms grade their own homework.
- On fraud and toolbar scandals, he agrees with the panel: if the last click gets the money, people will game the last click. Programs must be actively managed with expert judgment and tools, not set and forgotten.

chunks.heading: Keep human judgment in the loop
chunks.text:
- Volume is not the key; judgment is. Check whether a human reviewed the content, the outreach and the attribution rules.
- Self-driving analogy: AI is cruise control and cooled seats, but he still wants to "feel the road."
- Don't send AI-written outreach or content blindly. Panel consensus: audiences, especially younger ones, bounce from obviously AI-written pages and partners will be burned by sloppy AI replies.
- Vibe-coded site changes can open security holes (form-to-system leaks, injections). Have a developer or expert check them.

chunks.heading: What AI frees affiliate managers to do
chunks.text:
- Affiliate managers spend an estimated 95% of their time pulling reports and logging into systems, leaving little for strategy and relationships. AI should reclaim that time for human work: strategy, client communication, partner relationships.
- His company's tool Alfie (XP Flow) automates affiliate recruitment and outreach: identifying niche content partners, sending over 1,000 outreach emails a month automatically, saving managers an average of 14 hours a week without adding headcount.
- Practical setups from the panel: a morning agent that briefs you from email, calendar and call notes and drafts follow-ups (never sent unreviewed); a Notion workspace connected to frontier models; sub-GPTs per partner that store their repeat questions; local-drive agents that run gap analysis.

chunks.heading: Monthly action items for program managers
chunks.text:
- Do: connect AI to your own tools (email, calendar, call transcripts, workspace) so it handles reporting and admin.
- Do: set up background monitoring to flag affiliates whose traffic dropped, pages that were removed, whether your merchant ID is still in their source code, and what top performers have in common.
- Do: clear data use with legal and prefer the local desktop version over the web version for security.
- Stop: communicating blatantly with AI. Stop writing all content with AI only; people want to know who the real people are.
- Stop: treating affiliate as set-and-forget last-click.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts a panel with affiliate operators from HubSpot/Instantly, an affiliate agency and a tracking platform. His own contributions: audit before recruiting, respond fast to partner interest, build co-branded landing pages, coach partners, treat affiliate types differently, and pitch internally for test budget.

chunks.heading: Audit and activate before you recruit
chunks.text:
- Dustin hosts the panel (Nancy Harnett, Victor Moen, Ed Seballos); his own contributions are the framing and the emphasis on practical, tested advice. He says B2B affiliate is among "the most scalable and lowest cost acquisition channels in the entire marketing mix."
- He agrees that auditing an existing program is "an absolute must" before jumping into recruitment. Recruitment is necessary and you want early traction, but the audit comes first.
- Vanity metrics such as partner count are not the goal. He backs the panel's view that the aim is revenue-driving partners, not a big roster.

chunks.heading: Recruitment: volume, persistence and fast response
chunks.text:
- Dustin highlights a four-email drip campaign he received from Victor's team as a model of good recruitment outreach. He liked three things:
  - It presents what the possibility is.
  - It gives a time frame to get into an exclusive opportunity.
  - It ends with a question aimed at getting him on a call.
- He was "really impressed by the persistence" of that sequence. He says recruitment is a volume game, and that a 10% response rate is excellent: "10% is a good response rate" given he gets a dozen outreach emails a day as a small-time B2B affiliate.
- He sees recruitment as one of the biggest time drains for affiliate managers. A tool that sends over 1,000 outreach emails a month automatically can save an average of 14 hours per week (this is the sponsor's claim, Alfie by Everflow, which he promotes).
- When an affiliate replies and asks for a call, jump on it immediately. He shared a bad example: a brand replied "to save us both time on a call... we're not looking for paid placements at the moment." He calls this "a very bad way to respond to an email to an affiliate" and says to take the call with "no questions asked."
- He works by talking to people directly. His own preference is a 15-minute call to confirm the audience, product and offer fit before committing.

chunks.heading: Conversion rate and co-branded landing pages
chunks.text:
- Optimizing the conversion rate for your affiliates is "absolutely optimal" for the program.
- Build partners a co-branded landing page: "that's going to convert better and you're going to be in a much better spot."

chunks.heading: Different affiliates sit at different funnel stages
chunks.text:
- Dustin stresses that every affiliate is a little different and "treating them all the same way is the wrong answer."
- Some affiliates are top of funnel and some are bottom. Find the right way to pay each and give top-of-funnel partners the credit they deserve, same as bottom-of-funnel ones.
- Attribution and commission structure get complicated, so he recommends bringing in experienced people to build the commission structure properly.
- He notes Everflow is extremely helpful for building out commission structure: a brand can come with an idea and the team will slow it down and ask what will actually appeal to the affiliates being targeted.

chunks.heading: Coaching affiliates is underrated
chunks.text:
- He calls coaching "a big part of affiliate management that people don't recognize how important it is."
- Spending time with affiliates is "extraordinarily valuable" to them and to the program, provided it is done the right way.

chunks.heading: Paying creators who want upfront fees (his take as a creator)
chunks.text:
- Dustin's advice to a brand facing creators who want flat fees instead of pure revenue share: beg for an exploration budget from your team.
- Pitch it internally with a concrete number, for example "just give me $2,000 a month to check this out."
- He argues a performance deal alone is slow with creators: "if you pay me up front I am much more likely to get things done immediately" than "I'll get to it when I can."
- Frame the proposition to leadership as more content, faster, than a performance-only structure would deliver.

chunks.heading: Practical filters on the audience's questions
chunks.text:
- On the stat that only 16% of affiliates run B2B programs, Dustin said he wasn't sure of the source and couldn't confirm it, though it "sounds right." He treats the thin B2B pool as a reason to seek out the right partners rather than a barrier.
- He fields audience questions on auditing dormant partners and tracking events in the funnel, and says tracking all events across the affiliate journey is the real goal.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes hosts Erica, who was thrown an affiliate program in 2020 and ended up running a huge budget by age 25. Dustin mainly frames the episode and endorses her points: don't fear looking stupid, ask for help and forgiveness, lean on community, and don't pretend you know everything. Most tactical advice is Erica's.

chunks.heading: Getting thrown an affiliate program and learning it fast
chunks.text:
Erica's story is the case study here, and Dustin frames it as common: many managers are handed an affiliate program with no background, or run a massive network as a one-person show.

- Erica was asked to take over affiliate at a startup in March 2020, with no prior knowledge. She read articles, watched YouTube, and listened to podcasts at the same time.
- Dustin points to acceleration Partners blog posts as a core resource (partner type definitions, CPA vs CPC, first click vs last click). She printed them into a binder.
- Her network rep at PepperJam gave her hour-long calls explaining how to find partners.
- Dustin's takeaway: you can bring a lot of value without knowing everything, and being willing to ask for help prevents many mistakes.

chunks.heading: Networking, asking questions, and not caring what people think
chunks.text:
The "subtle art of not giving a duck" theme is applied to fear of looking dumb. Dustin and Erica both argue the fear is mostly in your own head.

- Dustin says he has "no shame whatsoever" and doesn't mind feeling stupid when asking follow-up questions in communities.
- Erica's rule: if anyone thinks you're stupid for asking, shame on them, and you think about it more than they do.
- Her first question to a well-known community figure was the difference between coupon and loyalty partners. It felt scary then and is basic now.
- At conferences: walk up and say "I've seen you on LinkedIn, I like your work, nice to meet you."
- After about 70 episodes and growing branding, Dustin had 20+ strangers approach him at Affiliate Summit. He wants to be friends with and mentor exactly those people.
- He and Erica share an "ask forgiveness rather than permission" outlook, but not in your first three months at a company, to avoid getting fired over something ridiculous.

chunks.heading: Continued education: why veterans should keep learning
chunks.text:
Dustin describes a pattern in affiliate managers.

- At 2-3 years of experience, many feel they know everything and stop learning.
- By year six they see how little they knew at year three. By year 14 he still feels there is plenty he doesn't know, which is why he started a podcast and invites people smarter than him.
- Erica's current education mix: trial and error with data, learning from teammates on an agency team, impact.com's PXA course, webinars and podcasts.
- Dustin's own communities: MTech Record, his own community and inner circle, and the PMA. He calls community essential to continual learning and to not falling behind day to day.

chunks.heading: Running programs solo: organization, data, and confidence
chunks.text:
How an affiliate manager (AM) works on an island, using Erica's experience at TruthFinder, where she managed a roughly $5 million monthly affiliate budget at about 25 years old and six months into affiliate.

- **Organization drives efficiency.** She uses task management tools, notes, and spreadsheets, with daily, weekly, monthly, and quarterly task lists. Impact.com has a spreadsheet template that breaks out AM tasks by cadence, and a QBR template listing talking points for quarterly business reviews.
- **Data backs decisions.** She made a friend in the business intelligence director's team and used data to justify spend, for example backing a proposed spend into an implied CPA from existing conversion rates.
- **Confidence.** She had to remind herself she was in the seat on her qualifications rather than assume someone with a master's should be there. Dustin notes acting like you know what you're doing, and confidence in the program's vision, matters in the role.
- Dustin's observation of her: very efficient with a chill attitude, unlike many successful people in the industry who are neurotic. She was named employee of the year at a 100-person company at 25.

chunks.heading: Staying motivated and educating the business as an in-house AM
chunks.text:
- Erica's motivation is largely intrinsic: she takes pride in her work even though she doesn't "give a duck."
- Discouraged days usually signal she needs help with something, so she identifies it and asks. She used a 20-minute call feature with acceleration Partners account reps for questions.
- In-house, a large part of the job is educating higher-ups and advocating for affiliates. One bad actor in a program can make leadership hostile to every affiliate.
- Dustin's addition: AMs often work from home and are the only affiliate person at the company, so a community outlet (friends or virtual) is essential. Erica said MTech tends to surface network outages or updates before anyone else.

chunks.heading: Tools for partner research and recruitment
chunks.text:
- Erica's favorite tool is SimilarWeb. She uses it to find new partners, monitor where top affiliates send traffic, see what share goes to competitors, and catch who is bidding on branded keywords when they shouldn't be (compliance).
- Dustin notes that his own tool, AffiStash, integrates a SimilarWeb API, so users get the same stats in the tool for $97 a month, and that it is positioned as an easy way for agencies or brands to recruit affiliates.

chunks.heading: Getting value from conferences and defending "be valuable, not successful"
chunks.text:
- Erica's best conference connections are often unplanned: chatting next to someone ordering a drink at a Top Golf event, or at a women-in-affiliate meetup where she met a new partner who will drive traffic to her brand.
- She says she will stop whoever is walking by and say hi, and it always leads to a positive outcome. Dustin's summary: "just be nice to people, have a fun time, network."
- Defending her old LinkedIn post: "the goal is not to be successful, the goal is to be valuable. Once you're valuable, instead of chasing success it will attract itself to you." She still believes it, adding that you can be valuable without knowing everything and that success comes with time and hard work.
- Dustin's point on small voices: "a whole bunch of little old mes make up our whole affiliate community."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes (solo, guest no-show) walks through common affiliate manager hurdles gathered from LinkedIn responses: publisher education/activation, application overload and fraud, "lazy" affiliates, and finding long-term partnerships. His core fix is making education easy and paying for partners' time.

chunks.heading: Why affiliate partners don't activate, and how Dustin gets them moving
chunks.text:
- Dustin's core problem: an affiliate goes from one cold email to promoting a product with a big gap in between. They have no time to evaluate random products, so the manager has to bridge it.
- He says "making it as easy as possible for them to get the education" is essential.
- Free samples for physical products and free trials for SaaS let partners educate themselves.
- Short videos about what the product does help.
- A personalized video is better. Share your screen and show where your brand could fit on their site or in an existing YouTube video.
- This is his quickest route to activation.

chunks.heading: Paying for a partner's time
chunks.text:
- Dustin says money talks, because a publisher's time is valuable.
- Ask what an hour of their consulting costs. Buying an hour at $200 to $300 can be a good investment.
- Use the hour to ask how they would promote the product, how they would approach others, and what their expertise is.
- It builds loyalty and may lead to a real partnership.
- He has traditionally paid for these hours out of his own pocket.
- His order of operations: get information and promotion for free first, then offer sponsorship opportunities, and if the partner is out of budget, ask "can I buy an hour of your time, what does that cost?"
- He charges $200 an hour himself.
- Some people don't recognize their own hourly rate. His cheapest call was $25 an hour, and he'll happily pay $25 for an hour of someone's information.

chunks.heading: Handling too many low-quality and fraud applications
chunks.text:
- Dustin calls a high application volume "a good problem to have", because it means the program is doing something right.
- He says he enjoys going through applications every day, since there can be "real gold" in there.
- He cites a peer who reviews about 50 applications a day, even with filters.
- Auto-decline certain countries that traditionally have low affiliate value.
- Put a line in the decline message: if a mistake was made, reply to your email for a second look.
- Train a virtual assistant to review applications.
- Reviewing is 15 to 20 minutes a day, about one application per minute, and he says to shift your mindset to liking it.

chunks.heading: "Lazy" or unresponsive affiliates
chunks.text:
- Dustin says managers often don't recognize what affiliates go through with content calendars.
- Getting into a calendar means talking someone into pausing something else.
- A publisher with high traffic, high value and strong domain authority is not lazy, just not motivated enough.
- The fix is motivation: pay for their time, offer sponsorship, or buy an hour of consulting.
- He says "they are not lazy, you just have never been in their shoes."

chunks.heading: Finding long-term, consistent partnerships
chunks.text:
- If you can't find long-term partnerships, Dustin says you're likely not deep enough in content.
- Lists and rented traffic are flashes in the pan.
- Content affiliates matter, even the long-tail ones making one or two sales a month. A hundred of them make the difference.
- Finding content sites is a consistent battle.
- Joint ventures and list sharing can be powerful short term, but long-term value is in Google and SEO rankings.
- Tactic: use Semrush to find who ranks for your target keywords and reach out to them.

chunks.heading: Relationship building on calls
chunks.text:
- Dustin dislikes using a headset and microphone on one-on-one partner calls, because it takes away from the personal conversation.
- He says building a connection is an intricate part of being a good partner manager.
- He uses a mic for podcasts for audio quality but avoids it in one-on-one conversations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes hosts Adam Weiss, a publisher-side affiliate consultant, on Affiliate Nerdout. Weiss carries the consulting playbook; Howes contributes short remarks on network profile keywords, community value, and networks as a career entry point.

chunks.heading: Defining the publisher side as the underserved opportunity in affiliate
chunks.text:
- Adam Weiss's consultancy is built on a gap Dustin agrees with: many agencies manage advertiser programs and many technologies support advertisers, but the publisher side is "a little bit underserved."
- Dustin says he builds his courses to serve the do-it-yourself advertiser before they reach the agency level, and that he rarely hears of anyone servicing publishers.
- Newcomers to affiliate need a map of the space: whether to work with every network, what a sub-network is, which agency to call, and when to call an advertiser directly.
- A consultant with that map can speed up a publisher's entry into the space.

chunks.heading: Validating a consulting niche by calling people first
chunks.text:
- Adam's approach, which Dustin highlights as the way he found his niche: before launching, he called people he knew from his years at a network and described what he was thinking.
- He asked about their pain points and the problems they wanted solved, all on the publisher side.
- That feedback shaped the offering, and he says he is still "refining and tweaking" it years later.
- Starting simple also worked: he did not agonize over the company name or website. A friend told him to go get business and learn, and the main name criteria were an available domain and LLC name.

chunks.heading: Publisher consulting is more than affiliate revenue
chunks.text:
- Dustin and Adam frame publisher problems as three layers that must work in lockstep: the revenue piece (partnerships and economics), the product itself (content site or technology), and customer acquisition (traffic, readers, newsletter subscribers).
- Partnerships create no value without audience, so a consultant who fixes only the revenue stream is not enough.
- Dustin cites Adam Enfroy's approach: publish genuinely helpful content with organic links first so Google sees you as an authority, then monetize once page visits reach a certain level.
- Adam's principle, which Dustin endorses: focus on doing the right thing for the customer and let monetization follow. Non-monetized helpful links are fine.

chunks.heading: Sub-networks versus direct partnerships
chunks.text:
- Sub-networks (the Skimlinks and Sovrn type) give publishers an easy entry, with tens of thousands of potential partnerships and the fragmentation across networks aggregated for them.
- Fragmentation is the core publisher pain: an advertiser sets up on one network, but a publisher may need to join Impact, Rakuten, CJ, Awin and more.
- Rule of thumb: manage roughly your top 20% of partners directly, and let sub-networks cover the long tail, unless you have resources to run everything directly.
- Tools Dustin and Adam name for publishers: Affilimate, Trackonomics and FMTC.
- Dustin uses Geniuslink-style link management; his own affiliate links are standardized and redirect through dustinhowes.com/affiliate, and he stopped using Affluent's tool because of limits.

chunks.heading: Using AI and keywords in affiliate
chunks.text:
- Dustin's current publisher workflow: build content on high-volume, low-difficulty keywords, then look up "best [keyword]" lists from other bloggers and join the affiliate programs listed. He expects someone to build a better brand-matching product, possibly with AI.
- Adam's view, which Dustin engages with: AI can help networks surface partner recommendations from benchmarks of publishers that worked for similar advertisers, and help optimize economics.
- On the publisher side, AI can flag content gaps and stale posts for operational efficiency and margin, but not replace first-hand content.
- Dustin's tactical advice to advertisers: stuff relevant keywords into your network profile page, because publishers search networks by keyword and affiliate managers too often neglect this.

chunks.heading: Pitching and matching brands with publishers
chunks.text:
- Adam leads with goals rather than a publisher pitch: company goals, affiliate program goals, what is working, which publisher mix they want, and where they invest or don't (for example, coupon sites or influencers).
- Brands should likewise share who they are and what they stand for so there is alignment on messaging and values.
- Sometimes it is not a fit, and that is fine.
- Dustin says these basics are what he plugs in his course, since people with a couple of years of experience often forget them.

chunks.heading: Publisher landscape map and when affiliate is the right time
chunks.text:
- Dustin praises Adam's quarterly Performance Marketing publisher landscape: a visual map of publishers by category, which Dustin calls a one-of-a-kind resource.
- His use: when he lands a new client or job, he goes to it to build a hit list of potential affiliates.
- Adam's takeaway for advertisers: there is a lot of quality distribution available, and roughly 20% of advertisers are not in affiliate today.
- Advice on timing, from Adam: the right time is a recognizable brand with traffic seeking alternate monetization, or a funded startup with a growth plan. Put operational infrastructure in place before traffic arrives so you are not scrambling.
- On perfectionism, the advice Adam took from Mike McNerney: publish it, because "it's good."
- Dustin also stresses community: martech record's Slack, the PMA (he cites its $9.1 billion industry size figure) and conferences, where people make introductions and help each other.

chunks.heading: Why network jobs are a breeding ground for talent
chunks.text:
- Dustin's first industry job was at CJ, and it took him three positions and five interviews to get hired, since he had no industry expertise.
- Both agree networks are the interchange of the ecosystem: advertisers, publishers, tracking, payments, product feeds and reporting all pass through, giving a "30,000 foot view" that few other roles give.
- Alumni go on to brands, publishers and agencies, or start their own agencies.
- Dustin points newcomers to performancemarketingmanager.com, his online course on creating and scaling an affiliate program.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts Vic Giurgiu, who walks through AI tools for affiliate recruitment, cold email, fake follower detection and onboarding. Dustin's own contributions are short practical takes: use lookalike search to replicate winners, train the algorithm with thumbs up, keep the human relationship in partnerships, and stay focused on one product.

chunks.heading: Affiliate recruitment with AppyStash
chunks.text:
- Dustin and Vic Giurgiu (his business partner on AppyStash, which Vic builds) say the most time-consuming affiliate manager tasks are recruitment, sending emails, spotting fake followers and onboarding new partners.
- The recruitment workflow in AppyStash starts from a brand URL, which the tool turns into a list of potential affiliates and influencers. The brand's keywords, target audience and description are extracted automatically.
- AppyStash supports 10 platforms, including social platforms, and the AI Partner Finder takes just a partner type and a platform. Dustin's view is that this removes the need for separate keyword analysis or expensive SEO tools.
- The Lookalike feature finds more affiliates similar to a good one. Dustin says it is the feature he uses most: "I'm in there almost every day. If I find a good affiliate and I want to replicate it, that's the thing I use."
- Dustin says he spends a little extra time giving thumbs up to the results he wants, to train the algorithm toward similar results in future.

chunks.heading: Building a 150-lead YouTuber list in under five minutes
chunks.text:
- The "800 YouTubers" lead-gen list was built from repeated manual-search exports in AppyStash, using the YouTube search with keywords such as "best products for better sleep" and "sleep product review".
- The search tool allows multiple keywords at once, exclusion keywords and hashtags for social platforms.
- One search returned 150 results, all ranking for the target queries, which Dustin calls "really good quality publishers".
- The CSV export includes the source, contact example, URL, contact email and referral link.
- Referral-link types (Genius Link, ShareASale, Amazon links, Bitly) signal existing affiliate activity.
- Only emails that are public can be scraped, so sorting A to Z puts the leads with emails first and leaves the rest for manual outreach.
- Dustin's comparison: the usual pain with YouTubers is the number of clicks (and a CAPTCHA) needed to reach an email address, and this skips it. A list takes "literally under five minutes" to get to a CSV ready for outreach.

chunks.heading: Email outreach automation tools
chunks.text:
- Dustin and Vic point to Instantly and Smartlead for bulk affiliate email outreach. Instantly was used internally and "worked really well", and both are described as very affordable.
- Instantly allows AI-personalized icebreakers. The workflow: put each prospect's content example into a custom variable, then prompt a GPT model to compliment their video.
- Example icebreaker: "I saw you have a video about fast and efficient car chargers... I was just looking for one for my new car."
- The point of the approach is that it sounds far better than bulk "join my affiliate program" or "can you review this product" emails, because the pitch shows the creator's content helped you and offers them a chance to earn.

chunks.heading: Spotting fake followers with HypeAuditor
chunks.text:
- Vic's favorite tool for fake-follower detection is HypeAuditor, and he says fake followers are a big problem in influencer marketing. Its "check any influencer" feature is free.
- Engagement rate is the first signal, since it usually indicates suspicious follower activity, and HypeAuditor compares it to the industry average.
- Subscriber growth rate is the second. A big spike followed by much slower growth can mean bought followers or views, unless it was a genuinely viral video that can be checked.
- It also shows total video views and average views.
- AppyStash shows similar audience data (views, likes, audience interests), but Vic recommends running candidates through HypeAuditor for checking stats.

chunks.heading: Onboarding new affiliates
chunks.text:
- Vic suggests an onboarding email sequence for each new affiliate, and Dustin confirms that is standard practice. For email, Vic recommends MailerLite as super cheap and affordable, and Mailchimp for a more enterprise solution.
- Vic says to keep three things in mind: emails, onboarding materials and affiliate support.
- Boost Box (built by Ru from Australia) trains an AI chatbot on a program's materials, past work and policies. Affiliates ask it questions first and escalate to the affiliate manager or support team only if needed.
- This takes repetitive support emails off the manager's plate.
- Dustin's caveat: it sits "on that cusp of how much is too much automation", since the last thing partnership marketing should lose is the face-to-face relationship, but he finds its effectiveness valuable.

chunks.heading: Advice for young entrepreneurs
chunks.text:
- Dustin's view is that you should not work so hard that you burn out. He tells Vic to get life experiences and says he does not want him "living behind a computer", because you only get one childhood and one set of college years.
- Vic's tips, which Dustin endorses with "great points": outsource as much as possible, build a quality team, focus on growth over profitability early, and pay for help (social media, features) if the budget allows.
- Vic also advises learning the fundamentals of business from the start, taking breaks, traveling, and surrounding yourself with the right people, who may even work for little or nothing to be part of a bigger mission.
- AI lets a high-school student ship features, new products and bug fixes faster than would otherwise be possible while balancing school and work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts affiliate agency owner Ish and shares his own bar for choosing affiliate networks (flexible commissions, locking periods, two-tier), how product feeds now serve content affiliates, and how to staff affiliate management by pairing relationship and data skills.

chunks.heading: Network settings that matter for e-commerce programs
chunks.text:
Dustin's guest (not Dustin) did most of the talking on network setup, but Dustin endorses and adds the following requirements when choosing or configuring an affiliate network:

- **Flexible commissions.** "Anything that has a flat fee that you can't change is not a network for me." Coupon sites should earn much less than content sites, so commission must be adjustable per partner type.
- **Vanity code (voucher) tracking** is required to measure coupon-driven sales.
- **Flexible locking periods.** For native-ad buyers he trusts, he wants a 10-day lock instead of 30 days so they are paid faster.
- **Two-tier commissions.** He wants to recruit affiliates into a program and be paid in perpetuity on their activity, and to let affiliates invite other affiliates. He calls it "a big motivator" and says not every network supports it.
- **Multiple networks as a workaround.** He dislikes running several networks, but sometimes it is the solution: coupon sites on one network and content sites on a CPA model on another. He accepts some overlap and possible double commissions on a sale.

chunks.heading: Product feeds are an essential, not just for shopping sites
chunks.text:
Dustin says product feeds are making a comeback and are no longer only for comparison and shopping platforms.

- Content affiliates now use feeds to pull products and calls to action into articles.
- Tools like affiliate.com and Gizmo let affiliates build content from feeds, so a data feed with strong calls to action matters to them.
- YouTubers can put feed-powered links in video descriptions, which makes the call to action "so much hotter."
- His rule: he does not work with networks that lack product feed capability, because he finds it "super necessary in e-com."

chunks.heading: Where he stands on the affiliate-manager skill mix
chunks.text:
Dustin cut his teeth as an affiliate manager and says you should keep doing the hands-on work.

- If you are not working on strategy and technology yourself, "you shouldn't be qualified to be talking about it."
- He still recruits affiliates for the programs he runs himself rather than delegating all of it.
- He finds strategy the fun, easy part and the grunt work the hard part.
- He is a relationship and outreach person, not a data person ("analytics and me are not great"), so he pairs with a data specialist.
- His most successful program, WP Engine, was run with a partner (Oswin) who was the data head and who talked to executives about results, while Dustin did relationships and outreach.

chunks.heading: Eight types of affiliate manager and how to staff a team
chunks.text:
Dustin wrote a blog post breaking affiliate managers into eight types:

1. Relationship architects (people like him who are good at talking to people and likable)
2. Organizational types
3. Knowledge fountains
4. Problem solvers
5. Data heads
6. Strategists
7. Partner supporters
8. (He listed these as his categories; the transcript names seven explicitly in the list above.)

His staffing guidance:

- A good affiliate manager needs roughly four of these skills. Having all of them is rare.
- You do not have to be best at everything. Hire a complement: if you hire a relationship guru, also hire a data head to fill the gap.
- Pairing a relationship person with a data person makes "one really good affiliate manager."

chunks.heading: Hiring, outreach and gender observation
chunks.text:
- Dustin says that in his experience female affiliate managers are often better than male ones, and that if he were to hire another affiliate manager it would be a woman. His reasoning is that likability and building connections come easier.
- He has hired virtual assistants to do outreach on his behalf and bring in deals, and says female VAs consistently get better response rates.
- He notes only a finite number of men in the industry are good at the job, and he does not consider himself a very good affiliate manager overall, only strong in certain aspects.

chunks.heading: Training and documentation for agency teams
chunks.text:
- As an agency owner he says you must train everyone in "the ways that are working right now."
- Good documentation for turning a young marketing specialist into an affiliate manager is "an art."
- He has done this for years through his Performance Marketing Manager course.
- He says these skills develop over time and only through experience plus the right training.

chunks.heading: Boutique agencies and award shows
chunks.text:
- Dustin defines "boutique" as being dialed into what you do and serving clients well, and says it is not a negative regardless of size.
- He favors boutique agencies, saying they give "the most bang for your buck."
- He agrees with the guest's critique that awards are often not merit-based because small agencies doing strong work cannot afford entry fees.

chunks.heading: Sponsor and format notes
chunks.text:
- His show is "Affiliate Nerd Out," held Thursdays at noon on LinkedIn Live, and guests can apply at dustinhowes.com/nerd.
- He is recruiting partners for the brands he works with on the inflection platform, which he describes as personalized funnels for partnerships marketing aimed at health and wellness, with landing pages built for partners in minutes.
- His stated view of coupon sites: they are on the downtrend, and inflection only takes on clients that want content partners.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes hosts Adam Glazer of Partner Commerce on how B2B affiliate programs get built, from discovery to a go-to-market plan to partner personas. Most of the substance comes from the guest; Dustin's own contribution is framing on why B2B differs from B2C and where agencies get their edge.

chunks.heading: What B2B affiliate programs look like and how they differ from B2C
chunks.text:
Dustin's guest, Adam Glazer, runs Partner Commerce, an agency that works only with B2B advertisers.

- Dustin says B2B is an underserviced corner of affiliate marketing.
- He sends B2B leads to Adam's agency and lists it among his preferred agencies.
- B2B is not coupons, discounts, cash back or toolbars.
- B2C programs can be "robust" with 30-40 affiliates and a few big names, run by junior staff.
- B2B is a "much longer tail" of partner types, so it is more partner development and less classic affiliate marketing.
- Low-value coupon and cash-back partners are avoided in favor of high-value, incremental, net-new customers.
- Dustin notes that nobody searches coupon sites for which business to buy from, so the B2C coupon and loyalty game does not carry over.

chunks.heading: The onboarding game plan: discovery, go-to-market plan, implementation
chunks.text:
The first deliverable is a deep discovery phase that feeds a go-to-market plan.

**Discovery covers:**
- Who the customer is and what their buying journey looks like.
- The unit economics of the business.
- Any history with affiliate or partner marketing and what was learned.
- Other marketing channels, plus the KPIs and benchmarks that matter.
- Appetite for testing different payment models, including pay-for-play.

**The plan then defines:**
- A commission structure.
- Which partner personas to prioritize.
- What each partner type needs (discounting, co-branding) and the SLAs and requirements on both sides to deliver it.

**Timeline:**
- Planning takes 2-3 weeks.
- A technical spec and implementation take another 2-3 weeks.
- The program is live in market by about week 6, with a focus plan for the first 90 days.
- After launch the agency handles recruiting, onboarding, campaign activation, performance monitoring, platform operations, brand safety, affiliate support and application review.

chunks.heading: Aligning on commission structure and testing budget up front
chunks.text:
Dustin endorses locking down payment models before launch so deals don't bottleneck later.

- The default is a rev share, for example in year one.
- Some partners will require CPL or flat pay-for-placement, so agree in advance whether the brand will test those.
- Agree on when to test and how much budget to allocate, for example "three of these types of deals this quarter".
- Evaluate each deal through a calculator and proceed only at roughly 80% confidence that it backs into allowables.
- Early alignment lets the client communicate to leadership, finance, the web team and dev resources.
- Capabilities that can't ship at launch (such as a lead-referral form) go onto a strategic roadmap for Q2 or Q3.

chunks.heading: Platform choice
chunks.text:
- The agency is platform-agnostic but works mostly on impact.com, PartnerStack and Everflow, which it considers best-in-class for B2B.
- Processes, certifications and economies of scale are built around those three.
- Newer platforms carry unknowns about whether they can do what the leaders can.
- If a client has no preference, the agency audits and helps them evaluate.
- Dustin likes all three platforms and the people who work at them.

chunks.heading: B2B partner personas to recruit
chunks.text:
Adam calls the approach "modern partner marketing", centered on incrementality and quality. Segments include:

- **Influencers:** primarily YouTube and LinkedIn.
  - Macro influencers with millions of followers are an awareness play handled at brand level.
  - The affiliate focus is micro influencers, say 50,000 followers in a very specific niche; there are thousands of them, so it is a scale motion.
- **Agencies:** advisors and intermediaries who steer small-business decisions. Adam cites a Forrester figure of about 76%, nearly two-thirds, of small-business spend going through an intermediary.
- **Content sites:**
  - Endemic B2B publishers such as Forbes, Fit Small Business and small-business advice portals.
  - Niche blogs and trade publications aimed at a vertical (medical practices, restaurants) or at a solution (a site about expense management suits fintech clients).
- **Member groups:** banks, co-working communities, associations, chambers of commerce and gated networks, where members get perks and deals.
- **Creators:** course and template builders on Coursera, Udemy, Udacity or LinkedIn Learning, or in Notion or ClickUp.
  - Example: search Udemy for courses on scaling an HVAC business that recommend moving from spreadsheets to a CRM.
  - A creator might reach only 900 people a year, but those buyers paid $200-500, trust the creator and onboard with templates and a playbook, so they stick and succeed.

chunks.heading: Card-linked offers and influencer attribution
chunks.text:
**Card-linked offers (CLO):**
- Adam is enthusiastic about CLO and says it can reach "phenomenal" volume.
- Blocker one: clients want to incentivize net-new customers only, but many card offers can't exclude existing customers.
- Blocker two: large brands (Google, TikTok) see a perceived need to share customer data, which means legal and infosec review; smaller SaaS brands can move faster.

**Influencer attribution:**
- Influencers sit high in the funnel and often don't drive a direct click.
- A viewer may watch a YouTube video, then search Google or click a retargeting ad, so other channels win last-click credit.
- The fix is educating clients on how to evaluate these campaigns properly.

chunks.heading: Tools and operations
chunks.text:
- HubSpot serves as the agency's CRM, "the brain of our organization".
  - It tracks every partner and all correspondence, plus deal pipeline waterfalls.
  - Example list pull: influencers in Brazil in the HVAC vertical.
  - A team of about 30 can check whether a colleague is already talking to a partner before outreach.
- Notion handles project management, process documentation, a repository of AI hacks, task tracking and a client-facing portal.
- The agency also uses outbound email warm-up and campaign tools.
- Custom AI tools are used to query client program data and assist with recruiting.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin walks through his six-step process for building a list of 500 targeted affiliate partners for a brand. He shows how to mine competitor backlinks, ranking content and influencer databases, enrich contacts, and score and prioritize partners by persona.

chunks.heading: How Dustin builds a "Perfect Partner 500" affiliate recruitment list
chunks.text:
- **Six-step process per brand:** (1) learn the brand, (2) audit the existing program, (3) build partner personas, (4) run a gap analysis of which affiliates the program is missing, (5) build a list of 500 ideal targets with contact info, (6) write email templates for each persona.
- **Learning the brand:** the brand fills out a survey of about 30 minutes for someone on the marketing team. It covers the marketing campaigns that work for them.
- **Live demo brand:** Truly Free, organic non-toxic cleaning supplies (fabric softener, cleaning products). The top target is moms who are cautious about chemicals, so "mommy bloggers" are a priority. The brand already sends influencers a free product pack.
- **Where he sources targets:**
  - Competitor backlinks (Semrush for the backlinks, Afy Stash for contact enrichment).
  - Existing content that doesn't use affiliate links, found with manual YouTube searches.
  - Brand followers, competitor followers and existing customers, using Phantom Buster to pull followers from a competing brand's Instagram and Influencer Club to enrich them.
  - Content sites found by keyword.
