  - Influencers via Upfluence.
  - Podcasts via PodMatch.
  - His own lists of high-potential big publications from past work.

chunks.heading: Mining competitor backlinks for partners already on performance deals
chunks.text:
- In Semrush, he enters a competitor's URL and opens the Backlinks report.
- He filters to the "Sponsored" link type first. Sponsored links show the competitor is partnered with that site on some performance basis, so he can see which affiliate partners they work with.
- He downloads the list and takes the source URLs (his example from another client, Backbone: PC Gamer is a great fit).
- He pastes the domains, or uploads a CSV, into Afy Stash's bulk contact finder.
- Afy Stash returns roughly 5 to 10 contacts per company, with LinkedIn and email.
- He picks the right person (for example a writer or editor) and adds them to the list.
- A competitor with few backlinks and weak domain authority is a weak source. He moves on to find a better-established competitor, since low traffic means little to spy on.
- Competitor discovery tip: Semrush's organic competitors are "hit or miss". A plain Google search such as "[brand] competitor" and checking the first non-sponsored results works too.

chunks.heading: Finding content sites by ranking keywords
chunks.text:
- In Semrush's Keyword Magic Tool, he searches a keyword the brand would want to rank for (example: "organic cleaning supplies").
- He exports the first 100 ranking results to CSV and uploads it to Afy Stash to get contacts.
- He strips out results that aren't recruitable: Walmart, Amazon, YouTube, Target and similar. Anything already ranking and not a content partner is eliminated.
- He downloads the contacts as a CSV, or stars them to push them into the CRM.
- Afy Stash counts a credit for every contact downloaded.
- He also looks at the brand's organic keywords with the brand name removed, to see what the brand wants to rank for and is missing.

chunks.heading: Finding influencers with Upfluence
chunks.text:
- Dustin calls Upfluence "incredibly powerful" but "pretty expensive". He thinks it's about $500 a month for 500 credits, and says he could be wrong on that.
- Filters he uses:
  - Platform: Instagram.
  - Followers: 20,000 to 200,000.
  - Engagement rate: 2% as a baseline, higher if you want.
  - Keyword set as a must-have in their content (example: "safe cleaning products").
  - Show only creators with emails.
  - Country: United States.
- A keyword filter can cut millions of creators down to a handful, and with looser filters he could pick from hundreds or thousands.
- He likes the "area of expertise" filter because creators may still work on a performance basis with just gifting.
- Caveat: some creators are represented by agencies and are hard to land on a real sponsorship.
- Upfluence shows an estimated price range per creator. It's negotiable but gives a baseline.
- He reviews each profile, adds good fits to a selected list (for example a creator with a dryer ball in her content and 21,000 followers) and exports.
- The standard export has no emails; the email export is what he uses. Upfluence gives about 50 extra columns he doesn't need. He keeps URL, subscribers, views, engagement rate, engagement growth, price suggestions, blogs and visits.

chunks.heading: Scoring and prioritizing the list
chunks.text:
- He scores each prospect from 1 to 5 based on partner type, category fit, follower range of 20,000 to 200,000, and US location.
- Only 4s and 5s go on the sheet. A 3 won't make the list of 500.

chunks.heading: Partner personas and client alignment
chunks.text:
- He sorts partners into two top-level types: influencers and content sites.
- He doesn't work with coupon or loyalty sites. He is "strictly looking on content creators".
- Each type gets subcategories (for example gaming news, Minecraft influencers, toys), with an example of each.
- He takes the personas back to the client and asks whether they agree, which to pursue and how much time to spend on each.
- Prioritizing matters. Example: build 50 Minecraft influencers and only 20 toy influencers.
- For content sites, the list is what's already ranking online that the brand could be part of on a listicle. It includes the people at each company and their contact information.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A casual live show where Dustin Howes hosts affiliate industry friends in short guest slots. Most of the substance comes from guests; Dustin's own contributions are a help-first view of relationships, the idea that AI users (not AI itself) will take jobs, and his pitch for affiliate manager training.

chunks.heading: Affiliate Summit's evolution and where new affiliates get lost
chunks.text:
- Dustin asks long-time industry peers what Affiliate Summit was like in its early days versus now, and the answers shape his view of how the industry changed.
- Early on the industry networked through conference calls hosted by one company that had a conference line, with about 20-25 people on them.
- The first Affiliate Summit was roughly 150 people, one day to a day and a half, all panels in one room, with networking over lunch and dinner.
- Today the show is far bigger, and newer content producers and small affiliates get lost in "the sea of CPA networks."
- Dustin's takeaway: the relationships between merchants, agencies and newer publishers are where value sits, and communities like the PMA (Performance Marketing Association) and brunches at the show help fill that gap.

chunks.heading: Pitching PPC affiliates to merchants (no-risk positioning)
chunks.text:
- Dustin's guests pitch PPC affiliates to merchants as a risk-free channel, and he engages with and endorses the framing.
- The argument: if a merchant runs PPC in-house, they carry the risk of not knowing what they're doing and of spending money with no positive ROI.
- In the affiliate channel the merchant only pays commissions on actual sales, so they aren't fronting ad spend and the channel "should always be a positive ROI."
- Dustin's use: send merchants who want PPC to PPC publishers rather than having them front the media budget.

chunks.heading: Three topics the affiliate industry must level up on
chunks.text:
- Dustin draws out a guest's view of what is coming and treats it as the agenda for affiliate managers.
- Compliance: confirming partners are compliant and that it's tracked.
- AI and automation: conversational search (ChatGPT, Bard) now gives product recommendations, and the industry has to figure out how that is tracked and credited. Younger buyers may use comparison sites, blogs and newsletters less.
- Integration of affiliate with influencer and creator marketing: Gen Z and Gen Alpha lean on TikTok, Snapchat and video, and affiliate tracking hasn't yet figured out how to convert and attribute in those channels.
- Dustin's own stance on AI: "AI is not going to come and take our jobs as AMs, but the people that are using AI will." He frames the real risk as tracking, conversions and crediting contribution to a sale.

chunks.heading: Using ChatGPT for affiliate managers' prep and content
chunks.text:
- Dustin agrees ChatGPT is "magical" for content creation: brainstorming, drafting talking points and doing research.
- Meeting prep: if you run out of time before a meeting, ask for 10 bullet points on a brand's value propositions, its main competitors, or a publisher's audience.
- Campaign matching: ask it to match your campaigns to a particular brand and tell you which to pitch, so you arrive with a stronger, targeted offer.
- Caveat he endorses: you need someone who knows how to use it well.

chunks.heading: Impact's creator and affiliate platform and manager organization
chunks.text:
- Dustin discusses a platform that handles both affiliate and creator programs in one place, with a toggle between the two.
- The problem it solves: creators already sit inside affiliate programs but want things affiliates traditionally didn't get, like free products, referrals, flat rates and sponsorships.
- Organization tools he draws out and endorses for managing a big team: calendar discipline ("if it's not on the calendar it doesn't exist"), Gmail snooze and Slack reminders, Lattice for one-on-ones, shared Drive folders, and Wiki/Confluence/Seismic to document processes so people don't recreate the wheel.
- Managers should meet each person, including indirect reports, at least quarterly and keep notes in one centralized place tied to goals and feedback.

chunks.heading: Mentorship and "help first" as a career approach
chunks.text:
- Dustin describes his own approach, learned from a mentor, as "help others first": sit down with people and ask how you can support them.
- He asks every guest "how can I help you?" and treats helping as the default way to build relationships.
- He uses the show itself as a relationship tool: short five-minute guest conversations to spread the word about affiliate marketing, with guests invited via dustinhouse.com/nerd.
- His stated long-term goal is to move to the other side of the equation and be an affiliate full-time.

chunks.heading: Dustin's training offer for affiliate managers
chunks.text:
- Resources he points people to: dustinhouse.com and performancemarketingmanager.com.
- The Performance Marketing Manager course is about eight hours of training covering fundamentals and advanced tactics for growing affiliate programs.
- It includes coaching sessions with him and a hot seat to discuss your own program.
- Guarantee: affiliate channel growth "guaranteed or I'm going to give you your money back."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes interviews Robert Glazer (Acceleration Partners) on the evolution of partnership marketing, AI and the agency model, and career paths. Most insight is Glazer's; Dustin's own contributions are brief reflections on relationships, podcast side benefits, and course-selling difficulty.

chunks.heading: Partnership marketing is business development at scale
chunks.text:
- Dustin's guest, Robert Glazer, frames the industry as "business development supported by technology."
- Dustin's view of the opportunity: partnership marketing is business development at scale, which he calls a multi-trillion dollar market. The question is how to scale all the Business Development Partnerships in the world.
- The name "partnership marketing" is a change for the better. "Affiliate" is confused with "affinity" and implies a loose relationship.
- The term has also widened the tent to include influencer, B2B and other partnership types enabled by technology.

*Note: the opinions in this source are mostly Robert Glazer's; Dustin is the host and asks the questions.*

Because the source's substantive views belong to the guest, not Dustin, I'm cutting the output down to what Dustin himself says or clearly endorses.

chunks.heading: What Dustin says about his own path and podcast
chunks.text:
- Dustin built an affiliate marketing course after hearing a talk advocating it. He says six years later he wishes he had never done it, because "beating my head against the wall trying to get people to buy a product that they don't think they need" is hard.
- He started his podcast (this was episode 80 of it) to drum up business for his course and consulting.
- It turned into two benefits: educational upskilling for himself, and a large growth in his connections across the industry.
- He says it is very time consuming, and he is winding it down because he can't do that much content alongside everything else.
- He prefers to stay in his lane: "on the phones and talking with people" doing partnership development, not compliance.

chunks.heading: Dustin's view on where affiliate managers are headed
chunks.text:
- Dustin favors a partnership-first skill set: relationship building, recruiting, and open-the-door deal making.
- He is waiting for AI that takes a brand, lists every affiliate in a database that fits its exact niche, and reaches out with their contact information automatically.
- He notes Robert's point that this is machine learning rather than generative AI.
- He admires people who sustain long-running projects (Robert's 17 years at his agency, 330 podcast episodes, 425 newsletters) and asked how they stick with it.
- He also highlights John Labruto's move into a "director of affiliate marketing" title, and says that title is rarely seen in the industry.

chunks.heading: Publisher advice Dustin endorses: lead with passion, not monetization
chunks.text:
- Dustin agrees that the less you push a podcast, or any content effort, for other business goals, the more it helps.
- Robert's framing, which Dustin responds to as matching his own experience, is that successful publishers loved a topic (barbecues, cell phones) first and monetized after earning trust.
- Starting from "what do I get out of it" instead of "how do I give value" rarely works.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts creator Gigi Robinson, who explains how she pitches brands, negotiates paid sponsorships and why she avoids affiliate-only deals. Dustin's own contributions are brief: creators deserve pay, influencers sit at the top of the funnel, and recorded kickoff calls document scope.

chunks.heading: Gigi Robinson's creator-first view of paid partnerships vs. affiliate
chunks.text:
- Dustin hosts Gigi Robinson (speaker, creator-preneur, founder of Host of Influence) on "Affiliate Nerd Out". Gigi is the one making these points; Dustin's own contribution is framing influencers as top-of-funnel.
- Dustin agrees influencers sit at the top of the funnel for brand recognition and getting a customer in the door. Other affiliates act as "closers" who retarget and close the deal.
- His view is that every influencer and creator deserves to get paid for their time and effort, and that affiliate marketing can be unfair on that point.
- He flags that Gigi is not a fan of affiliate marketing and that this is fine with him. He wanted her perspective so affiliate managers can learn how creators think.
- Dustin promotes Inflection as the sponsor: personalized funnels that help influencers convert more, with co-branded landing pages, discount codes for the influencers, and a quote from them about why they like the product.

chunks.heading: Why many creators decline commission-only deals
chunks.text:
These are Gigi's arguments, which Dustin treats as a valuable creator perspective:

- Link clicks do not equal conversions. Hundreds or thousands of story link clicks may produce only a handful of purchases.
- Her example: five people buy a $45 Stanley bottle at a 3 to 5% commission, which does not compensate days or hours of production time or travel.
- Not every creator is a converter. Many share wins and never post links, so brands should check tracking data and know who they are targeting before pitching an affiliate deal.
- She only considers affiliate for high-ticket products aligned with her niche (air and water purifiers, tech she uses). She says fashion and home creators are where affiliate money is made.
- Dustin's takeaway for managers: match the deal type to the creator's niche and audience behavior.

chunks.heading: Hybrid models and the "Honeygate" risk
chunks.text:
- Dustin raises Honeygate, where the Honey browser extension is accused of taking last-click commissions from influencers who drove the sale.
- Gigi's response: this is a reason to value guaranteed paid partnerships over performance-only income.
- Hybrid models (flat fee plus affiliate) are good in principle, but she often sees flat fees of only a couple hundred dollars.
- She describes agencies that boost a creator's organic content containing affiliate links and split the income with the creator 70/30, 60/40 or 50/50. This suits hardware or fashion creators, not her.

chunks.heading: How brands should approach creators
chunks.text:
Answering Dustin's final question for affiliate managers, Gigi's guidance, which he summarizes as "budget and creative freedom":

- Lead with budget. A couple thousand dollars is enough to build something productive.
- Let the creator pitch the idea. Her example: telling her own story of using Squarespace since age 10 and how she built her business on it, tied to a product launch, rather than reading a script.
- Scripted ads perform worse because audiences realize it is just an ad. Some creators now tell audiences "I have an ad coming, please engage" so they can keep creating.
- Collaborate on ideas that align with the creator and comply with FTC guidelines.

chunks.heading: Running brand deals smoothly (creator workflow)
chunks.text:
- Gigi works inbound and outbound deals the same way and says it makes no difference; what matters is reaching the negotiation stage.
- Hold a Zoom call before production to align on the brief and prevent endless back-and-forth.
- Dustin's addition: record the call and keep notes as proof of what was agreed if the brand later asks for changes.
- Bake in edit clauses limiting revisions to one or two rounds.
- Creators are not commercial producers with one shot on location, and brands should not assume anything can be redone on a whim.

chunks.heading: Storytelling and authenticity framework
chunks.text:
- Gigi's background in fine arts taught her "show, don't tell". She defines authenticity as transparent storytelling and vulnerability, not just posting outfits of the day.
- Use a hook, know the target audience, and choose what resonates (photo, video, headline). Put the detail in the caption.
- She says roughly 94% of creators earn under $100,000 a year, which is why many take deals for the money.
- Her stance: the creator should use the product and give an authentic review. She focuses on long-term brand building rather than going viral.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes interviews the CEO of TrackDesk about hidden ceilings in affiliate platform pricing. His framing: "unlimited" on a pricing page is a hook, and click caps, contact-sales walls and overages are where growing programs get burned. Most substance comes from the guest; Dustin's contribution is the buyer's checklist.

chunks.heading: What "unlimited" means at Trackdesk
chunks.text:
- Dustin raised a concern from his own experience: he has "been burned by this before" in affiliate programs where "unlimited" on a pricing page didn't mean unlimited.
- He frames the buyer's job as reading the small print behind the "unlimited" hook and asking vendors to state on the record where the ceiling is.
- The question he wants answered before signing with any vendor, Trackdesk included: what happens to your bill once the program starts producing sales?
- The ceilings he names as common: a click cap, a "contact sales" wall, or a traffic spike that turns into a support ticket.
- Trackdesk's stated position (from its CEO Martin, whom Dustin interviewed): no fees on affiliates, transactions or conversions. The one limit is clicks, set by default at 20 times the closest competitor's, and the smallest plan carries that same default.

chunks.heading: Why click-based pricing hurts low-value traffic verticals
chunks.text:
- Dustin's point of view as an operator: click caps and overage charges matter most in verticals where a click is worth a few cents, not $10-15.
- If overage fees per click approach what the network earns per click, a network owner ends up asking affiliates to stop sending traffic. That is the failure mode he wants buyers to screen for.
- The questions he asks any vendor:
  - Where exactly does "unlimited" end (clicks, contacts, support)?
  - What does the bill do when a program does well?
  - Why is a platform charging more when the program succeeds?
- Martin's answer, which Dustin accepted as plausible: old click-based pricing dates from when servers were costly and software was built 15-20 years ago. A platform rebuilt from scratch to handle billions of daily clicks can carry healthy margins without per-click overages.

chunks.heading: Vetting a vendor's handling of traffic spikes
chunks.text:
- Dustin tests vendors with a concrete scenario: an affiliate "blows up" overnight and sends 100,000 clicks. He asks whether anything breaks and whether the bill goes up.
- What he wants to hear is a process, not just capacity:
  - Someone monitors volume around the clock across time zones.
  - The vendor contacts you on your preferred channel (Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack) and decides with you whether to keep the traffic or block it.
  - Fraud signals are checked, such as conversions firing milliseconds after the click.
  - Because the vendor serves many customers sharing the same affiliates, it can warn you when a traffic source is behaving badly elsewhere too.
- He values this because forced or fraudulent clicks happen, and not every network will listen when you ask to reverse them.

chunks.heading: Evaluating postback setup and AI features
chunks.text:
- Dustin calls postbacks the "scary" part of the affiliate space, from his experience as both an affiliate manager and an affiliate.
- The Trackdesk feature he highlighted: an AI agent that builds postbacks. You tell it who you are connecting with and send a URL, and it returns a URL to pass over Telegram, WhatsApp or whichever channel you use with the advertiser.
- The business case, as relayed in the interview: larger networks employ full-time staff just to set up postbacks between affiliates, networks and advertisers. Automating this frees managers to spend time with affiliates rather than with dev and tech teams.
- Dustin's own view is that the value of affiliate management is relationship time with partners, so he rates tools that remove technical busywork.

chunks.heading: Criteria for choosing affiliate software
chunks.text:
- Dustin asked the guest for the deciding factors and treats them as a checklist for buyers. The three offered:
  - Support where the customer already works, with no extra charge for being in your Slack or Telegram.
  - Reliability: nothing breaks during traffic spikes and there is no downtime.
  - Features and AI readiness: over 300 features launched in a year, and chat-based control of the platform (sending affiliate links, adjusting offers, setting postbacks) rather than read-only reporting.
- Dustin noted that he plans to run his own program on the platform and share the experience, so he treats the vendor's claims as something to be tested rather than taken on faith.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts a panel on the "constellation strategy": pairing influencer reach with affiliate retargeting and measuring publisher-level incrementality. His own contribution is mostly framing and questions; the substantive tactics come from the panelists (Kim Murray, Annie Laro, Tom Wthbone).

chunks.heading: The constellation strategy: aligning influencer and affiliate along the purchase path
chunks.text:
Dustin hosts this panel, and his own framing is that influencer buzz alone isn't enough and affiliate conversions are increasingly scrutinized. He presents the "constellation strategy" (a concept from panelist Kim Murray) as a way to align influencer content distribution with affiliate retargeting and close the loop with data-based performance.

- Brands need measurable action, a scalable approach to growth, and a way to move customers down the funnel predictably.
- He wants to track incrementality and ROAS at the publisher level.
- He frames the aim as helping brands scale affiliate and influencer programs creatively, especially in the early stages of growth.

chunks.heading: Incrementality as the real question in partnerships
chunks.text:
Dustin introduces incrementality as a buzzword the panel unpacks, asking why it matters "more now than ever." He pushes the point that the lack of standardized data hurts publishers too.

- He notes there is a huge gap in a standardized way of delivering data to publishers so they can optimize.
- If publishers provide brand growth and recognition but can't see the data, it is harder to optimize toward that and quantify it.
- He points out that affiliate tracking solutions are "not all built the same": some give far more dynamic visibility into what happens in the funnel, and asks what gaps most networks are missing.

chunks.heading: Where the funnel measurement breaks
chunks.text:
Dustin probes where attribution fails and where each partner type sits in the customer journey.

- He asks how a major media publisher (USA Today) views its role from awareness to conversion.
- He asks how influencer content can "actually convert or play a role in driving performance," since many brands treat influencer as purely top-of-funnel.
- He asks what top-of-funnel strategies help close on the funnel, and what tools give merchants insight into traction through each stage.
- He observes that the data partner-level tools collect also lets agencies tailor campaigns for new brands to the part of the funnel where they find value.

chunks.heading: Cookie windows, budget caps and "too successful" campaigns
chunks.text:
Dustin raises tough practical objections and relays audience questions.

- On cookie windows, he relays a viewer question that extending tracking beyond the standard 30-day window would help surface publishers driving high-quality upper-funnel traffic. He adds the brand-side counterpoint: a longer duration means paying partners more, since internal email and retargeting campaigns still have to pay out the affiliate.
- He asks whether a publisher would avoid a brand with a 10-day cookie versus one with 90 days.
- On budget caps, he calls it "ludicrous talk" when brands say a campaign is too successful and want to stop it, because "it's on performance." He asks how to respond when brands say they need to halt campaigns.
- He asks about vanity or closing coupons: whether publishers request a closing coupon when creating content with brands.

chunks.heading: Content, boosting and CPC
chunks.text:
Dustin steers the discussion to tactics that are hot in the space.

- He asks whether boosting influencer posts that make great content has good value.
- He highlights CPC as "super hot" right now, with more and more affiliates adopting the model and finding value, and asks how premium editorial placements are evolving as brands want more measurable ROI, ROAS and incrementality.
- He names Linkby, Beehiiv and Goloot (as he describes them, "super hot right now") among the tools in that space.

chunks.heading: Practical close: getting started and unifying programs
chunks.text:
For brands under eight figures, Dustin asks for low-lift, high-impact tactics to scale affiliate and influencer programs. He closes by asking what to do first tomorrow if influencer and affiliate are run separately.

- He asks Kim about the tactic specifically for sub-eight-figure brands.
- He asks the panel for the single first step to unify a split affiliate/influencer approach.
- He sponsors the session with Inflection, a tracking solution he describes as evolving affiliate tracking toward personalization and conversion optimization. He cites brands like Ring, Backbone and Power Plate, and says a brand manager can build a fully customized landing page "in less than 10 minutes" that tells the influencer's story to lift conversion rate.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes hosts Joe Campanella of Complyy on AI-driven FTC compliance monitoring for affiliate programs. Dustin's own points are short: compliance gets ignored until something breaks, monitoring gets exponentially harder as programs scale, and affiliate managers should automate it rather than do it by hand.

chunks.heading: Why affiliate compliance monitoring matters for brands
chunks.text:
Dustin hosted Joe Campanella, CEO of Comply, for an "Affiliate Nerd Out" SaaS review. Dustin's first job in the industry was working compliance at CJ, over 15 years ago. He notes that affiliate compliance "is usually ignored until something actually breaks." He frames the core idea this way:

- Affiliates are an extension of the brand's marketing and sales team.
- The brand is ultimately held responsible for what affiliates say, not the affiliate.
- Most programs vet affiliates before onboarding but do little ongoing monitoring.
- Manually checking even a couple hundred affiliates' social accounts is too time consuming for affiliate managers.

chunks.heading: Where compliance risk actually sits
chunks.text:
Dustin treats compliance as more than disclosures and cleanup. The risk is in what is being said, and the FTC looks at the intent of the claim.

- Tracking links and gaming of the system are separate issues from what can get a brand sued.
- Implied earnings claims count: suggesting a product lets people "make money online" or generate a set revenue amount is a potential earnings claim.
- Health claims need substantiation: a claim like "reduce wrinkles by 22%" needs a study or evidence behind it.
- Express performance claims such as "guarantees results" are not allowed.
- False scarcity ("only five spots remaining today") is a violation.
- Trigger words the FTC watches for include "step by step" and "easy." Combined with a line like "so easy even a 5-year-old can follow," they become a problem.
- The point of tooling is to mitigate risk, since a business can never remove it fully.

chunks.heading: How an affiliate compliance monitoring workflow runs
chunks.text:
The platform Dustin reviewed (Comply's ACM) works as follows:

1. Upload the affiliate list, including each affiliate's referring URL.
2. Add brand name, primary website, YouTube and TikTok channels, and custom brand keywords.
3. The tool crawls the web, social accounts, YouTube videos, websites and sales pages for each affiliate.
4. It scores each piece of content out of 100 (the demo showed 44/100) and flags violations in red.
5. It tracks original versus current score and trends over time in an alert center.
6. It generates a PDF report listing each warning, why it is a violation and how to fix it.

Dustin's takeaway for affiliate managers: this saves hours of manual review and turns monitoring into something that runs continuously.

chunks.heading: Automating affiliate outreach when a violation is found
chunks.text:
The tool lets a brand act on violations without manual follow-up:

- One-touch email to the affiliate, with the PDF report attached.
- Reusable email templates, created from several factors.
- Automation settings: scan weekly, every two weeks or monthly.
- Automatic emails when a warning or violation triggers, with the PDF optional.
- Exclusion of select affiliates, such as your top five, from automated outreach.
- Monitoring of paid ads to catch affiliates bidding on trademark or brand keyword terms.

chunks.heading: When to start compliance, and what onboarding looks like
chunks.text:
- Dustin asked whether a brand needs to reach a certain size first. The answer given: start now.
- The FTC can look back three years, so a brand doing $500,000 a year today can be investigated for earlier periods when it assumed it was under the radar.
- The FTC has gone after small companies for $22,000 and large ones for hundreds of millions.
- Cost of an investigation, from Joe's own experience at a digital publishing company: multiple millions in fines and legal fees, plus time shut down.
- Onboarding: about a week from signed agreement to use, 15-25 minutes of account setup, then alerts appear after 24-48 hours of crawling across Facebook, TikTok, Instagram and LinkedIn.
- Follow-up: an onboarding call, a check-in a couple of weeks later, then roughly monthly touch points.
- Dustin's own advice to affiliate managers: it is never a bad time to start monitoring, since disclosure monitoring gets harder as a program grows.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin interviews Bob Sparkins of Leadpages on moving from a flat 30% lifetime commission to a performance-based tier. Dustin's own takeaways cover keeping offers competitive, explaining complex structures simply, why rev share reduces fraud versus CPA, and how to put yourself in affiliates' shoes.

chunks.heading: Commission structure: performance-based tiers that reward ongoing engagement
chunks.text:
Bob Sparkins (Leadpages) describes a restructure Dustin endorses and teaches as a model for SaaS programs.

- Old structure: a flat 30% lifetime commission. Problem: affiliates who promoted in 2014-2015 stopped promoting, moved to competitors, and still received checks.
- New structure: 10% base rate, 40% if the affiliate brings at least $49 in new sales in a rolling 30-day window, and 50% for super affiliates above $3,000 in new sales in 30 days. The higher rate applies to renewals as well as new accounts.
- The qualifier is based on new sales, so affiliates must keep engaging to hold the higher tier.
- Two goals when setting commissions: attractive enough to get people out of bed, and profitable enough to protect cash flow.
- Dustin's take: a commission structure that is hard to understand needs a short explainer video in the first onboarding email.

chunks.heading: Why lifetime value and no CPA
chunks.text:
- Dustin and Bob favor rev share with retention over upfront CPA for quality: affiliates have to bring customers who renew into year two and three.
- Leadpages offers annual plans and pays within about five weeks (sales in one month are paid by the 13th of the next).
- CPA carries fraud risk. Dustin: if an affiliate gets a $200 payout and only has to pay $30 for a subscription, "they're going to do that all day long until you catch them."
- Rev share lowers fraud risk, because self-submitted sales at 40% don't make sense logistically.
- To answer partners who ask for CPA, show them lifetime value: average months retained times the 40% tier shows they can earn several times a flat CPA.

chunks.heading: Changing a program: communicate and gather feedback
chunks.text:
- Before the change, Leadpages surveyed top affiliates by email, group chat and one-on-ones. Some said they were out, some all in. Expect to lose some and gain others.
- Give several months of lead time and over-communicate the deadlines and effective dates.
- Dustin: asking for feedback makes affiliates feel heard and creates more interaction with partners.
- Dustin's warning: keeping a commission structure stale is one of the worst things you can do, since competitors change payouts constantly.

chunks.heading: Ideal affiliate and understanding their side
chunks.text:
- Best partners for Leadpages teach audiences how to do business online: course creators, workshop and live-event hosts, and coaches who build the tool into a module ("go get your leadpages account, then your email provider").
- Other fits: YouTubers who showcase use cases and PPC affiliates who know the math, but the focus is course creators.
- Dustin's advice: build your own landing page and try being an affiliate yourself so you can empathize with partners and improve outreach.
- Use varied incentives, since different people respond to different rewards.

chunks.heading: Recognition and engagement
chunks.text:
- About 90-95% of Leadpages affiliate revenue comes from the top 5-10% of affiliates.
- Leadpages sends periodic leaderboards (a top 15 for the quarter) mainly to acknowledge and thank top performers rather than run contests.
- After a top affiliate asked for a badge, Leadpages created quarterly badges: number one, top ten, and top one percent. This also incentivizes those outside the group.
- Dustin likes leaderboards because affiliates are competitive and want to know where they rank. He had never considered badges but found the idea appealing.
- Leadpages has run roundtables but no in-person events yet, which Bob calls a shortcoming.

chunks.heading: Migrating affiliate platforms
chunks.text:
- Bob's first ten checklist items: don't do it unless you have substantial reasons. Leadpages outgrew a platform built around CPA and e-commerce and moved to PartnerStack for a cleaner dashboard and support for the commission structure.
- Give about six months' notice and explain why.
- Make sure the new platform can import historical data and referrals so no one is lost.
- Run both programs in parallel (Leadpages ran about seven months, paying both platforms' fees) and send private outreach to affiliates still sending traffic to old links.
- Always use a redirect (such as Pretty Links) instead of raw affiliate links, so links can be changed in one place when programs move.
- Dustin's view: a migration pauses growth, and most of your time goes to begging people to move over; affiliates don't love change.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin hosts Get Response's affiliate head on B2B partner recruitment and migration off an in-house program. His own contributions are brief: judge affiliate networks by reachable partners, not vanity counts, raise experimental budget early, and let product features power partner landing pages.

chunks.heading: Evaluating an inherited affiliate program
chunks.text:
- Dustin's guest (Erica) starts with a look "under the hood": program size, partner quality, where partners came from, and how new partners get in.
- She defines health as "sales active", not email-responsive. Affiliates are busy, so the test is whether they consistently publish content and drive sales.
- A big roster of inactive partners is a weak program; she saw that at Get Response as the opportunity.
- On arrival she sent a few intro emails to build legitimacy, promised no changes that would hurt existing partners' commissions, and applied any changes to new partners only.

chunks.heading: Choosing and migrating from an in-house program to a network
chunks.text:
- She made an external platform a condition of taking the job, rather than inheriting an in-house tracking setup.
- She chose PartnerStack over Impact for B2B because of its network (about 18,000 affiliates and partners) and because "for B2B, I find that everyone is on PartnerStack or at least most of the best ones." Impact has more reach for B2C.
- Migration was for new partners only; legacy partners could opt in to the new commission structure but weren't forced.
- Main work was internal education for leadership and developer work on the integration, with her as liaison to the platform. Rollout took about eight weeks.
- Lesson: she wishes she had asked in the interview for budget for non-traditional or experimental deals (sponsorships, hybrids).

chunks.heading: Recruiting inside a network marketplace
chunks.text:
- She uses the network's weekly email allotment and maxes it out every week.
- She filters by region (for example US, Germany, Poland), and uses the platform's AI recommendations of relevant partners.
- Result: roughly a 15% join rate from invites sent, which she attributes to network members being quality people who understand the space.
- Tooling: PartnerStack discovery/recruitment heavily; Conneto to find publishers writing about the brand and its competitors (a prompt to reach out and say "we're here too, and here's why we're different").

chunks.heading: Recruiting outside the network
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn is the main channel for off-network outreach; many publishers aren't on it, but influencers increasingly are.
- Passion Fruit is used to connect with influencers, though influencers are a small part of the program.
- About 90% of recruiting comes from the PartnerStack network.
- She tailors recruiting to company campaigns: for a "simplify your tech stack" promotion, she targets writers on that topic and consultants who simplify tech stacks.
- Campaign activation includes an ebook, landing pages for partners, and PPC alongside the affiliate push.

chunks.heading: Outreach message and commission terms
chunks.text:
- Principle: "be the easiest person for people to work with." Make the email clear so partners don't have to decipher it.
- She states the commission openly (40% for 12 months, going up from there) instead of gatekeeping, with a join-now button and links to content resources.
- She disagrees with "take it or leave it" programs: that doesn't work in 2025, and managers need flexibility.

chunks.heading: Negotiating CPA, hybrid and sponsorship deals
chunks.text:
- Every negotiation is backed by data. She sets a target CPA (example: $250), takes the partner's traffic and conversion numbers plus her own conversion rate, and sees whether she can back into the target.
- If the math lands near $1,000 instead, she declines.
- She has done a few CPA/CPL deals and works with leadership on guardrails so she can say yes quickly.
- Trend: influencers who asked "$5,000 for a video, no questions asked" a few years ago are now open to hybrid structures and video packages.

chunks.heading: Landing pages, coupons and trends
chunks.text:
- Landing pages work when they echo the content that sent the visitor ("you read about us on so-and-so's blog, here are the main points, start a free trial"). She did more of this at previous roles; at Get Response bandwidth limits it, as a one-person team.
- Coupons stay in the program for brand reasons, but they drive few conversions and her biggest affiliates aren't coupon sites. She prefers individual promo codes (for example 15% to help close one affiliate's audience).
- She is a believer in Cart-level/CLO-style loyalty offers when done right, citing a B2B client success at her agency (via Cartlytics).
- 2025 trend: everyone is an "AI expert" with an AI blog or newsletter, so she is deciding whether to be listed everywhere or be selective. No standout AI-guru partner yet.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes, an affiliate manager and course creator, shares what he teaches about running affiliate programs and being a successful affiliate. Core ideas: relationship-first partner management, focus on one strength before expanding, email as the cheapest conversion channel, and embracing AI while editing it with your own voice.

chunks.heading: Background and path into affiliate marketing
chunks.text:
- Dustin spent six years in the Marine Corps, then college (psychology degree), then worked as a poker dealer and a professional poker player for a year before going "dead broke."
- His first affiliate job was in the fraud department at Commission Junction (CJ). Poker's fraud awareness, Marine Corps discipline and the psychology degree made it the best fit when he had zero affiliate experience.
- Fraud work let him audit how affiliates making six and seven figures operated, including "the really dirty parts of affiliate marketing." That gave him a sharp eye for fraud when later running merchant programs.
- That led to roles in sales and managing programs for merchants. He has worked for networks, agencies, merchants and publishers, and now owns his own publications, agency and brands, with 14 years in the industry.
- He worked at WP Engine (hosting) and at Volusion before it.

chunks.heading: Why he built an affiliate management course and community
chunks.text:
- At WP Engine the program was doing well, but he wanted to get better and found conferences too unstructured: no clear path to success, and they cost thousands to send a representative to.
- He put everything he knew about running affiliate programs into an online course: roughly 200-300 slides and eight hours of video in step-by-step modules. He has sold it for five years.
- Pricing ladder:
  - Course: $300 entry fee.
  - Mastermind: another $700 to join, or $100 a month as a membership.
  - Done-for-you affiliate program management: price points of $2,500 and $15,000.
- Every course buyer is a candidate for upsell into the next tier. He notes many course creators use the course as lead gen for higher-priced services.
- The course became a community of affiliate managers helping each other. He calls the recurring membership his "inner circle" and mentors members when they need help growing a program.
- He also runs the podcast Affiliate Nerd Out, created to pick other people's brains.
- He owns a SaaS product, Affstash, that uses AI to find affiliates to recruit based on search keywords, and doubles as a tool for finding backlink opportunities on high-domain-authority sites, with contact information.
- On courses: he says there is "nothing passive" about owning one. You are constantly updating content and marketing it. Passive only describes waking up to overnight sales after the hard work. He has "pounded my head against a wall" for five years working out why people are not buying, and would not advise building one without a real need and a large email list.

chunks.heading: Core principles for affiliate managers
chunks.text:
- **Relationships first.** Affiliates are "not just a number on a page" with dollar signs; they are people. The more love you give, the more they give back.
- **Stay organized and prioritize.** Pay more attention to your favorites at the top of the list, without ignoring the people at the bottom making barely any sales. Where you spend your time each day is a staple of his course.
- **Keep learning.** In year three managers think they know everything, by year six they realize how little they know, and at year 14 he still learns from others. Find mentors and communities.
- **Spot potential in lower-tier affiliates** and work with them to become big ones later. He says this is the hardest thing to teach.
- **Reporting.** He doesn't enjoy data, but it is necessary. He teaches what to look for and how to present it to executives so they see the program is working.
- **Don't be a ghost.** Managers can't help affiliates who don't talk to them. Affiliates work alone, so he urges finding communities (he names PMA, MarTech Review's Slack, and his own inner circle), which he says is a social necessity after 60 hours a week at a computer.

chunks.heading: The affiliate-turned-manager path: Adam Enfroy
chunks.text:
- Adam Enfroy was Dustin's first student in the affiliate management course. He had digital marketing and partnership skills and had just taken the job at BigCommerce.
- He increased affiliate channel revenue by over 200% in his first six months and got promoted in six months.
- Seeing the affiliates, he built his own sites, went from 40 to 80 hours a week, reached $10,000 a month on the side, quit, and a year later was making six figures a month and netting about a million dollars a year.
- Dustin says it is a slow burn for most people with full-time jobs and not a get-rich-quick scheme. The people with Lamborghinis and tigers worked very hard early. He calls courses that sell it as a scheme "pretty irresponsible."
- He recommends Adam's website SEO and YouTube SEO course, which he has taken himself. Dustin himself has never maximized his own affiliate efforts and describes affiliate income as "my retirement plan."

chunks.heading: His affiliate marketing playbook
chunks.text:
- **Focus.** Pick one brand and one medium (writing and SEO, or on-camera video and YouTube) and get good at it before moving on. Lessons transfer: replicate what worked and cut what didn't.
- **SEO is a long game** measured in years, with a small cost (hosting and your time).
- **Content authenticity.** Only recommend things you actually believe in; lack of passion shows. He warns Google can recognize AI-generated content.
- **Amplify everything.** Use a tool like Buffer or eClincher and post every piece of content to free places such as Reddit, and anywhere you can get a link back to your site, especially content-relevant sites.
- **Backlinks.** Hire virtual assistants to get backlinks to both transactional and informational articles.
- **Paid amplification.** Spend $50-$100 to boost a good YouTube video. Or pay around a quarter per click on a transactional keyword that sends traffic to a listicle blog post. The extra traffic helps Google see you as an authority, which lifts rankings.
- **Every link is an opportunity.** Use short links via the Pretty Links plugin on his own domain that redirect to affiliate links. When people ask what tools he uses for podcasting, he sends a short link for Opus (clip tool), which is word-of-mouth marketing combined with affiliate marketing. Anyone with a full-time job can be an affiliate for tools in their own workflow.
- **Channels.**
  - Quora can work if you stay active.
  - Reddit does not allow affiliate links, but he knows affiliates with a secret workaround.
  - Pinterest is "still a monster" for affiliates (memes, pictures, suggestions, videos).

chunks.heading: Email marketing and lead capture
chunks.text:
- Email is the cheapest route to conversions at every company he has worked for. Affiliate is often number two, and when done right has a lower cost per acquisition than paid social ads.
- His regret: he wishes he had collected emails much earlier. He has 13,000 LinkedIn followers he is trying to convert to email, and an email list in the low 10,000s that "should be easily at 50" had he started sooner.
- He says lead capture is one of his weakest assets, but describes a four-step process:
  1. Offer a downloadable lead magnet on the site that requires an email address, valuable enough to lead to a later purchase.
  2. Put the lead magnet in the right-hand column of the blog.
  3. Add popups: exit-intent, time-on-page or scroll-based.
  4. Build a second piece of content and A/B test which brings in more subscribers; keep the winner, test a third against it, and repeat.
- Final step: place topic-specific lead magnets on matching pages (a cat page gets the cat lead magnet, not the dog one).

chunks.heading: Marketing innovation, courses and AI
chunks.text:
- **Innovation.** Make something that works first, then tweak it. Go to conferences to learn what worked "last year," and look for the next thing. Copy the latest from people like Frank Kern, make it work for you, then adjust it slightly.
- **Promoting others' courses.** Easier than making your own. Course creators can pay affiliates 20% to 90% of revenue because overhead is low and they hope to upsell. He suggests only promoting a course you have taken and believe in, and building your own splash pages to drive traffic.
- **Weakness of course affiliate programs.** There's no affiliate network that caters to courses, and good affiliates don't like joining the internal programs in Kajabi, GoHighLevel or ClickFunnels. That makes it hard for creators to run a profitable affiliate program.
- **Free education.** Take free courses from big merchants (he says SEMrush's SEO course taught him much of what he knows). He notes free courses bundled with paid courses may be upsell-driven.
- **AI.** Embrace it or lose your job; learn tools beyond ChatGPT (he mentions Jasper and Opus). He says AI content isn't top-notch yet and calls out words like "dips, dives and delves" as AI tells. He uses Speedy Brand, edits heavily to put in his own voice, and expects AI to get much better within two years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes walks through the 15-step journey an affiliate manager takes from finding a partner to replicating wins with them. His core claim is that time management is the biggest success metric: spend time nurturing high-potential partnerships and be patient while content ranks.

chunks.heading: The 15-step affiliate growth process Dustin follows
chunks.text:
Dustin frames affiliate programs as slow-build channels: "You can't just turn them on like Facebook ads and see instant results." The manager has to be "the right mix of aggressive and patient" with high-potential affiliates, and the job is never done because there are always more affiliates to recruit.

He lays out 15 steps, split between what the manager does (recruit, enable, negotiate) and what the affiliate does (research, write, rank).

### Recruiting and onboarding (steps 1-4)
1. **Find the program.** Good affiliates mostly have to be found and convinced, not just discovered via the network. Dustin sends media kits and one-sheeters, offers incentives to join and drive volume, and asks engaging questions.
2. **Review the program, product and site.** The goal is to get the affiliate excited. Give them free product, share reviews with great selling points, show which landing pages convert best, and share how much other affiliates earn. "Do what it takes to get your foot in the door."
3. **Request to join.** Send an official offer, usually with special terms and VIP commissions.
4. **Get accepted.** Harder than it sounds: affiliates forget to accept terms or move on. Follow up as much as necessary and supply all marketing materials.

### Affiliate-side content steps and the manager's role (steps 5-10)
5. **Keyword research.** The affiliate finds high-volume keywords with tools like SEMRush. Provide free trials and product so they can test and pick a main keyword.
6. **Content research.** The affiliate studies what ranks and reads positive and negative reviews. The manager recommends where products fit on their site, with example evergreen posts, competitor-style posts and upcoming promos.
7. **Create the content.** A review of 500 to 10,000 words requires product knowledge, so the manager supplies "all the ammo": the best selling points.
8. **Optimize the content.** Skilled partners know how to rank. To go further, offer to edit the first draft and give feedback.
9. **Monetize the content.** Affiliate links, call-to-action buttons and banners go in. Give the affiliate the latest closing coupon to round out the article.
10. **Start ranking on Google.** Rankings take time and don't happen overnight. Managers and executives "need to be patient here and believe in the process."

### Traffic, conversion and optimization (steps 11-12)
11. **Bring in clicks.** Reach drives early clicks. Ask the internal social team to share strong content or include it in the next affiliate newsletter.
12. **Convert clicks to sales.** Use click data to see what converts and tweak content. Landing pages may need to adapt to the affiliate's audience, so make sure deep linking is enabled for tracking.

### Relationship and expansion (steps 13-15)
13. **Connect with the affiliate's manager.** Someone on each site owns affiliate revenue. Find them and reach out by email, Skype or phone. Dustin uses Calendly to save time scheduling calls.
14. **Calls and negotiating commissions.** Trade more commissions or bonuses for more exposure. It "takes finesse" to get a partner to promote you over competitors, and every conversation is unique.
15. **Create new campaigns.** Once a winning formula exists, repeat steps 5 through 9 with the same partner instead of starting over. "Convincing someone with money in their pocket of doing more is a much easier conversation than starting from scratch."

chunks.heading: What an affiliate manager actually does day to day
chunks.text:
Dustin lists the recurring daily and weekly tasks:

- Review program applications.
- Find affiliates that fit, hunt down contact info, send recruitment and follow-up emails.
- Protect brand trademarks with tools like BrandVerity.
- Answer detailed emails and zero out the inbox for themselves, affiliates@ and support@.
- Hold a weekly team call and one-on-ones with the boss.
- Run week-over-week and month-over-month reports for forecasting.
- Give strategy and recommendations to top affiliates and message them on Skype.
- Post group Slack updates for the marketing team.
- Review new partner sales for fraud.
- Plan and write next week's newsletter.
- Report all wins to executives weekly.

chunks.heading: Time management is the deciding success factor
chunks.text:
Dustin says the biggest success metric for an affiliate manager is time management, not years of experience or percentage of revenue growth (though growth helps job security). Each day the manager must choose where to spend time among daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly and annual tasks, including executive reporting.

His answer to where time should go: "Spend time nurturing high potential partnerships." He says the execution is the hard part. The manager's job is to recognize high potential in a partner and "do whatever it takes to make magic happen." Without knowing where to spend effort, he argues, a program never reaches its full potential.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes breaks the affiliate manager role into six core jobs (recruit, activate, build relationships, enforce compliance, optimize, direct creative) and compares three ways to staff it: in-house, agency, or a trained junior marketer. He stresses that affiliate programs don't grow on their own and that relationships are the core asset.

chunks.heading: What an affiliate manager is and why the role matters
chunks.text:
- Dustin defines an affiliate manager as the person who manages an affiliate program on behalf of a merchant.
- The role covers the people, tools and systems responsible for bringing in revenue from the program.
- Affiliate marketing is a performance marketing strategy: you partner with independent marketers who promote your product in exchange for compensation.
- He cites a projection that US affiliate marketing spend will reach $15 billion by 2028.
- His bottom line: "Affiliate programs will not magically grow on their own." A manager optimizes the program, drives relevant traffic, builds relationships with the network and creates effective recruiting and marketing campaigns.

chunks.heading: The six core responsibilities of an affiliate manager
chunks.text:
1. **Recruiting new affiliates.** Build target lists, find contact information, craft an outreach email sequence, accept applications and follow up with high-potential affiliates.
2. **Activating affiliates.** Having hundreds of affiliates on the roster is not enough; the job is keeping accounts active by giving new and stagnant affiliates information, incentives and tools.
3. **Building relationships.** Includes support, payouts and friendship (see the relationship section below).
4. **Monitoring compliance.** Protects the brand, saves money on payouts and keeps affiliates within government regulations and program rules.
5. **Optimizing the program.** Analyze performance data and find the most effective channels.
6. **Directing affiliate creative.** Help affiliates produce effective content for their sites, since content decides whether they succeed at promoting the product.

chunks.heading: Recruiting and activating affiliates
chunks.text:
- Recruitment takes up a huge chunk of the manager's time because program success depends on growing the network.
- Dustin says every manager should "fill their pipeline by recruiting new partners every week."
- Recruitment tasks: target lists of potential partners, hunting contact info, outreach email sequences, accepting applications, following up high-potential affiliates.
- Activation means motivating both new and stagnant affiliates to promote.
- A welcome email sequence is a "clutch time-saver" that helps affiliates "hit the ground running."
- Grovia is his go-to solution for recruitment.

chunks.heading: Relationships: the four hats an affiliate manager wears
chunks.text:
- **Human resources:** managing affiliates, collecting payment info, ensuring accurate, on-time payouts.
- **Customer support:** helping with coupon codes, dashboards, links and troubleshooting.
- **Brand liaison:** educating affiliates on brand guidelines and positioning.
- **Friend:** building long-term relationships and professional networks.
- When you help partners succeed, you become vested in their journey and they in yours. Dustin says he has made hundreds of friendships this way and stays in touch after his time managing a program ends: "This type of networking is priceless."
- A good manager must be a people person who can empathize with both the affiliates and the brand they represent.

chunks.heading: Compliance and optimization
chunks.text:
- Compliance protects brand image, saves payout money, keeps affiliates within regulations and program rules, and creates a safe environment for advertisers and publishers. He calls it integral to program longevity and success.
- Optimization means monitoring performance, analyzing data and discovering the best marketing channels.
- Four goals of optimization:
  1. Increase the efficiency of the affiliate manager
  2. Improve the quality of traffic affiliates send
  3. Increase conversion rates of landing pages and offers
  4. Drive more sales and revenue
- Hitting and exceeding revenue goals makes executives more likely to invest additional budget in exploratory campaigns.

chunks.heading: Three ways to staff an affiliate program
chunks.text:
**1. Hire in-house.**
- Best for companies that want to really invest in program growth.
- Pros: dedicated to your brand, reacts quickly to promo strategy shifts, easy collaboration with the marketing team, 40+ hours a week on program growth, can help affiliates with product questions.
- Costs: salary of $40,000 to $80,000, equipment, office space if onsite, benefits, and training to keep up with industry trends.
- Works best when you already have a growing network generating revenue that can sustain the hire.

**2. Hire an agency.**
- Best for brands that have already had an in-house manager and want to scale.
- Pros: faster initial growth, expertise in recognizing big players in your niche, access to advanced tools, an extensive affiliate network, cheaper than a full-time manager, and frees your time for the core business.
- Cons: agencies charge $2,000 to $10,000 per month and may require a minimum six-month retainer; they are not fully integrated into your business, so collaboration and execution can be slower.
- Dustin partners with Grovia and praises its affiliate recruitment work.

**3. Train a junior marketer, intern or VA.**
- Aligns with your culture, values and mission, and the person learns your product well enough to craft tailored campaigns.
- He calls it one of the most cost-effective options and "an investment you'll benefit from for years."
- His Performance Marketing Manager course offers eight hours of conference-style video training with over 50 tips, tricks and hacks, covering time management, recruiting the right affiliates and building profitable partner relationships.

chunks.heading: Skills to look for, pay, and how to find good managers
chunks.text:
**Skills:**
- Strategic thinking
- Detail orientation, especially with data, analytics and income reports
- Organization and multitasking
- People skills (trust, relationships, motivation)
- Basic HTML/CSS for emails that display properly on all devices
- Graphic design for banners, buttons and promotions
- Newsletter formatting, as newsletters are central to campaigns and affiliate communication
- Content creation and monitoring, including SEO-optimized content

**Pay:**
- He cites Payscale's average base salary of $54,046, varying by experience, location and industry.
- He recommends adding an incentive bonus or commission structure.

**Finding good managers:**
- Search LinkedIn for "affiliate manager"; good ones have a strong network and profile.
- Look for diversified experience across agencies, merchants and publishers.
- Years of experience don't always translate into greatness, so don't pass on junior managers: "You will want creative thinkers to run your program."

**Becoming a good one:** get proper training from a teacher or mentor, since there are many facets to master.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 10-step playbook Dustin follows when taking on any new affiliate program: audit first, define partner personas, scrub unproductive partners, layer in quick-win technology partners, then chase review placements, paid-search publishers and media buyers. He stresses judging partners by traffic and revenue produced rather than by partner count or brand name.

chunks.heading: Treating the audit as the foundation of an affiliate program
chunks.text:
Dustin starts every new affiliate program with a thorough audit. It positions the affiliate manager as the "expert" in the client's eyes and gets the manager familiar with the program. He documents notes on each area in the final audit deliverable.

- **Sales funnel audit:**
  - Examine product detail pages, landing pages and presells for optimization opportunities.
  - Check bounce rate and time on page for sales pages in Google Analytics.
  - Read the reviews on product pages.
  - Use tools like Mouseflow for user experience and behavior analytics.
  - Walk the checkout flow to spot friction points.
- **Product audit:**
  - Identify best sellers or hero products.
  - Learn product margins, especially which products have the highest margins.
  - Find out which products are seasonal.
  - Find out which products have inventory or return rate issues.
- **Partnership audit:**
  - Check which publisher types (content, loyalty, technology, etc.) are missing from the program.
  - Check the state of coupons and trademark bidding.
  - Review creative assets.
  - Visit top referring pages and look for non-affiliate links or broken links.
  - Run a short gap analysis against other clients.
  - Review the current offer strategy (dynamic commissions, term templates).

chunks.heading: Defining partner personas and scrubbing unproductive partners
chunks.text:
Dustin builds partner personas: detailed evaluations of the best partner fit for a brand. For each persona he works out what type of partner they are, their job title, how to find them and their motivation to partner. Once the ideal persona is identified, he builds a list of who they are.

He calls total affiliate count a vanity metric and argues managers should focus on partner productivity instead of recruiting as many affiliates as possible.

- **Productive partners:** they drive traffic, or traffic and sales. Keep them and maximize their output. A few usually produce the lion's share of traffic and revenue.
- **Dormant partners:** they produce no traffic or revenue. Some have potential to become productive and some do not.
- **Action:** the manager decides which dormant partners have no potential and removes them from the program.

chunks.heading: Using abandonment and retargeting partners to bridge the waiting period
chunks.text:
New partners can take weeks or months to produce valuable traffic and sales, which frustrates clients who are investing but not seeing returns. Dustin onboards abandonment and retargeting partners during this period.

- **Abandonment partners:** they detect exit intent (hovering over the tab's "X", switching windows, hitting back) and deploy pop-ups offering a discount or free shipping, or capture the email.
- **Retargeting partners:** they show ad units to previous visitors, via paid social or publisher sites, to keep the brand top of mind.
- **Examples named:** Upsellit, Revlifter, Addshoppers, Retargeted AI, Klickly, NMPI and Cybba.
- **Why:**
  - They generate more revenue attributable to the affiliate channel.
  - They produce results quickly and need little upkeep.
  - They bring incremental value while content, deal, mobile app and influencer partners ramp up.
  - They scale proportionately as traffic grows.

chunks.heading: On-site partners and conversion optimization
chunks.text:
Dustin calls conversion rate optimization the affiliate program's best friend. Affiliates who see a high-quality, converting site send more traffic. On-site technology partners run in the background and need little effort after implementation.

- **Raise AOV:** partners like Revlifter and Increasingly offer discounts at spend thresholds, bundle products and suggest recommended products. He sees them as helpful in fashion, cosmetics, technology and tools.
- **Chat and assisted shopping:** companies like Envolve Tech add virtual shopping assistants that answer questions and guide shoppers to products through question-led funnels.
- **Trademark plus (TM+) partners:** they bid on "Brand Name" + a term, e.g. "Nike Shoes".
  - The affiliate world debates their value, and some brands ban TM+ bidding.
  - If the client permits, partners like Savings.com and Bravo Deal can save brands CPC budget on branded searches.
  - They are scalable because they work through Google, Bing or other ad networks.
  - Attributable revenue rises whenever the brand's search volume rises.
- **Tracking technology:** he notes not all tracking attribution platforms are equal, and names Inflektion.ai as his favorite solution of 2024.

chunks.heading: Landing review articles and finding the right publishers
chunks.text:
Review articles are the toughest placement to win. Dustin says managers should care less about vanity (placement count, publisher name recognition) and more about direct results.

- A premium publisher (Forbes, Business Insider, CNN) is a benchmark, but niche review sites with product reviews, round-ups and gift guides may be more valuable.
- Premium does not mean authoritative for a given industry or product.
- To find the right sites, research which sites rank highest for the client's relevant consumer searches, using Semrush, Similarweb, Ahrefs and Spyfu.
- What matters most is how much traffic a site drives to the client's program. "High trust and high relevant traffic will lead to high performance."
- Evaluate a publisher's messaging, appearance, credibility and professionalism. Bounce rate and time on page indicate how much consumers trust it.

chunks.heading: Paid search publishers and outsourced media buyers
chunks.text:
Some publishers buy paid search traffic to their review pages. If a publisher's earnings per click from commissions exceed the ad cost per click, it makes sense for them to keep buying that traffic. For the brand, this accelerates traffic and revenue.

- **Examples named:** buyersguide.org, bestreview.guide and consumerrating.org. Managers should comb their reviews for client fit.
- **Premium publishers do it too:** The Spruce bids on "best vacuum cleaner" and around 100 other keywords. Semrush estimated about 8,800 monthly visits via sponsored listings, which he puts at around 400% more than the page gets organically (estimates not exact).
- **Outsourced media buyers:** they specialize in Meta, Google Paid Search, Google Shopping, native, TikTok and similar channels. They audit past campaigns, performance and average CPA, and usually work on commission (percentage of spend, revenue or cost per action).
- **Fronted ad spend / CPA model:** the partner invests its own ad money so long as the CPA it is paid stays profitable. Example: if the brand's Google Paid Search CPA is $40, the partner might charge $50 per customer, keeping $10 per referral for its investment and risk. NMPI and Imwave work this way, as do several partners on the Squaredance marketplace.
- **Non-traditional partnerships:** he defines affiliate as a model where a promoter gets paid for driving outcomes. Look beyond the affiliate network for traffic sources: app stores, advertising marketplaces like Nift, DTC blogs, podcasts and innovative brands in the industry.

chunks.heading: Social and market listening, reporting, and ongoing learning
chunks.text:
Dustin has managers set up listening alerts to spot recruitment and placement opportunities.

- **Search terms:** product, competitor and market terms, plus publication, influencer and industry voice names. For a vacuum client: "Dyson", "best vacuum cleaners".
- **Tools:** Google Alerts (free, web pages only, daily email); Awario, Brand24 and BuzzSumo for social platforms like X, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok.

On reporting, he wants less time number crunching and more time growing the program.

- Use reporting tools (Affluent, Google Data Studio, Tableau) plus network reporting.
- Affluent only works with affiliate network data, so use an extension such as Schedule and Send Email in Spreadsheets for outside data like profit analysis in Google Sheets.
- Customize reports to the metrics the client cares about: customer lifetime value, ROAS, CPC, CPA, earnings per click.
- Questions to ask the client: top three metrics; new customers vs. repeat purchases; target CPA; publisher types wanted; month-over-month growth target; seasonal periods; target share of total revenue from affiliate.

He also tells managers to keep learning through network newsletters, webinars, courses (Google, Datacamp, Udemy) and agency development teams, using as many resources as bandwidth allows.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes catalogs affiliate management tools by function: recruitment, tracking, CRM, automation, AI, communication, payments and fraud. The core idea is that manual program management doesn't scale, and the right stack saves time, improves accuracy and unlocks growth. Much of the piece is a tool list with affiliate links, so the durable insight is thin.

chunks.heading: Affiliate recruitment is the most time-saving category to tool up
chunks.text:
Dustin says recruitment is his favorite tooling category, partly because he's "a nerd with it" and partly because it saves the most time on the most tedious work. When he started managing programs, everything was manual: the most sophisticated method was searching Google for organic results and hoping to find an email address on a site. He has spent years giving product feedback to recruitment-tool companies including 5IQ, Grovia, Media Rails and Affistash, so he says he knows what affiliate managers need to be efficient.

His recruitment stack, by job:
- **Prospecting and outreach automation:** Alfie (finds affiliates, writes personalized outreach, automates follow-ups), Affistash (AI platform for finding affiliate and influencer partners plus contact info), AffiliateFinder (scans the web for creators already promoting competitors or relevant products).
- **Influencer discovery and data:** Upfluence, Influencers Club (data enrichment), Influencity (search by performance, niche, engagement), GRIN (discovery and recruitment, integrated with ecommerce tools).
- **Scraping:** Phantom Buster for scraping Instagram followers at scale, combined with Upfluence or Influencers Club.
- **Existing affiliate databases and lookalikes:** Publisher Discovery (huge database of existing affiliates), Similar Sites (find similar websites for partnership opportunities).
- **SEO and audience research:** Semrush, Respona (SEO player discovery with a built-in outreach drip system), SparkToro (where the target audience spends time online).
- **Outreach management:** Buzzstream (outreach and backlink campaigns), Affiliate Email Pro (AI tool for unique recruitment messages aimed at opens and responses).

chunks.heading: Network sourcing and LinkedIn prospecting
chunks.text:
For finding people and offers inside the affiliate ecosystem, Dustin leans on three tools:
- **LinkedIn:** the "ultimate networking platform for business." He says affiliates are on there but "hidden in plain site"; use filters and search to prospect the right contact at companies.
- **Waalaxy:** LinkedIn automation for cold outreach to affiliate partners.
- **FMTC:** aggregates affiliate offers, deals and merchant data.

chunks.heading: Tracking, analytics and conversion optimization
chunks.text:
Dustin groups tracking and analytics tools by what they do for a program:
- **Partnership platforms and tracking:** Impact.com (tracking, payouts, fraud detection, partnership management), Everflow (advanced partner tracking with granular analytics and optimization tools).
- **Dashboards and insight:** Vstat (visualizing program performance), Affluent (analytics for agencies and brands), Refinery (turns complex data into insights to drive revenue, acquire customers, optimize spend and reduce risk).
- **Verification and creators:** Get Affirmative (quickly check whether publisher sites have confirmed affiliate links), Favikon (tracks creator performance across social channels, AI categorization for finding influencers in any niche).
- **SaaS:** Rewardful, affiliate management software built for SaaS businesses.
- **Tracking accuracy:** Stape provides server-side tracking and Google Tag Manager hosting, capturing data that browsers and ad blockers would otherwise miss.

chunks.heading: Landing page conversion as part of affiliate tracking (Inflektion)
chunks.text: Dustin pairs affiliate tracking with conversion rate optimization through his own firm, Inflektion. His example is Oura Ring with Lindsey Vonn: a dedicated lander that speaks to her fans and to the benefits she finds valuable, with her recognizable face, her accolades and a quote. He says these elements together improved conversion rates by 200% over the basic home page. He describes this as what Inflektion does for all its clients so that affiliate and influencer programs "shine."

chunks.heading: Influencer and creator CRM
chunks.text:
For managing relationships and pipelines, Dustin lists:
- **HubSpot:** powerful CRM with customizable pipelines for affiliate and influencer campaigns.
- **HighLevel:** all-in-one marketing platform with tracking, automation and CRM; he calls it great for agencies and consultants.
- **Copper:** CRM that integrates with Gmail and helps manage influencer outreach.
- **Aspire:** influencer marketing platform with CRM features and campaign workflows.
- **CreatorIQ:** enterprise-level influencer CRM with integrations and performance tracking.
- **Modash:** influencer discovery and CRM for UGC and affiliate programs.
- **Influencer.co:** influencer relationship platform for managing campaigns.

chunks.heading: Automation, AI and virtual assistants for the manager's own workflow
chunks.text:
Dustin's time-saving stack for the affiliate manager:
- **Scraping and email finding:** Instant Data Scraper (browser extension for tabular data), Hunter.io (professional email addresses), Browse AI (no-code extraction of affiliate info from sites and marketplaces).
- **Workflow:** Make (Integromat) to connect tools and data, TextExpander for text shortcuts on repetitive emails and outreach, Notion (notes, tasks, CRM, wikis), SaneBox (declutters inboxes).
- **Dictation:** Typeless converts speech to text and corrects grammar.
- **Link checking:** Redirect Path, a Chrome plugin that finds broken or redirected links affecting affiliate tracking.
- **Delegation:** OnlineJobs.ph to hire affordable virtual assistants for program management tasks.
- **Access:** NordPass password manager to streamline logins across affiliate platforms.
- **AI writing and analysis:** ChatGPT (email templates, outreach copy, reports), Jasper (content, emails, blogs at scale), Grammarly (polishing), Relevance AI (clustering influencer content and analyzing creator fit), Prezi (AI presentations).

chunks.heading: Fraud, compliance, payments and engagement
chunks.text:
Dustin treats compliance and payouts as their own layer of the stack:
- **Brand and traffic compliance:** Integrishield (monitors campaigns for brand compliance), Rightlander (finds affiliates' and sub-networks' active traffic sources and monitors sites and social content for non-compliant marketing), BrandVerity (monitors paid search and coupon use), Revvim (stops wasted SEM spend, also good for trademark-plus protection).
- **Fraud detection:** FraudBlock (coupon and attribution fraud), Anura (ensures clicks and conversions are human), Forensiq (affiliate fraud across channels), Voluum (performance tracking for affiliates and media buyers).
- **Payments:** Tipalti (global mass payments with compliance and tax features), PayPal Payouts (bulk payments to affiliates worldwide).
- **Communication and engagement:** Slack (affiliate communities), ActiveCampaign (email automation and CRM), EZ Messenger (Facebook Messenger automation), TubeBuddy (YouTube channel management), SocialBlade (track influencer performance), Keywords Everywhere (keyword research).

chunks.heading: How he frames choosing tools
