chunks.text: Dustin says program effectiveness "hinges on selecting the right tools tailored to your goals and program scale." Whether recruiting high performers, optimizing UGC campaigns or tracking complex multi-touch attribution, he argues the tech stack "can make or break your efforts." He positions the right tools as saving time and effort while adding insight and automation that can streamline processes, optimize budget and lift a program's results.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes recaps his conversation with Partner Gap CEO Vik Ratomske on moving from data analyst to executive. The core idea is to treat the affiliate role as executive training, prove relationship value with hard data, and learn to delegate and pick your battles.

chunks.heading: Affiliate analytical skills as a launchpad to executive roles
chunks.text:
Dustin presents the affiliate background as a launchpad, not a ceiling. His central claim: affiliate managers get a wide view of every marketing channel because partners work in SEO, PPC, newsletters and more, so the role is "the ultimate training ground for executive leadership." He argues you stop being "just the affiliate person" by acting like a business leader who manages growth rather than links.

- Treat the current role as training, not a dead end.
- Partner conversations give a free "masterclass in marketing."
- Negotiation and relationship management are the skills the C-suite requires.
- Stop thinking of yourself as a channel manager and start acting like a business leader.

chunks.heading: Traits that move a partner manager up
chunks.text:
Dustin lists the qualities a great partner manager needs to excel and get noticed by leadership:

- **Communicate constantly:** don't just report numbers, explain what they mean.
- **Suggest upgrades:** look for gaps in the current strategy and offer solutions.
- **Stay data-driven:** use an analytical side to back up every negotiation.
- **Be bubbly and bold:** build relationships by being the most engaged person in the room.

Analytical skills show the "why" behind the "what." Proactively suggesting upgrades, updates and insights is what gets a CEO's attention and can lead to a commercial role.

chunks.heading: Career progression framework from coordinator to C-suite
chunks.text:
Dustin maps the affiliate career path by phase:

| Phase | Core focus | Key skill developed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinator | Execution and support | Technical tracking |
| Manager | Relationship building | Negotiation |
| Director | Strategy and planning | Cross-channel integration |
| VP / C-suite | Business growth | Ecosystem management |

At the executive level you have to "speak C-suite." Executives don't do tangible tasks every hour, which can feel stressful at first. You must learn to delegate and focus on the big picture. Dustin notes that making this mindset shift took one executive he profiled about a year, and that mentors who reassure you during the transition are essential.

chunks.heading: Proving intangible value to executives with concrete data
chunks.text:
Dustin's guidance on getting buy-in for relationship-driven work:

- Executives want numbers, not "good vibes." Use data to bridge intangibles (a coffee meeting, a long-running relationship) to the bottom line.
- Don't just say a partner is important. Show how three years of connection turned into revenue for the brand.
- Become an educator: prove how affiliate marketing supports the whole business ecosystem.
- Use historical data on traffic and money from partner connections to show networking is a long-term revenue investment.
- The goal is to move from cost center to profit leader.

chunks.heading: Skills for a future CMO
chunks.text:
Dustin's advice for someone aiming at a CMO seat by 2030:

- Keep a wide outlook. Don't narrow yourself to one channel like media buying or content.
- Be an expert on traditional affiliate strategies but stay open to every new trend, which makes you the most versatile player in the marketing department.
- Pick your battles. Affiliate can be high-stakes and emotional. If a conversation becomes unproductive, use a "pause button": suggest revisiting in ten minutes or the next day, which keeps focus on results rather than hurt feelings.
- Use tooling such as Alfie to automate recruitment and manual lead generation so you can focus on executive-level strategy.

chunks.heading: Emotional discipline, learning and boldness
chunks.text:
Dustin endorses advice from the guest's mentors (a CEO, CFO and direct manager): never take things personally.

> "In business, you keep emotions outside… just be there for the business. That's it."

Other points he endorses:

- Many affiliate managers plateau after their first two years because they think they have it figured out. Counter this with a fear of missing something and keep learning new verticals and markets.
- Learn from people "underneath" you and invite your team to challenge your ideas. That is a sign of a true leader.
- Be bolder sooner. The executive he profiled became one at 26 in a male-dominated industry and regretted holding her tongue when her first instinct was right. Voice your opinion, trust your gut and lean on data to support claims.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes, who started his affiliate career policing fraud at CJ Affiliate 17+ years ago, defines affiliate fraud as anyone breaking brand T&Cs to earn a commission. He lays out red flags, seven fraud types, an evidence-first escalation path, and daily, weekly and quarterly monitoring habits. Most fraud is opportunistic, not sophisticated.

chunks.heading: Dustin's definition of affiliate fraud and why it matters
chunks.text:
- Dustin defines affiliate fraud as "anybody breaking the terms and conditions established by the brand to make a dollar."
- It is not just technical exploits or stolen credit cards. Any violation of your T&C that earns commissions someone didn't earn counts.
- The principle is an even playing field: if one affiliate gets an unfair advantage over legitimate partners, that is a problem, sophisticated or not.
- He notes a technical difference between "fraud" (intentional deception) and "non-compliance," but says they look the same on a dashboard and cost the same, so he deals with all of it.
- Most fraud isn't sophisticated. It is opportunists and hustlers breaking rules for a quick buck, and daily monitoring plus evidence collection catches the vast majority.
- "You can't stop hustlers from hustling." The goal is managing and catching it early, and making your program a harder target than the one down the street. Fraudsters "just want to stay in the shadows" and move on when watched.
- Context he cites: about $3.4B in annual affiliate fraud (2022, up from $1.4B in 2020), roughly 17% of affiliate traffic, about 17 cents of every program dollar. He also cites the top 10% of affiliates generating about 90% of revenue, so one bad top partner is high stakes.
- His background: first job in affiliate marketing at CJ Affiliate doing trademark compliance and cookie stuffing monitoring, later compliance work at Impact Radius, 17+ years in the space.

chunks.heading: Rule out false positives before accusing anyone
chunks.text:
Dustin says not everything suspicious is fraud. Check these first:
- Tracking misconfiguration (pixels firing wrong).
- Attribution window mismatches (conversion happened outside your window).
- Cookie overrides or browser cookie blocking (a platform issue, not a partner issue).
- Self-referrals being blocked by your own anti-fraud settings.
- Conversions marked ineligible in the fine print of your program terms.

"Fix your tracking before you accuse anyone." Outright scamming is rarer than these config issues.

chunks.heading: Red flags he watches for
chunks.text:
1. **Conversion rates far above baseline.** Healthy e-commerce affiliate rates are 1-3%, content affiliates 3-5%. 25% points to cookie stuffing, click injection or attribution manipulation.
2. **Click-to-purchase under five minutes.** "If something's happened within five minutes from their first click all the way to checkout... somebody's doing something serious and stealing that last click somehow." Under 10 seconds means automation.
3. **Site doesn't match your niche** (e.g., a recipe blog as top B2B SaaS affiliate).
4. **Suspicious country origins.** He says there are schools teaching fraudulent commission tactics, which he saw from the network side at CJ.
5. **Sudden spikes.** "If you see a guy going from one sale to 15 sales, you're going to need to investigate."
6. **Same IP across conversions** (self-submitted leads with disposable emails, stolen cards, synthetic identities).
7. **Low customer LTV.** High refunds, quick cancellations and few repeat purchases suggest incentivized traffic posing as organic.
8. **Gut feeling.** "When there's smoke, there's fire." If you can't find evidence yourself, ask the network about the traffic, since they have data you don't.
9. **Identical email patterns** in lead data (e.g., first initial + last name @gmail.com).
10. **Form completion under 10 seconds.**
11. **Chargeback rates above 0.9%** (Visa VAMP merchant threshold).

chunks.heading: The seven fraud types and how to catch each
chunks.text:
- **Browser extension commission replacement.** The biggest modern threat. Honey (20M Chrome users) swapped creators' affiliate cookies for its own at checkout, even when no coupon was found. MegaLag exposed it in December 2024. Fallout: 25+ lawsuits consolidated, about 8M users lost, Rakuten and Impact.com terminated network access, Google banned extensions claiming commissions without real discounts. Dustin calls it "one of the grossest accounts of fraud in the history of affiliate marketing." Capital One Shopping faced similar allegations (settled about $4M). Catch it by monitoring for extension-driven last-touch at checkout, especially with no discount applied.
- **Cookie stuffing.** Hidden iframes, JavaScript or pixels inject cookies. He says the crude version is rare now (better browser protections, shorter windows), but it evolved into extension-based replacement. Up to 60% of fraud cases per TrackAd. Catch via anomalous conversion rates.
- **Brand/trademark bidding.** Affiliates bid on your brand terms. Smart ones geo-fence to dodge your monitoring location. Use BrandVerity or The Search Monitor (Similarweb) for geo-targeted scans.
- **Coupon code abuse / last-click stealing.** A customer at checkout opens a tab, searches "[brand] coupon," and a coupon site takes the commission. Catch it with the 5-minute rule and coupon sites appearing as last click with no coupon used.
- **Self-submitted leads/fake orders.** Look for same IPs, random-character or disposable emails, sub-10-second forms, identical contact info, and concentrated refunds.
- **Incentivized traffic misrepresentation.** Rewards or paid clicks presented as organic. Compare affiliate-referred LTV, churn and returns to direct customers.
- **Click injection.** Mobile apps inject fake clicks on installs (15-30% of Android install campaigns). Watch click-to-install under one second and clustered IPs, mainly for CPI campaigns.

chunks.heading: Tools by program size
chunks.text:
Dustin's core line: "you don't need expensive tools to catch fraud. You need a system. The tools help you scale that system."

- **Free, any size:** network built-in tools, TrafficGuard free tier (up to $2,500 ad spend), manual daily monitoring.
- **Starter ($10K-50K/mo affiliate revenue):** add Complily or RightLander, about $200-500/mo.
- **Growth ($50K-250K/mo):** add BrandVerity or The Search Monitor plus TrafficGuard paid, about $500-2,000/mo.
- **Enterprise ($250K+/mo):** IntegriShield or ImpersonAlly plus multiple monitors, about $2,000-10,000+/mo.
- His top seven: Complily (FTC disclosure), IntegriShield (holistic monitoring), BrandVerity (paid search), RightLander (promo transparency), The Search Monitor (geo-targeted PPC), Sitebee (regulatory, strong in iGaming), TrafficGuard (real-time fraud, free tier).
- Cited results: Rhino Affiliates found 100+ violations, disputed EUR 11,000 and prevented EUR 131,000 in losses. TrafficGuard helped a streaming brand save $1M+ by blocking 66,000 invalid conversions in 12 months.

chunks.heading: How to handle an affiliate you catch
chunks.text:
- Confrontation is rarely hard: "It's never really a hard conversation. When they get caught, they understand what they've done is wrong. A lot of them will beg for the money." He has confronted hundreds and has had death threats at the extreme end, but most move on to easier targets.
- Evidence first: "Collect that evidence and make sure that it's locked tight before we do anything else." Gather timestamped screenshots, transaction logs, IP records, click-to-conversion timing and network reports before emailing or freezing anyone.
- Escalation path:
  1. Professional email citing the violated T&C, evidence attached, deadline to respond.
  2. Firmer follow-up with a compliance deadline.
  3. Freeze the account and hold pending commissions.
  4. Reverse commissions by submitting documented evidence to the network.
  5. Report the affiliate to the network so they're flagged ecosystem-wide.
- At CJ, outcomes ranged from a slap on the hand to reversing commissions on a first offense, and sometimes a "rabbit hole" with hundreds of thousands of dollars of fraud.
- Big-affiliate exception: even if the bad actor drives 10-20% of revenue, the process doesn't change. Evidence first, escalation second, because a gamed program poisons legitimate partners.
- Example: for affiliate manager Nick Polano he found coupon sites stealing last clicks and trademark bidding, built an evidence case, sent it to the network, reversed commissions and saved over $10,000.

chunks.heading: Building a prevention system and when to escalate
chunks.text:
- **Vet applicants.** Check site quality and niche fit, require traffic-source disclosure, consider KYC-style identity checks for high-commission programs. A healthy approval rate is 20-50%; approving everyone invites fraud.
- **Write specific T&Cs.** Vague terms can't be enforced. Include bans on brand bidding, cookie stuffing and cloaking, incentivized traffic disclosure, FTC disclosure requirements, and clear penalties (reversal, suspension, termination).
- **Cadence:**
  - Daily (5 min): conversion-rate anomalies, spikes, click-to-conversion under 5 minutes.
  - Weekly (30 min): 7 KPIs (conversion rate, EPC, AOV, commission outlay, affiliate CAC, revenue by affiliate, refund rate), affiliate vs direct LTV, new suspicious affiliates.
  - Quarterly (half-day): full audit of every active affiliate, geographic analysis, reversal history, T&C and tool review.
- "Fraud is invisible at low volume because anomalies blend with noise. Build the system before you need it." Small programs are more vulnerable because they monitor less.
- **Handle internally:** first-time T&C violations, small coupon abuse, single self-submitted leads, ignorance-looking non-compliance.
- **Escalate to the network:** repeated violations after warning, large-scale or coordinated fraud, or when you need data you can't see.
- **Involve legal counsel:** stolen identities, credit card fraud, systematic deception across programs, losses over $10,000.
- **FTC:** fines up to $53,088 per violation, with each non-compliant post counting separately. Disclosures must be "clear, conspicuous, and unavoidable" under the June 2023 Endorsement Guides, and fake reviews are banned (August 2024).
- **Framing for a boss:** present prevention as revenue protection and ROI, since about 17 cents of every program dollar is lost to fraud.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin explains why ecommerce-style affiliate tracking breaks for subscription businesses, drawing on a conversation with FirstPromoter's Tautvydas Vasiliauskas. He covers subscription-native commission structures, long B2B sales cycles, and a personal lesson from paying a flat $200 CPA at WP Engine on $30 plans that cancelled.

chunks.heading: Why ecommerce affiliate tracking breaks on subscription revenue
chunks.text:
- Dustin says ecommerce affiliate tracking is built around one moment: a customer clicks, buys, and the transaction is done. Any return visit looks like a brand new, disconnected sale.
- Subscription customers keep paying month after month, sometimes for years, and that continuity has to be tracked and rewarded correctly.
- Without subscription-native tracking, every renewal, upgrade, downgrade, refund and chargeback becomes manual reconciliation, with developers editing the database by hand.
- What he wanted (and found in FirstPromoter 10+ years ago): an affordable platform that integrates directly with billing providers like Stripe and pulls new sales, recurring payments, refunds, chargebacks, upgrades, downgrades and cancellations straight from billing data.
- Quote from the guest he interviewed, which he endorses: "If you have a subscription pricing for your product and you want to do partner marketing, you need a subscription-native commission tracking tool."

chunks.heading: The flat CPA mistake at WP Engine
chunks.text:
- At WP Engine, Dustin ran affiliate programs without a subscription-native model.
- The team had to guess at a flat CPA that was attractive to partners without eating margins, and landed on $200.
- Partners learned they could send a customer on a $30 plan, collect the full $200 commission, and the customer would cancel the next month.
- The company paid full price for revenue it never got to keep.
- Lesson: a rigid, one-size-fits-all commission structure invites gaming, and it can quietly torch margins without anyone noticing.

chunks.heading: Designing commission structures around your business
chunks.text:
- Commissions should fit how the business makes money: "You have to always structure the reward model around your business case."
- Options he highlights as useful guardrails against gaming:
  - Delay the commission until the customer reaches their third month of subscription.
  - Pay 50% on the first payment and 10% on renewals after that.
  - Pay a one-time or lifetime commission.
  - Set rules per individual partner, not just per campaign, so a top partner can have a different structure than a new affiliate.
- Rule of thumb: if the business depends on customers sticking around, smaller, longer commissions keep partners invested in bringing the right customers. If the business is built on a large initial sale, front-loading may make more sense.
- Trade-off he flags: "with flexibility comes complexity", so the tooling should keep setup simple. On Stripe, a campaign can go from zero to launched in about fifteen minutes.

chunks.heading: Attribution for long SaaS sales cycles
chunks.text:
- Ecommerce sales happen fast, so a cookie window of around thirty days (click to sale) is usually enough.
- B2B software sales cycles can run eight months to a year before a lead becomes a paying customer.
- Cookie-based click-to-purchase tracking fails there. Programs need a tool that tracks the lead itself, not just a short click-to-purchase window.
- This matters most for freemium and free-trial models, where the real event to track is the registration or signup, not an immediate purchase.
- Standard ecommerce platforms generally aren't built to capture that lead-to-sale relationship.

chunks.heading: Ecommerce vs. SaaS affiliate tooling at a glance
chunks.text:
| | Ecommerce tools | Subscription-native tools |
|---|---|---|
| Core event | Single order | Ongoing subscription lifecycle |
| Attribution | Cookie duration, click-to-sale | Click-to-lead, no cookie cutoff before conversion |
| Upgrades/downgrades | Manual updates | Pulled automatically from the billing provider |
| Refunds/chargebacks | Manual reconciliation | Synced automatically |
| Typical sales cycle | Days | Up to 8 to 12 months for B2B SaaS |
| Commissions | Usually flat, one-time | Per-partner, tiered, delayed, recurring or lifetime |

chunks.heading: What a day-to-day affiliate platform should include
chunks.text:
- Link and coupon-code tracking side by side, plus CPL and CPA tracking and built-in fraud protection, so paying customers can be traced to their source without stitching tools together.
- Partner activation: broadcast emails, contests and leaderboards, aimed at the point where most affiliate programs quietly go quiet after partners sign up.
- Automated payouts end to end, including payments, tax forms and invoicing, so nobody manually cuts checks or chases a W-9.

chunks.heading: AI assistants for affiliate managers, with guardrails
chunks.text:
- Dustin highlights FirstPromoter's experimental AI assistant: it can build a campaign, run research or pull a report on request, and the vendor is also building an MCP server so teams can plug it into their own tools.
- The detail he singles out: the assistant is intentionally locked out of anything financial and cannot move money.
- Every other change it makes is visible before it takes effect, so nothing happens that the manager didn't approve.
- The goal is to give affiliate managers back time spent on CSV reports so they can focus on building real partner relationships.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes explains why affiliate programs need dedicated tracking software, what makes a platform good, and ranks eight platforms by best-fit use case (SaaS, SMB ecommerce, enterprise, mobile, coupons, budget). Includes pricing and pros/cons per tool.

chunks.heading: Dustin's criteria for a good affiliate tracking platform
chunks.text:
Dustin frames affiliate tracking software as the fix for manual tracking of clicks, leads and commissions across spreadsheets. It assigns unique tracking codes or cookies so each conversion is attributed to the right affiliate. He lists five benefits:

- Accurate tracking that prevents revenue leakage.
- Transparency, so both sides trust the data for fair payouts.
- Time savings from automated commission calculations and reporting.
- Performance insights that identify top affiliates.
- Fraud prevention, such as catching invalid clicks.

A good platform, in his view, does these things:

- Tracks clicks, conversions and other metrics accurately, with real-time analytics.
- Is easy to use for both businesses and affiliates.
- Allows customization of tracking links, commissions and reports.
- Has built-in fraud detection.
- Integrates with CRMs and e-commerce platforms.
- Is not just about management; "it should empower growth and drive success."

chunks.heading: Best picks for SaaS and B2B: Everflow, PartnerStack, Inflektion
chunks.text:
**Everflow** is his "best for overall affiliate tracking" pick. It works with any vertical (software, B2B, e-commerce), is cheaper than the big networks, and he calls it the biggest up-and-comer in the industry.

- Pricing starts at $750/month with a 6-month commitment.
- Pros: intuitive, robust tracking and reporting, quick support, mobile management.
- Cons: initially complex, occasional bugs and API issues, campaigns with broken links need manual pausing.
- In 2025 Everflow partnered with Skimlinks for a full transparency integration, giving brands a picture of sub-affiliate network traffic.

**PartnerStack** is the platform he says currently leads the industry for SaaS partnerships and affiliate programs.

- Strengths: easy partner onboarding, advanced analytics, automation, customizable programs, integrated payouts.
- Weaknesses: learning curve, fewer integrations than some competitors, cost for smaller businesses.
- Pricing is not public; it is quote-based.

**Inflektion** is his pick for high conversion rates and health and wellness.

- It makes co-branded, personalized landing pages and funnels that drive high conversion, especially for unique products influencers like.
- Integration takes under two weeks, and pricing starts at $495/month.
- Cons: needs regular updates, complex setups may need outside support, and the free trial may feel too short.

chunks.heading: Best picks for e-commerce and coupon programs: ShareASale/Awin and Refersion
chunks.text:
**ShareASale/Awin** is his "best for SMB eCommerce" pick.

- It integrates with Shopify, WooCommerce and Wix, and connects merchants to over 1 million pre-screened affiliates.
- Pricing: a one-time non-refundable $625 setup fee, a $125 minimum deposit, a $35 monthly platform fee starting one month after launch, and a 20% tracking fee on commissions for qualified transactions.
- Cons: learning curve, premium features cost more, and a platform transition planned for 2025.

**Refersion** is his "best for coupon strategy" pick because it creates vanity codes for partners, which keeps coupon-driven sales trackable.

- It integrates with Shopify, WooCommerce and BigCommerce, automates affiliate payments, offers first-party and multi-domain tracking, and complies with GDPR and CCPA.
- Pricing (annual / monthly billing): Starter $79 / $99 (up to 10 monthly conversions), Professional $99 / $119 (50 conversions), Business $249 / $299 (200 conversions), Custom for unlimited conversions. There is a 14-day free trial.
- Cons: cost for smaller businesses, limited customization.

chunks.heading: Best picks for large programs and mobile: Impact and TUNE
chunks.text:
**Impact** is his "best for big programs" pick, trusted by brands like Walmart and Nike.

- It manages affiliates, influencers and referrals in one platform, automates recruitment, contracts, tracking and payment, and includes fraud detection.
- Dustin says it is "not recommended for SMBs with less than $10 million in revenue."
- Pricing is not public (sales quote); a free trial is available.
- Cons: complex setup, higher cost, steep learning curve.

**TUNE** is his "best for mobile tracking" pick.

- It offers native postback tracking across apps and web, an API with over 650 endpoints, white-labeling, real-time data streaming, SOC 2 Type II certification and GDPR compliance.
- Cons: complexity can overwhelm small teams, steep pricing for small businesses, limited support for custom needs.
- Pricing is quote-based.

chunks.heading: Best budget option: FirstPromoter
chunks.text:
**FirstPromoter** is his "best for companies on a budget" pick and the most budget-friendly on his list.

- It integrates with Stripe, Paddle and Recurly, reports 18 key data points, offers customizable branded affiliate dashboards, automated email, and one-click auto-payouts.
- Pros: easy setup, strong reporting.
- Cons: limited e-commerce features, the Starter plan restricts campaigns and affiliates, no support for one-time purchase models, and the interface may feel basic.
- All plans include a 14-day free trial.

chunks.heading: How Dustin suggests choosing
chunks.text:
His takeaway is to pick the tool that fits your workflow and stage rather than guess at attribution:

- SaaS: Everflow or PartnerStack.
- Small e-commerce: ShareASale/Awin.
- Coupon-heavy programs: Refersion.
- Enterprise-scale programs: Impact.
- Mobile apps: TUNE.
- Influencer-heavy health and wellness: Inflektion.
- Tight budgets: FirstPromoter.

His closing point is that "every click and commission matters," so a proper tracking system is "non-negotiable."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin ranks seven affiliate platforms for subscription businesses, arguing that commissions must follow the billing lifecycle (renewals, upgrades, downgrades, cancellations) rather than a one-time sale webhook. He picks FirstPromoter as best overall and lists the features that matter. The piece is heavily affiliate-link driven.

chunks.heading: Affiliate software for subscription businesses must follow the billing lifecycle
chunks.text:
- Dustin argues that affiliate tracking for subscription businesses is not "click, sale, commission."
- A customer might sign up on a $49 plan, upgrade to $99 two months later, apply a discount code, then churn for a billing cycle and come back.
- A generic tool built for one-time ecommerce purchases has no model for any of that.
- The result is overpaying affiliates on canceled accounts or underpaying them on upgrades that were never tracked.
- That is why he treats subscription-specific affiliate software as its own category.
- These platforms sync to the billing provider (Stripe, Chargebee, Paddle, Recurly, Braintree) so commissions follow renewals, upgrades, downgrades, refunds and cancellations automatically, instead of being reconciled in a spreadsheet each month.
- Ecommerce tools track a single purchase event. Subscription tools need a direct billing-provider integration, not a one-time "sale" webhook.
- Without billing sync, he says you typically track the initial sale only and adjust everything afterward by hand.

chunks.heading: Checklist for choosing subscription affiliate software
chunks.text:
Dustin lists what to confirm before picking a tool on price alone:

- Native billing-provider sync (Stripe, Chargebee, Paddle, Recurly, Braintree), not just a purchase webhook.
- Lifecycle-aware commissions that adjust on upgrades, downgrades and cancellations.
- Self-serve setup, so you don't sit through a sales demo just to see pricing.
- Transparent pricing tied to affiliate-driven revenue, rather than vague "contact us" tiers (unless you are already enterprise scale).
- Built-in fraud protection, since subscription businesses are a common target for self-referral abuse.
- Room to add referral and influencer programs later without switching platforms.

Budget guidance: most self-serve subscription tools start around $49-$99/month for programs generating up to $15,000/month in affiliate-driven revenue, then move to custom Enterprise pricing. Full B2B partner platforms and enterprise tools (PartnerStack, Everflow) are quote-based and typically cost more.

chunks.heading: FirstPromoter: his top pick for subscription businesses
chunks.text:
- Dustin ranks FirstPromoter best overall because it is built specifically for subscription businesses, not adapted for them.
- It syncs to Stripe, Paddle, Recurly, Chargebee or Braintree, so a renewal, upgrade, downgrade or refund reprices the affiliate's payout without anyone touching a spreadsheet.
- Affiliate, referral and influencer programs run from one dashboard, which replaces duct-taping three tools for partner types that all send paying customers.
- Setup is self-serve, typically under 15 minutes, with no developer.
- Features: multi-tier and dual-sided rewards, custom rules per partner or plan, sub-affiliates up to three levels deep, link and coupon-code tracking, CPL/CPA, fraud protection, broadcast emails, contests and leaderboards, and automated payouts with tax forms and EU invoicing.
- Stated proof points: over a decade running subscription partner programs, $2B+ affiliate revenue tracked across 3,000+ SaaS customers, and JustCall driving $2.4M ARR through its affiliate channel.
- Pricing: Starter $49/month (up to $5,000/month affiliate revenue), Business $99/month (up to $15,000), Enterprise from $149/month above $15,000. 14-day free trial, no credit card.
- Downsides he names: a smaller G2 review base (30+) than PartnerStack (900+), custom pricing above roughly $15K/month, and less useful if you aren't subscription-based.

chunks.heading: Rewardful: best budget pick for Stripe or Paddle startups
chunks.text:
- Dustin recommends Rewardful for early-stage SaaS that runs entirely on Stripe or Paddle and wants the simplest possible setup with no sales process.
- 0% transaction fees on every plan, unlimited affiliates and visitors on every tier, self-referral fraud detection, PayPal and Wise bulk payouts.
- Pricing: Starter $49/month (up to $7,500/month tracked revenue, 1 campaign, 2 team members), Growth $99/month (up to $15,000, unlimited campaigns, branded portal with custom domain), Enterprise $149+/month above $15,000. 14-day free trial, 30-day refund guarantee, month-to-month.
- Downsides: Stripe and Paddle only (a dealbreaker for Chargebee, Recurly or Braintree), no influencer-program management, and the custom domain is locked behind the $99 tier.

chunks.heading: Tolt and Tapfiliate: portal branding vs mixed business models
chunks.text:
**Tolt** (best for a highly branded affiliate portal):
- Stripe, Paddle and Chargebee only (no Recurly or Braintree). 0% commission on payouts at every tier.
- Custom-domain branded portal on the entry tier, where competitors often gate it higher.
- Pricing: Basic $69/month (up to $10,000/month affiliate revenue, manual payouts, 2 programs), Growth $99/month (up to $20,000, auto payouts with a 2% processing fee, 5 programs), Pro $199/month (up to $50,000, unlimited programs, dedicated Slack), Enterprise custom above $50,000.
- Lower revenue ceilings mean an upgrade comes sooner. It is a newer, smaller player.

**Tapfiliate** (best for subscription brands that also sell one-time products):
- Fits a SaaS tool with an add-on marketplace or a subscription box that also sells gift cards.
- Supports recurring, one-time and multi-level commissions (multi-level on Scale and above), 30+ native integrations, and coupon-code tracking.
- Pricing: Launch $89/month ($74 annual; 1 program, 50 affiliates, 5,000 clicks/500 conversions), Scale $179/month ($149 annual; unlimited programs and affiliates, 100,000 clicks/10,000 conversions), Enterprise custom with full white-label.
- Downsides: overage fees on click and conversion caps, and it is less purpose-built for upgrade and downgrade events than FirstPromoter or Rewardful.

chunks.heading: PartnerStack, ClickGo and Everflow: when you need more than affiliate tracking
chunks.text:
- **PartnerStack** suits B2B SaaS building a full partner ecosystem (affiliates, referral partners, reseller deal registration).
  - It has a partner marketplace that actively matches partners to programs, CRM integrations, and partner onboarding/certification tools.
  - Pricing is quote-based across Launch, Growth and Enterprise, and implementation takes weeks.
  - It is heavier than most subscription businesses need if they only run an affiliate program.
- **ClickGo** is built for networks, agencies and advertisers running programs at volume.
  - Strengths are proactive fraud interception before payout and full-funnel multi-source attribution.
  - Dustin notes its site mentions no subscription billing or Stripe/Paddle/Chargebee integration, so it earns its place for fraud protection, not billing sync.
  - Pricing is quote-based.
- **Everflow** is the enterprise option, unifying affiliate with paid (Google, Facebook, TikTok) and organic attribution in one layer.
  - It tracks recurring revenue and upsells but is not natively tied to subscription billing events.
  - Includes SOC 2 compliance, HubSpot/Salesforce integrations, a Customer Success Manager, and Everflow Pay.
  - Pricing is quote-based with a 6-month minimum contract.

chunks.heading: Dustin's decision rules
chunks.text:
- Single best fit for a subscription business: FirstPromoter, as the only tool he lists built around billing-lifecycle commissions while unifying affiliate, referral and influencer programs, with fast self-serve setup and transparent pricing.
- Stripe- or Paddle-only and want the simplest, cheapest start: Rewardful.
- Building a full B2B partner ecosystem rather than a straightforward affiliate program: PartnerStack.
- Need affiliate unified with paid and organic attribution: Everflow, accepting a sales process and 6-month contract.
- Mixed subscription and one-time products, or multi-level commissions: Tapfiliate.
- Fraud detection and multi-network volume over billing sync: ClickGo.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes reviews Affistash, an affiliate partner discovery and CRM SaaS he helped shape and later became CMO of. He lays out its feature set, SMB target buyer, pricing and competitive positioning. This is a promotional review by an interested party, not a general framework.

chunks.heading: Affistash: what it is and who it is for
chunks.text:
- Dustin describes Affistash as a SaaS platform launched in 2023 with the mission of being the most helpful tool available for affiliate managers.
- It is built for SMB brands that already have an affiliate program, which often lack resources and manpower, so time-saving features matter most to them.
- Dustin says he is "ALWAYS looking for the next game-changing tool." When he found Affistash he "recognized the power behind it" and wanted to be involved.
- Over about a year he helped shape it into what he calls "the ultimate affiliate management time saver," and he became its CMO after recognizing its potential.
- Core promise: generate a high-potential partner hitlist in minutes and save affiliate managers hours.

chunks.heading: Partner discovery features Dustin highlights
chunks.text:
- **Whole-internet search.** Unlike competitor tools that rely on limited databases, Affistash scours the entire internet for potential affiliates and influencers.
- **Real-time ranking identification.** It finds partners currently ranking for relevant keywords, so you target affiliates already performing in your niche and more likely to produce results.
- **Lookalike discovery.** Give it the URL of an ideal partner and it finds hundreds of similar partners, which lets you replicate a successful partnership.
- **Competitor partner finder.** It surfaces websites that link to your competitors, so you can tap established affiliate relationships and try to sway them to your brand.
- **Traffic stats.** Every potential partner comes with detailed traffic data, so you can decide which affiliates to pursue based on data.
- The platform pulls from several APIs of top industry tools rather than relying only on its own algorithms, which gives users broader and more current data.

chunks.heading: Relationship management and outreach features
chunks.text:
- **Centralized CRM portal** built specifically for partnership managers. It tracks existing and potential partners in one place and includes note-taking and relationship tracking.
- **AI-powered outreach.** It creates personalized outreach messages and timed email drip campaigns, which saves manual work while keeping a personal touch.
- **Custom AI assistant** that helps craft personalized messages that resonate with potential partners.
- **Integrations** with other marketing and analytics tools, so it slots into an existing stack with minimal disruption.
- **Support.** There is an Affistash Academy with educational resources on using the features, plus a dedicated customer support team.

chunks.heading: Pricing and positioning
chunks.text:
- Starts at $97 per month.
- 20% discount for annual purchases.
- 30-day money-back guarantee.
- No free trial.
- Dustin claims it is the most affordable partner discovery tool and offers the highest value for money compared with enterprise-level tools.
- His stated edge: it can find partners ranking in real time across the entire internet.

chunks.heading: How Dustin frames who should use it
chunks.text:
He says Affistash fits an SMB brand with an affiliate program that wants to:

- Streamline partner discovery.
- Manage relationships more effectively.
- Save time and resources.
- Make data-driven decisions about partnerships.

His broader view is that tools like this will play an increasingly crucial role in building sustainable partnership programs, whether a program is brand new or being taken to the next level.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sales page for Dustin Howes's Affiliate Manager Mastermind, a 10-day, one-hour-a-day course on affiliate program setup, recruitment, fraud prevention and reporting. It shows how he frames the affiliate manager role and the value of a well-run affiliate channel.

chunks.heading: Who the course is for and what it promises
chunks.text:
- Dustin sells a 10-weekday affiliate manager training ("Performance Manager Training", $697 one-time) built from 12+ years of experience compressed into 200+ PowerPoint slides.
- Target buyers: business owners training themselves or their team, agencies wanting a certified performance/affiliate manager credential, students, and marketing employees.
- Time commitment: one hour per day for 10 consecutive weekdays. Optional 30-minute assignments follow each session, though he strongly suggests implementing lessons while they're fresh.
- His framing: "You don't know…what you don't know." The biggest pitfall for an affiliate manager is not knowing where to focus, because the job is never done and there are always more partners to recruit.

chunks.heading: What an affiliate manager actually is
chunks.text:
- He defines an affiliate manager as a partnership development representative of the company.
- The focus is growing the affiliate program, but there are dozens of small daily tasks needed to maximize those efforts.
- His position is that a good affiliate program will represent about 20% of the revenue from marketing efforts and will likely have the lowest CPA of all marketing channels, besides organic.

chunks.heading: Curriculum: the order for building a program
chunks.text:
The course walks through the program lifecycle in this sequence:
1. Affiliate 101
2. Product research
3. Competitive analysis
4. Choosing the right platform
5. Creating the program
6. Publisher types
7. Recruitment strategy
8. Negotiations
9. Activation
10. Building partnerships
11. Fraud prevention and auditing
12. Creative campaigns
13. Program maintenance
14. Reporting
15. "The Little Things"

The implied approach: research the product and competitors and pick the platform before creating the program, then recruit, negotiate, activate, protect, and maintain.

chunks.heading: Fraud prevention and auditing as a core skill
chunks.text:
- Fraud prevention and audit processes are a dedicated module, not an afterthought.
- A student affiliate manager at Omnisend reported that the fraud prevention and audit processes were "eye opening" and would save the program much more than the course cost.
- Dustin also sells a separate compliance management service (linked from the course page).

chunks.heading: Recruitment as the main growth lever
chunks.text:
- Recruiting affiliates is where he says the work never ends.
- Course materials include recruitment email templates, recruitment strategy, and welcome-sequence templates, alongside legal terms templates.
- Reported outcome, from a client testimonial (BigCommerce, via Adam Enfroy): with his guidance on recruiting affiliates, the affiliate program doubled its revenue in less than a year.
- He positions training around the most coveted content sites, per a PR agency testimonial that the bootcamp helped teams optimize for partnerships with those sites.

chunks.heading: How he packages and prices training
chunks.text:
- Format: about 8 hours of screen-sharing video with commentary, 200+ slides, step-by-step program setup, dozens of affiliate network screen-share videos, and a program checklist with templates (recruitment, welcome sequences, legal terms).
- Support: 1:1 training with Dustin on a specific program, 2 consultation calls, email access, a Slack community with lifetime access, and weekly group coaching "community hours."
- Pricing: $697 one-time, anchored against "$5000 in total value" by stacking itemized values (setup and training $2000, daily assignments $500, checklist $500, email access $300, four bonuses totaling $1700).
- Lead-in: a free 15-minute exploration call before purchase.
- Positioning: tools, templates and a checklist let students "hit the ground running" and execute campaigns right after finishing, which he contrasts with a typical webinar.
- Social proof is leaned on heavily: client quotes citing cost savings (one CEO says hiring Dustin saved $10,000+) and program results.

chunks.heading: Proof points he uses
chunks.text:
- Doubled BigCommerce affiliate program revenue in under a year (via Adam Enfroy).
- A pet-door company CEO says the engagement saved $10,000+.
- Alumni outcomes include building a program from zero experience and moving into a senior partnerships strategist role.
- Team training used by agencies and brands (PR firms, WP Engine, Omnisend) for both newcomers and experienced affiliate managers wanting to benchmark their processes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Rewardful webinar recap where Dustin Howes lays out a five-step system for affiliate programs: define ideal partner personas, recruit outbound, personalize outreach, vet applicants, then onboard so partners earn their first commission fast. Recruitment is treated as ongoing pipeline work, not a one-time task.

chunks.heading: Defining the Ideal Affiliate Profile and partner personas
chunks.text:
- Dustin says no ICP means no IAP: if you don't deeply know your Ideal Customer Profile, you can't define your Ideal Affiliate Profile.
- He writes five partner personas, like customer personas, that fit the category and goals.
- For each persona he lists:
  - **Who they are:** blogger, listicle site, YouTuber, LinkedIn creator, newsletter owner, community admin, media buyer, emailer, or coupon/loyalty/extension closer.
  - **Audience fit:** keywords or topics they rank for, platform, niche relevance.
  - **Motivation:** fee vs. free product vs. commission, backlink, co-marketing, traffic support.
  - **Your pitch:** what you can offer (EPCs/conversion rate, exclusive deal, content ideas, tracking, creative).
- He argues quality beats quantity. Total affiliate count is a vanity metric; revenue concentration is real, and a tiny fraction of partners drives most sales.

chunks.heading: Why affiliate recruitment feels hard
chunks.text:
- Dustin: "Too many brands expect affiliates to just show up, grab a link, and go. Recruitment and activation end up last on the task list—yet they're the engine of the program."
- Three root causes he sees repeatedly:
  1. **Mis-set expectations.** Networks pitch "set it and forget it," but outbound recruitment is what wins. Recruitment must be an ongoing system, not an afterthought.
  2. **No ICP, so no IAP.**
  3. **Underinvested "exploratory" budget.** Competitive partners, especially creators, rarely engage without some combination of fee, free product, and commission.
- Common management mistakes he lists:
  - Treating recruitment as a one-time task instead of ongoing pipeline work.
  - Chasing celebrity macro-influencers before testing a dozen micro/niche partners.
  - Over-collecting info on applications, which kills signups.
  - No clear rules on paid search, brand bidding, coupons, or extensions.
  - Onboarding with nothing: no assets, no examples, no contact means no activation.

chunks.heading: Where to find high-quality affiliates
chunks.text:
Dustin prioritizes incremental partners who influence buyers before checkout:

1. **SEO content owners** (bloggers, reviewers, listicles) already ranking for your target keywords.
2. **Media buyers**, who can scale once messaging is dialed (stay on-brand, review copy closely).
3. **Emailers/newsletters** with curated, responsive lists.
4. **B2B and SaaS:** LinkedIn creators and niche reviewers, lower volume but high intent.
5. **Communities** (Slack, Discord, Facebook, Reddit) via group admins and mods.
6. **Lower-funnel closers:** coupon, loyalty, and extension partners, used with intent and rules.

Tools he and Rewardful's CEO recommend for discovery and outreach:

- Affistash: discovery, keywords, contacts
- Upfluence: influencers
- PhantomBuster: export competitor followers
- Semrush and Similarweb: research
- Hunter.io: emails
- Ahrefs: authority/links
- Waalaxy: LinkedIn outreach
- Matt McWilliams's affiliate email swipe copy

chunks.heading: Writing outreach that gets replies
chunks.text:
- Skip the mass blast; send targeted, human messages.
- The first message has three parts:
  1. **Proof you looked:** call out a recent post, video, ranking page, or newsletter issue.
  2. **Value fast:** what the product does and what's in it for them (commission/EPC, free product, backlink, co-marketing, traffic buys).
  3. **One question:** "Would this fit your audience?", "Want to try it?", or "Open to a quick test?"
- Ways to make yes easy:
  - Even a modest exploratory budget dramatically lifts response rates.
  - Always offer a free product or account, especially to creators.
  - Share concrete EPC/conversion-rate ranges and top-performer case studies.
  - Offer a backlink when pitching content sites.
  - Try a triple-touch (DM, email, LinkedIn) over a few days, polite, not spammy.
- Over-templated AI emails are obvious (he cites "dip/dive/delve" and random emojis). Use AI to draft, then humanize.

chunks.heading: Vetting and approving applicants
chunks.text:
- Keep the application short: name, company, URL, socials, how they'll promote.
- Green flags:
  - Content and audience match your niche/ICP.
  - Real site/socials, quality content, clear CTAs.
  - Transparent traffic/engagement and a specific promotion plan.
- Red flags:
  - Irrelevant sites (a "cat blog" for a B2B tool) with no plan.
  - Impossible stats, unclear business model, generic copy/paste answers.
  - Patterns tied to fraud or brand bidding: approve cautiously and monitor.

chunks.heading: Onboarding and activating new affiliates
chunks.text:
- He treats activation like product onboarding: the "aha" moment is their first commission.
- A 5-email welcome sequence over the first 5 days:
  1. **Welcome + link:** intro, unique link, how to reach you.
  2. **Assets:** logos, banners, deep links, screenshots, demo video, UTM guidance.
  3. **What works:** top content angles, best-converting pages, proven CTAs/titles.
  4. **Max earnings:** promo calendar, exclusive codes, suggested placements, do/don't list.
  5. **Open door:** office hours or Calendly, reminder of perks, invite questions.
- Give them a single home base (Notion or portal) with all of the above, plus case studies, competitor comparisons, media kit, and contact/booking link.
- Incentives that move the needle:
  - **Hybrid deals:** small fee plus commission for tests, especially for creators.
  - **Volume bonuses/tiers** and time-boxed boosts for new promos.
  - **Traffic support:** consider buying ads to a partner's high-ranking article for your key term.
  - **Newsletter shout-outs** that spotlight partner wins as social proof.
  - **Promote the program** on social, since your biggest fans may become long-tail partners.

chunks.heading: Commission structures and sponsorship-only creators
chunks.text:
- Which structure fits depends on LTV, upsells, and sales cycle, so he supports both:
  - **Rev-share:** aligns incentives; many programs cap recurring at 12 months to balance risk.
  - **CPA:** pegged to roughly the first 2-3 months of revenue, or a tested fixed amount.
  - **Hybrids:** use them to win competitive recruits and negotiate lower fees.
- For "sponsorship-only" B2B and SaaS creators:
  - Lead with relationship and value: product access, data they can use, co-marketing (webinar, case study, newsletter feature).
  - Share proof, e.g. a similar creator's conversion rate and estimated earnings on your commission plan.
  - When budgets are tight, be patient; friendship and genuine support often beat a one-off fee.
- He recommends measuring and tiering: focus on the few partners who drive the most while steadily testing new recruits.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin recaps a Real Talk Friday chat with Christen Evans on affiliate network failures (an eight-month tracking outage billed on estimates, removed affiliates still earning via bookmarked links). He also shares how a three-minute video and dedicated page got him a job interview, and urges early Q4 prep.

chunks.heading: Real talk with an affiliate manager: network failures that cost clients thousands
chunks.text:
Dustin recounts two cases from a conversation with affiliate manager Christen Evans in which affiliate networks failed clients.

- **Eight months of broken tracking.** A client's tracking was down for eight months. The network billed $7,000 in estimated commissions plus $1,500 to reinstate tracking.
- **Why the bill was unreasonable.** The estimates used general conversion rates rather than the client's actual data, so they were nearly impossible to verify. Dustin says that estimating commissions for a short outage might make sense, but "eight months is excessive."
- **The network's failure.** He argues the network should have flagged the tracking problem much earlier instead of blindsiding the client with a large invoice.

chunks.heading: Removed affiliates can still earn via "bookmarked links"
chunks.text:
Christen removed an affiliate from a program in February and found that same affiliate credited with two sales months later.

- **Cause:** a network feature called "bookmarked links" lets affiliates keep earning commissions even after removal from a program.
- **Network response:** the network's proposed solutions were unhelpful, so Christen had to reverse the sales manually.
- **Lesson Dustin draws:** this shows why you must stay hands-on with your own data rather than trusting network defaults.

chunks.heading: Takeaway: monitor network data closely
chunks.text:
Dustin's first of three takeaways is to stay hands-on with data.

- Network quirks such as "bookmarked links" and estimated commissions can cause major headaches.
- Diligent monitoring, rather than assuming the network will catch problems, is the protection.
- Early detection matters: a tracking outage caught in days is a minor fix, while one left for eight months became an $8,500 problem.

chunks.heading: Standing out in a job hunt with a video and a landing page
chunks.text:
Dustin describes how he approached a competitive job search while moving toward a more stable role at a major agency, keeping affiliate marketing as a side hustle.

- **Tactic:** he made a three-minute YouTube video and a dedicated page explaining why he would be a great hire.
- **Result:** it got him in the door and landed the crucial first interview; he was in the final stages when he wrote.
- **Principle:** going the extra mile with a personalized, creative approach helps you stand out in a crowded market.

chunks.heading: Seasonality: the summer slump and the Q4 rush
chunks.text:
Dustin and Christen discussed industry timing.

- **Summer** felt like a "graveyard," with many people out of office and little response to outreach.
- **After school restarts**, emails get responses again.
- **Q4:** with Black Friday approaching, everyone scrambles to secure placements and finalize strategies.
- **His advice:** prepare for Q4 early. Lock in placements and finalize strategy before the holiday rush hits.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A LinkedIn post and video diary from Dustin Howes covering CJU 2026. He shares practical travel tips and a candid verdict on the event app, meeting pacing and sponsor-heavy content, while interviewing attendees about why in-person networking events matter.

chunks.heading: Choosing and booking a conference stay
chunks.text:
Dustin advises against staying at the conference hotel because of the cost. For CJU 2026 in Santa Barbara he booked a small hotel near the venue instead:

- Small hotels around the venue are "just great enough to put your head at night" for roughly $100 to $200 a night.
- He booked two days before the event and was still able to get a place a block from the beach.
- The venue was about a mile's walk away, which he treated as a bonus for getting exercise in.
- Check-in was quick, with no line.

chunks.heading: Using live interviews as a networking tool
chunks.text:
Dustin took his Affiliate Nerd Out show on the road to CJU 2026 and filmed live interviews throughout the three days.

- He approached people at the event, on the beach, and at the party, and asked the same short question: what do you think of the vibes here?
- He interviewed network staff (Jon Thollander of CJ), agency and partner-side contacts (Matthew Wood of Hello Partner, Jake Fuller of JEBCommerce, Richard Jackson of Pion, Dan Sweeney of Coleman Digital Media, Matt Frary of XPFlow) and publishers (Allison Cirincione, Shawn Cowher, Marie Flores of Goloot, Beth Baratte of ShopHer Media).
- He published the footage as a multi-part series: Part 1 of the walkthrough, and Part 2 with his final score for the conference.
- He publicly thanked everyone who appeared, and framed the series as an honest look at "the good and the not-so-good."

chunks.heading: Why affiliate events are worth attending
chunks.text:
His takeaways on the value of CJU's format:

- It is networking-led. Attendees are relaxed and "you don't feel pressured to go meet everybody"; you can walk up, grab a coffee, and meet someone.
- The people you want to meet are mostly in one place: agencies, publishers, and network staff.
- Compact logistics help. One end of the conference to the other was under a 3-minute walk.
- Social events do real work. He called the beach party probably the best party at any conference he has attended, because people network with their feet in the sand.
- On day one he took roughly 10 scheduled meetings plus about 10 more informal conversations on the side.

chunks.heading: What he sees on the CJ side of the market
chunks.text:
From his conversation with Jon Thollander of CJ (a 20-year industry veteran), Dustin relayed the themes dominating the event:

- Marketers are worried about AI visibility and zero-click journeys.
- CJ is leaning into "connected commerce": an integrated approach that looks at the full funnel, how affiliate affects other channels, and how other channels affect affiliate.
- CJ's pitch to brands is that it sits at the intersection of these shifts, backed by Publicis and Epsilon data management and large funding.

chunks.heading: Critique of CJU 2026: where the event fell short
chunks.text:
Dustin gave a candid assessment of the weaker points:

- **Event app:** the biggest hit to the conference. It was clunky, not user friendly, and made scheduling meetings difficult. Attendees were frustrated and could not use it effectively.
- **Meeting pace:** too aggressive, with no time between meetings and no guidance on where to go next.
- **Content:** sessions were "pretty decent," but nearly all speakers came from CJ or a CJ sponsor. He wanted more outside voices.
- **Education focus:** the content centered on things within CJ rather than helping program managers get better at their jobs.

chunks.heading: How he runs the day
chunks.text:
- He works the schedule hard on day one, then goes to the evening party to keep mingling.
- He skips late-night events like karaoke to get a fresh start the next day, even though he hears they are a strong networking opportunity.
- He thanks sponsors and hosts of the evening events (such as Slick Deals) publicly at the end of the night.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A short LinkedIn teaser for an article on how US brands can capture Black Friday demand from expats and internationally minded shoppers in Asia. Dustin Howes points to a commission and a whitelisted address as the path, without altering how brands ship.

chunks.heading: Black Friday has gone international
chunks.text:
- Black Friday is no longer just an American shopping holiday.
- Expats and internationally minded shoppers across Asia plan their purchases around it.
- For many US brands, these are sales they are currently missing.

chunks.heading: Reaching Asian shoppers without changing fulfillment
chunks.text:
- With Q4 approaching, Dustin asked Jeff Unze of Buy&Ship how brands can reach these shoppers without changing how they ship.
- Per Dustin's summary, the answer comes down to two things: a commission and a whitelisted address.
- The approach lets a US brand keep its existing shipping setup while still serving international buyers.

chunks.heading: Positioning on "we don't ship there"
chunks.text:
- Dustin's framing (from the post's URL slug) is that "we don't ship there" is costing brands more than they think.
- The lost revenue comes from shoppers who want the product but are blocked by shipping restrictions.
- He treats cross-border affiliate and forwarding partners as a way to capture that demand.

chunks.heading: Channels and tags
chunks.text:
- Dustin files this under affiliate marketing, e-commerce, and cross-border e-commerce.
- The tactic is tied to Buy&Ship, with Jeff Unze as the source of the mechanics.
- The full breakdown, including how the commission and whitelisted address work in detail, sits in the linked article (https://lnkd.in/gCNE77_3), which was not included in this source.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes frames an Affiliate Nerd Out episode with a guest who holds a full-time job and an influencer side hustle with ADHD. The short post argues that the shift to remote work stripped away external structure and left ADHD workers without support. The guest's actual tips are not included.

chunks.heading: Remote work removed the structure that held a workday together
chunks.text:
- Dustin argues that the digital industry went fully remote and "quietly removed every external structure that once held a workday together."
- The office had built-in scaffolding: fixed hours, people around you, visible expectations. Remote work stripped these out without replacing them.
- He frames this as a structural problem rather than a personal failing. People for whom external structure matters most were hit hardest.

chunks.heading: Nobody was trained to work remotely
chunks.text:
- According to Dustin, no one was trained for remote work. Employers simply had to trust that people were responsible enough to manage themselves.
- That trust assumed self-management came naturally. For people with ADHD, it often doesn't, so the setup worked against them.

chunks.heading: Productivity apps and ADHD: "a recipe for failure"
chunks.text:
- Dustin notes that apps were built to make people more productive, but ADHD people ("ADHDoers") were "thrown into a world with a recipe for failure."
- His point is that tools alone don't replace the structure that was lost. They assume a level of self-direction that ADHD brains may not have by default.

chunks.heading: Why this matters for people in affiliate and digital marketing
chunks.text:
- Dustin positions this topic as relevant to anyone in the digital space who may be struggling quietly with the lack of structure.
- He frames the topic around a guest, Kyrus Keenan Westcott, who holds a full-time job and an influencer side hustle with an ADHD brain.
- The purpose of the episode, as Dustin describes it, is to share what is working for him in practice, plus tips for others, as part of the Affiliate Nerd Out #nerditorium series.
- The post is an introduction to the episode, so the specific systems and tactics the guest uses are not covered here.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Promo post for a live panel on the alleged Phia forced-click scheme. Dustin frames it as different from Honey-style credit theft: clicks and commissions were allegedly manufactured, leaving merchants as the victims. Light on detail, mostly a teaser with fraud-spotting and network-policy takeaways.

chunks.heading: Dustin's framing of the Phia accusation
chunks.text:
- Dustin describes the allegation as a shopping app that "opens a hidden tab on your phone, forces a click, and bills the merchant for a sale that it didn't earn."
- The alleged scheme ran quietly for seven months, right before the holidays.
- He says that if the accusation holds up, "this is not your usual affiliate fraud story."
- He treats it as a major event for the affiliate space and calls it a scandal for the whole affiliate marketing community.

chunks.heading: Manufactured clicks vs. stolen credit (Phia vs. Honey)
chunks.text:
- Dustin separates two kinds of affiliate misconduct.
- **Honey-style credit theft:** software allegedly took credit for another publisher's click, so a legitimate publisher loses a commission they earned.
- **Phia-style manufactured commissions:** the app allegedly created clicks that never happened, so the sale was never driven by any real referral.
- In the Honey model the victim is the publisher who earned the click. In the Phia model the merchant ends up as the victim, because they pay a commission on a sale the app didn't earn.
- This is why he frames Phia as a different and arguably worse category than Honey.

chunks.heading: How to spot a forced-click scheme
chunks.text:
- One of the tells Dustin flags for forced-click schemes is an implausibly high click-through rate.
- The other is an implausibly high conversion rate.
- Traffic that clicks and converts at rates far above what real shopper behavior would produce is a signal that the clicks are being generated, not earned.
- He plans to cover these tells in detail in the live session and ties them to what Ben Edelman's hands-on testing found.

chunks.heading: Where networks draw the line
chunks.text:
Dustin lists how the major networks handle this kind of behavior as a topic for the panel:

- **Awin:** the "soft click" approach.
- **Impact:** a per-program paid PQ (partner quality) check.
- **CJ:** an NQ team (network quality) and a software ban in subaffiliate programs.

He positions the comparison as a way for merchants and publishers to understand what protection each network actually offers.

chunks.heading: The panel and who sees what
chunks.text:
Dustin assembled people who each view the problem from a different seat:

- **Ben Edelman:** the researcher whose hands-on testing surfaced the issue and who laid out what the investigation found.
- **Dan Sweeney:** spent 20 years inside the affiliate networks and now builds tools to stop this kind of fraud.
- **Madeline Kaufman Sullivan:** a publisher who earns clicks and then watches software like this "walk off with a credit."

chunks.heading: Event and offer
chunks.text:
- The deep dive is a live LinkedIn session on July 29th at 9:00 am Pacific.
- Attendees can ask questions and add their own takes.
- Dustin offers a free audit of the attendee's own affiliate program as part of the session.
- Sign-up is through a link in the comments of the LinkedIn post.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes frames a conversation with ScaleVisible CEO Ewen Finser about winning in AI search. Negative Reddit sentiment can wreck paid spend, and brands build AI visibility by clustering content across Reddit, YouTube and niche publishers to create consensus. Most of the detailed playbook comes from the guest; Dustin's own take is the short framing.

chunks.heading: Reddit sentiment can wreck paid spend: the "villain" problem
chunks.text:
Dustin frames a common failure mode: someone sees a brand's ad on Meta or TikTok (or even a good editorial affiliate placement), then Googles the brand or checks Reddit, and finds a post from a random user ("Joey323") saying the brand sucks. That negative post becomes the prevailing sentiment and gets repeated across AI answers and search surfaces, so it can undermine an entire paid spend strategy. He says the Reddit user's identity doesn't matter; the sentiment is what spreads.

Dustin calls this the "villain archetype" and says it is more common than brands want to admit. Old reviews matter too: a two-year-old complaint can persist even after the product was fixed.

chunks.heading: Four brand archetypes for AI search: ghost, villain, challenger, defender
chunks.text:
Dustin and his guest Ewen Finser (CEO of ScaleVisible) sort brands into four archetypes, and Dustin asks audiences to say where their brand falls:

- **Ghost:** little to no context online. New or venture-backed startups that need to build reputation fast. With publisher traffic declining and less content supply, brands need to actively build context.
- **Villain:** negative Reddit or review sentiment that is damaging everything else.
- **Challenger:** brands with small share that can win by playing the new game early, like early-2000s SEO.
- **Defender:** big incumbents facing "death by a thousand paper cuts." Old SEO and affiliate spend still works but less well, and small players (a vibe coder on Reddit, someone optimizing for Perplexity) siphon off customers they never notice.

chunks.heading: The old KPIs trap and why defenders lose without knowing
chunks.text:
Dustin warns brands "still coasting on old KPIs" that the decline can happen without them noticing. Defenders watch affiliate or SEO metrics fall and respond by asking publishers to do more, instead of recognizing that discovery has shifted. He notes the work with defenders is largely education: showing them how they are losing.

He also points to org-chart silos as a blocker: affiliate only does CPA, Reddit touches PR, social, community and customer service, and no one owns it.

chunks.heading: The three-legged stool: Reddit, YouTube, and tier-two media
chunks.text:
The play for winning AI search, per the episode, is three legs: Reddit, YouTube, and tier-two (niche) media. The principle is to build clusters of content across channels to build consensus, so AI says nice things about a brand across multiple surfaces. Like a person's own cluster of YouTube, blog and LinkedIn, a review published as a video, an article and a post reinforces itself.

The mix varies by brand. For some, YouTube is 60-80% of the equation and Reddit matters less, so brands should analyze their own vertical and brand instead of trusting generic "Reddit is the number one source" claims.

chunks.heading: Measuring AI visibility: beyond citations
chunks.text:
The measurement approach shown covers SEO, LLM visibility and Reddit. Citations alone are not enough: some citations don't drive brand mentions. Brand mentions need to be assessed for position (first, second, below the fold) and sentiment (positive, mixed, negative).

Typical campaign shape: about 11 months, with an early period of strategy and testing, then a ramp, and a hockey-stick around a year in, depending on industry.

chunks.heading: Case result: bookkeeping software vs QuickBooks
chunks.text: A bookkeeping software client has roughly 2% market share against QuickBooks (about 80%) but reached about 50% parity in AI search. AI-driven signups are now one of its top customer acquisition channels. It doesn't tie out cleanly like performance marketing click tracking, but it correlates closely with citations and before/after changes.

chunks.heading: Audit-first approach and pricing transparency
chunks.text: Every prospect gets an audit of their online profile before a pitch, showing where Reddit sentiment, editorial (e.g., Forbes citing a brand) and YouTube influencers fill the landscape, plus a gap analysis. Dustin highlights that ScaleVisible is upfront with pricing at the end of each deck: four tiers (base, growth, scale, enterprise) starting at $4,400 a month for roughly 20 hours of work per cycle, plus a setup fee of about $2,500, with custom packages (for example 10-20 articles and videos plus a couple of Reddit campaigns).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Final part of Dustin Howes's series on building a B2B affiliate program from scratch. He argues for instant follow-up when an affiliate says yes, attribution that captures both influence and conversion, and hands-on coaching of partners who promote but don't convert.

chunks.heading: Speed to lead matters in affiliate recruitment
chunks.text:
- When an affiliate replies "yes" to a recruitment email and asks whether they accept paid placements, Dustin says to "get on that call. No questions asked."
- He calls speed to lead "everything" in affiliate recruitment.
- He cites a Harvard Business Review study: responding within 60 seconds increases sales by almost 400%. He says the same applies to affiliates.
- Waiting a day or two loses the interest: "They've moved on with their life."

chunks.heading: Measure influence and conversions together
chunks.text:
- Dustin says that without the ability to measure influence and conversions at the same time, "you're dead."
- Last-touch attribution "will lie to you."
- Example: one brand killed its Facebook ads because conversions looked low, and sales then dropped 25%. The brand had failed to understand what that touchpoint was doing in the buying journey.

chunks.heading: Coach partners who promote but don't convert
chunks.text:
- If a partner is promoting but not converting, Dustin says to hop on a call and see where they're getting stuck.
- Give them the angles that work.
- His framing: affiliate is "a relationship business."

chunks.heading: Topics in the full B2B affiliate program series
chunks.text:
This post is the final part of "How to Build a B2B Affiliate Program from Scratch." Dustin lists these topics as also covered:

- How to handle creators asking for flat fees upfront
- When a spreadsheet is enough and when it's not
- What to do when partners promote but don't convert

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes recounts how a flat $200 CPA at WP Engine got gamed by buyers of a $30 plan who cancelled in month two. In a conversation with FirstPromoter's head of marketing, he reinforces that SaaS affiliate programs need subscription-native tracking, flexible and delayed commissions, and lead-based attribution for long B2B sales cycles.

chunks.heading: Subscription-native tracking vs ecommerce-style tracking for SaaS affiliate programs
chunks.text:
Dustin ran affiliate programs without subscription-native tracking at WP Engine and it nearly cost him. His argument is that ecommerce-style tracking (one click, one sale, done) breaks on subscription billing because there is no continuity and no recurring logic. When a customer upgrades, downgrades, refunds or cancels, ecommerce setups force manual database updates and developer tickets, and the events no longer match what was paid out.

His recommendation for any SaaS or subscription company doing partner marketing is a subscription-native commission tracking tool that:
- Pulls data straight from the billing provider (Stripe and similar).
- Tracks new sales, recurring sales, upgrades, downgrades, refunds, chargebacks and cancellations automatically.
- Needs no manual reconciliation.

chunks.heading: The $200 CPA that got gamed at WP Engine
chunks.text:
At WP Engine, Dustin's team had to decide what flat CPA they could afford that was still appealing enough to attract affiliates without eating into customer lifetime value. They settled on a $200 CPA.

- People bought the $30 plan, canceled in month two, and kept the $200 commission.
- He calls this "gaming the system".
- The fix he points to is subscription-aware commission logic (delayed payouts, tiered structures) instead of a big flat bounty paid on the first charge.

chunks.heading: Commission structures that protect against churn and fit the business
chunks.text:
Dustin endorses flexibility in commission design as the most important feature when choosing an affiliate platform. His instinctive answer to "what's the most important feature?" is flexibility. Options he highlights:

- Delay commissions until a set month (for example, start paying only from the third month of a subscription).
- Tier payouts, such as 50% on the first payment and 10% on recurring payments.
- One-time, recurring or lifetime commissions.
- Per-partner custom commission structures, not just per campaign.

Principles he endorses:
- Structure the reward model around the business case. If the product depends on customers staying long, use smaller commissions over a longer time to keep partners invested. If the initial sale is very large, pay more upfront and less (or nothing) later.
- Talk to the partner and meet them in the middle ground on what works for both sides.
- Don't pay every affiliate type the same: "I'm not going to pay the coupon sites the same as I'm going to play the content and the content creators."
- The affiliate manager needs to be able to "pull those levers" to work with everybody.

chunks.heading: Lead-based attribution for long B2B sales cycles
chunks.text:
Dustin highlights a key difference between SaaS and ecommerce programs: ecommerce sales happen fast (click, then a 30-day cookie, then sale), while B2B software sales cycles can run up to 8 months or a year.

- Click-to-sale cookie tracking misses these deals.
- Tracking should be click-to-lead, so a sale that closes long after the cookie window is still attributed to the right partner.
- For SaaS with freemium or free trials, the main event is registration, so quality leads are what matters. Ecommerce platforms almost never track this.

chunks.heading: Speed of integration and flexibility without complexity
chunks.text:
Dustin values platforms that get a program live quickly. He has heard integration "nightmare stories" of three to six months on some platforms.

- His experience with FirstPromoter: the programs he put on the platform got up and running fast.
- The guest's claim, which he did not dispute: zero to a launched campaign in around 15 minutes with a Stripe integration.
- The usual trade-off is that flexibility brings complexity, and the best tools try to avoid that.

chunks.heading: Where he sees small SaaS affiliate programs
chunks.text: Dustin sent smaller SaaS brands to FirstPromoter as his first choice when they were not making much revenue yet and could not afford Impact or PartnerStack, but still needed the full feature set to start an affiliate program.

chunks.heading: AI assistants for affiliate management, with money locked out
chunks.text:
He is enthusiastic about AI tooling that lets lean teams do more with less, and plans to build on FirstPromoter's MCP server himself.

- The assistant described can create campaigns, run research and generate reports from a question, so affiliate managers spend time on partnerships and relationships instead of CSV reports.
- Guardrails he endorses: the AI is intentionally blocked from any financial operation (it cannot move money), and all other changes can be reviewed before they apply.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes's LinkedIn post and webinar recap on publisher outreach in 2026. His own framing: hard pitches get smelled instantly by overloaded publishers, AI visibility data should be layered, and publishers losing Google traffic are opening doors to whitelisting deals. Most substance in the transcript comes from guests.

chunks.heading: Soft-pitch outreach to selective publishers (the Wirecutter example)
chunks.text:
- Dustin describes Wirecutter as a premium publisher that is very selective about which brands and products it publishes content for, and notes it gets "hundreds of emails every single day."
- He backs the approach that landed Wirecutter as a top partner: a data-led, human, soft pitch instead of a hard pitch.
- Steps he describes:
  - Research first: check whether the publisher already has content in the brand's vertical or niche.
  - Acknowledge there are people on the other side who get blasted all day.
  - Lead with data, not just "here's the commission, can you join our program."
  - Include the brand, the product, what already ranks well for their site, how it converts, EPC for similar content, and where else it ranks.
- Research tools for the pitch: Ahrefs and SimilarWeb, plus a simple search on competitors' sites to see how many articles they have listed.
- His take: "It sounds like it's such a basic thing, but it actually worked." Having a brand the publisher was interested in also helped.

chunks.heading: Deal structures: independents, big publishers and whitelisting
chunks.text:
- Deal flexibility depends on publisher size. Independent publishers are easier to work with and more flexible (hybrid, CPC only).
