- Larger publishers are harder to get into and have flat-fee demands up front.
- Dustin points to a way in for the big mass-media publishers: whitelisting deals brokered by certain companies, which his team has launched for some clients in the last month or two.
- How he positions whitelisting to a publisher who is losing Google traffic:
  - Brands spend paid traffic against the publisher's content, so it's another traffic source: "you're losing Google on this side, but you're gaining meta on this side."
  - The content can be published at production cost or even free, with a set amount of spend directed at the page.
  - The publisher recoups commissions on that page long after it goes live.
  - Fee structures vary: commission payments only, a monthly handle/access fee, or another fee.
- For independents, he suggests being creative with the structure and thinking about keeping the relationship rolling long term so they earn passive commissions.

chunks.heading: Conversion rate and honesty as leverage
chunks.text:
- Dustin says conversion rate matters more than anything in the vertical and niche context. Working with many telehealth brands, he sees listicle sites that normally have flat fees or CPC deals bypass those terms when the vertical is lucrative and the brand converts well.
- "The conversion rate is supreme" because publishers know they will make money on it long term.
- On proving a claimed conversion rate: you never provide proof. It rests on trust, because publishers are smart and know the numbers, and if you lie you burn the bridge for any future relationship.
- Rule: "Reputation is everything. You do business from a place of honesty."
- If the offer has a weak conversion rate, don't oversell it as "the best thing since sliced bread." If it converts well, go for the big publishers.

chunks.heading: AI visibility data: layer it and pitch with it
chunks.text:
- Dustin's position (alongside what his team saw in their own data) is that a small set of domains, around 5 to 8, drives the vast majority of AI citations in a category. That data can be used to pitch those publishers.
- Deal progression he uses: start with a hybrid model to get in, then shift to performance as visibility and trending improve, while acknowledging there is always some sponsored element.
- Don't rely on a single AI visibility tool or dataset. Layer multi-touch attribution, AI visibility and SimilarWeb data, build a story, and constantly challenge the strategy. A single dataset can diverge sharply.
- Be skeptical of tools selling "prompts per dollar." Check whether prompts are neutral or have a persona behind them, because LLMs learn from user behavior and answer differently per audience (probabilistic models).

chunks.heading: Prioritizing publishers: Google rankings first, then AI citations
chunks.text:
- Workflow he describes using Profound:
  - Build non-branded comparison prompts (and incremental prompts) for the brand.
  - Load them in to see which publisher URLs are cited most (top 10, 20, 30, 50).
  - Examples of frequently cited publishers in his space: Healthline (often #1 or #2) and Fortune.
- AI citation rank doesn't always match SEO rank: a page may be #1 on Google but #10 for AI.
- His prioritization: from a revenue perspective, go after the publishers ranking on Google first, then work on AI citation targets afterward, because AI attribution is harder to show in an affiliate program unless you give secondary reports.

chunks.heading: Dustin's own affiliate position on LLM visibility
chunks.text:
- As an affiliate of productivity, SaaS and affiliate marketing tools, he is writing content intentionally to rank in LLMs.
- His current experience: he gets visibility, but LLMs consume his content and display it without sending clicks.
- He hopes affiliate marketing catches up on crediting AI-driven influence and says he needs to figure out how to earn credit in that channel, as many affiliates are trying to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Real Talk Friday episode of Affiliate Nerd Out where Dustin and co-host Christen Evans chat about finalizing Q4 plans, affiliate leaderboards, and a webinar that doubled in length. Mostly casual banter; the durable business insight is thin, centered on Q4 prep, gamification trade-offs, and building content from interviews with affiliate managers.

chunks.heading: Q4 planning and the "get it locked in now" mindset
chunks.text:
- Dustin says Q4 is "go time" and that anyone who hasn't finalized their Q4 plans should do it now, that week.
- He points to Karen Garcia as the go-to resource for prep and for knowing exactly how many days remain until Black Friday.
- He credits an episode of Affiliate Nerd Out where Karen came on, "all about prep," and a piece of Q4 prep content from Acceleration Partners as useful references.

chunks.heading: Affiliate leaderboards and public gamification
chunks.text:
- Dustin notes that some brands now publish scoreboards of which affiliates are winning.
- He is unsure whether that is a good idea. As a competitor, he likes seeing it.
- His theory is that affiliates want to be on the pedestal and get the extra attention.
- He sees gamification as great in some areas, but flags the risk when "you just see the same people win over and over again."
- He calls it a "mixed bag."

chunks.heading: Information sharing in affiliate has flipped
chunks.text:
- Dustin recalls a conference moment from early in the industry where he asked a 10-plus-year agency owner or program manager for his top five publishers. The person gave a rude answer and walked away, saying it was inappropriate to ask.
- His view: people guarded that information 15 years ago because it was hard to find. Now "everybody yaps about everybody publicly."
- It is one of his biggest pet peeves when people keep that kind of information locked down.

chunks.heading: Short-runway webinar that outperformed
chunks.text:
- Dustin ran a webinar with Alfie that walked through the whole platform. It was planned for 30 minutes and ran 60.
- Nearly 100 people commented, and the session was very interactive.
- He had roughly a one-week runway, effectively 3 to 4 days in a short week.
- The recording passed 1,000 views.
- Customers such as Wade Tonkin showed up, interacted and shared how much they like the tool.
- Result: the company asked him to do more webinars, so he is now building new ones and expediting the ones already in the pipeline.

chunks.heading: Affiliate recruitment masterclass
chunks.text:
- Dustin is building an Affiliate Recruitment Masterclass that teaches everything he knows about affiliate recruitment.
- It draws on interviews with hundreds of affiliate managers over the years, with notes on what is working right now in the industry and which tools are worth using.

chunks.heading: Conferences as content and networking
chunks.text:
- Dustin is heading to CJU after about 10 years away, with a ticket from CJ, to make conference content: video, interviews and hanging out with people.
- He made affiliate-related purchases through CJ and says the conferencing and networking there is outstanding.
- His one earlier CJU visit came while blogging, when he was one of two content creators there and most attendees were traditional publishers like coupon sites.
- That trip came right after CJ launched its Content Certified program, which he was feeding with a lot of bloggers. It is where he first met people like Sarah Margolis and Paresh in person.
- He cites the first-timer awkwardness: brands did not know how to engage with bloggers yet.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dustin Howes frames a LinkedIn post and interview with Viktorija Ratomskė around escaping the "affiliate person" label. His own points: partners teach you every channel, networking and adaptability are core skills, and you should keep learning from people below you.

chunks.heading: Moving from affiliate manager to executive leadership
chunks.text:
Dustin hosts the conversation with Viktorija Ratomskė (founder of Partner Gap), and his own framing is that affiliate professionals build skills across SEO, paid media, content, influencers and analytics, yet are still introduced as "the affiliate person" when executive roles open.

- The fix is to stop speaking "affiliate" and start speaking C-suite.
- He frames affiliate experience as a launchpad, not a ceiling.

chunks.heading: Why affiliate managers make good CMOs
chunks.text:
Dustin agrees that the most underrated thing affiliate managers do is develop a wide understanding of every marketing channel.

- Partners are so different (SEO, paid, content, newsletters) that the manager has to understand all of them.
- He says the education comes from partners, not formal courses.
- His own view: "my partners in the past have taught me the most out of all of the marketing channels."
- He notes that paid courses can cost money and some "will turn you down the wrong road."

chunks.heading: Learning from partners and your own team
chunks.text:
Dustin endorses the habit of asking the people beneath you to challenge you.

- He calls "I don't know anything" a great stance for a leader.
- Team members research and find new avenues, so keep learning from them.

chunks.heading: Relationship management and adaptability
chunks.text:
Dustin treats networking and adaptability as core affiliate-manager skills that carry into leadership.

- Adaptability to an environment is "one of those keys to a really good affiliate manager."
- The networking never stops.
- Being able to negotiate and get everyone in a room to reach the same agreement transfers directly to executive work.

chunks.heading: Keeping emotion out of business
chunks.text:
Dustin agrees with the principle of never taking things personally, especially in negotiations.

- He admits he has been emotional at points in his career.
- He says keeping it professional is key in this environment.
- He rejects the idea that holding back versus speaking up is a gender issue. He has held his tongue plenty of times and voiced his opinion plenty of times, and says you have to pick and choose your battles.

chunks.heading: Explaining intangible value to executives
chunks.text:
Dustin raises the problem that relationship and networking work produces results that are not directly visible in numbers.

- His question to guests: how do you show executives you are productive when the output isn't an obvious number?
- The approach he draws out: make the intangible tangible with data, for example showing that long-standing partner connections are the ones now driving traffic and revenue for the brand.

chunks.heading: What affiliate managers should do to reach the C-suite
chunks.text:
Dustin endorses staying broad rather than narrowing to one channel.

- Be an expert on traditional affiliate marketing while staying open to new channels.
- Don't specialize narrowly into only media buying, content or newsletters.
- Build a wide outlook and understanding of all channels.
- Network widely. He suggests going to Affiliate Summit West to see the many different ways people drive traffic, and calls educating yourself through networking "a really great practice."
